comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Dear Department of Homeland Security,

I am writing as an international student from a European Union member state, a country that maintains strong diplomatic, economic, and educational ties with the United States, to express my strong opposition to the proposed OPT fees.

Optional Practical Training is an essential part of my educational and professional journey. It provides a unique opportunity to apply the knowledge I have gained through my studies, demonstrate my specialized skills and abilities, and gain meaningful professional experience in my field. I believe students should be evaluated based on their qualifications, dedication, and potential contributions rather than their financial circumstances or their university's ability to pay substantial fees.

Coming from a European Union country with longstanding friendly relations with the United States, I see OPT as more than an individual career opportunity. The practical training, advanced knowledge, and professional experience I can gain in the United States will allow me to bring valuable expertise back to my home country and contribute to its professional and economic development. My country benefits from professionals who have received high-quality training in the United States, and such exchanges strengthen the longstanding cooperation, innovation, and mutual understanding between the United States and its European allies.

International students already make significant financial and personal sacrifices to pursue education in the United States. Many of us invest years of hard work, substantial tuition payments, and personal resources with the expectation that we will have an opportunity to gain practical experience related to our degrees. Introducing substantial additional fees would create financial uncertainty and could make OPT inaccessible to otherwise qualified students.

Although the proposed fees would formally be imposed on educational institutions, there is a serious concern that these costs could be passed on to students or result in universities limiting OPT recommendations. This would disproportionately affect students who cannot afford additional expenses, regardless of their academic achievements, professional capabilities, or the value they could bring to American workplaces.

I understand the importance of preventing fraud and maintaining the integrity of the immigration system. However, these objectives should be pursued through targeted verification, appropriate oversight, and enforcement against actual violations rather than financial barriers that restrict legitimate educational and professional opportunities.

International students bring diverse perspectives, specialized knowledge, creativity, and valuable skills to American universities and workplaces. OPT allows us to demonstrate these abilities, contribute to innovation, collaborate with American professionals, and build international professional relationships. Preventing students from accessing these opportunities would not only affect individual careers but could also weaken the educational and professional exchanges that benefit the United States and its international partners.

I respectfully urge DHS to reconsider and withdraw the proposed OPT fee requirements and preserve meaningful access to practical training without imposing excessive financial burdens on universities or students. I also ask DHS to consider the interests of students who have already invested in their American education and planned their professional development around the existing OPT program.

Thank you for considering my comment and the perspectives of international students from countries that value their close relationships with the United States.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly expresses strong opposition to the proposed OPT fees.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
This policy is throwing the baby out with the bathwater. That is probably the aptest description of what it is doing. In our obsession with preventing H1B abuse, we risk destroying higher education and our talent pipeline altogether. There are much better ways to prevent OPT fraud without shooting ourselves in the foot.

First, let’s look at what we are gaining. Yes, we might shut down shell companies and prevent OPT fraud. But how much does that help US workers if the students involved are not actually working—and therefore not taking anyone’s job? Given that students on OPT are allowed only 90 days of unemployment to search for a job, all they are doing is buying more time to search for a legitimate job. That does not excuse fraud, but it should make us question whether this tunnel vision on OPT fraud is proportionate to the problem. (Also, European countries like Denmark allows them to stay for 3 years to find a job! We were being extremely stingy with the amount of time!)

We should also keep the scale in perspective. So far, only 10,000 of OPT fraud cases are found. How large a share of the international student population do they represent?

Now let’s look at how much we stand to lose:
* The large fee could deter companies from hiring OPT students altogether. Students will choose to go to Europe and Canada instead—or, at worst for US competitiveness, China. Schools will admit fewer international students and lose a sizeable source of funding. Financial aid for domestic students could also suffer.
* We lose out on top talent. International students make up a substantial share of PhD students in the US. Would people like Elon Musk or Noubar Afeyan, a co-founder of Moderna, still choose to come here? Why go to a country where you cannot get hired?
* And if, by some miracle, they still choose to come, why train them only to send them away? What is the point?
Just look at where the world’s top AI researchers originally come from and tell me the US is not shooting itself in the foot by making it harder for international students to stay. We should go after fraud. But undermining the entire talent pipeline in the process is naive at best and idiotic at worst.
The cure is worse than the illness itself.

Why not just do a real-time E-verify + Tax Data tax check so that OPT with shell companies cannot clear?
comments.reason: The commenter argues the fees will harm US competitiveness and deter employers from hiring international students.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am a graduate researcher at Yale University, writing in my individual capacity to oppose the proposed OPT fees [proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)(1)–(2) and 214.2(f)(11)(ii)–(iii)]. The proposed $70,000 initial fee and $30,000 subsequent fee would create a substantial financial barrier to practical training and research employment after graduation.

American universities invest years of funding, mentorship, and research infrastructure in training international students. These students also contribute to research and teaching throughout their education. Making it prohibitively expensive for them to apply their specialized skills in the United States would undermine that shared investment, just when they are prepared to contribute as highly trained professionals.

In academic research, the consequences would extend beyond individual graduates. Research depends on sustained collaborations, specialized expertise, and projects that often take years to complete. If a university or employer cannot afford these fees, researchers could be forced to leave ongoing work, disrupting projects and affecting their colleagues, including American students and researchers. Passing the costs on to graduates would instead make access to practical training depend heavily on personal wealth.

I am also concerned that these fees would discourage talented students from choosing American universities and encourage graduates trained here to pursue opportunities elsewhere. This would risk transferring the benefits of American research and training investments to other countries while weakening the United States’ ability to attract and retain scientific talent.

DHS should assess these potential losses alongside its stated objectives, including the effects on research continuity, university budgets, and the recruitment of future students. Any concerns about program integrity should be addressed through targeted oversight rather than fees that create such a substantial barrier to participation.

I urge DHS to withdraw this proposed rule and preserve affordable access to OPT and the STEM OPT extension.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed OPT fees create financial barriers and harm academic research and student retention.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by S. S. Sane
comments.commentText: I am writing to oppose Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100. I am a domestic graduate student who has just started a PhD in Physics at Yale, having completed a Master's degree in Canada. My experience is with experimental nonequilibrium physics that applies in particular to exploring ways of more rapidly cooling systems. This rule would make it virtually impossible for an international student to pursue postgraduate research in the US; the proposed fee considerably exceeds the average postdoc's salary and universities are very unlikely not to pass the cost down to the student. The DHS may consider this desirable, but this would have disastrous consequences for the USA's scientific enterprise; international students are extremely valuable to any university and there just aren't enough qualified domestic students to fill the gaps. In my career, a significant fraction of my skills were acquired through personal training I got from international postdocs. Crucially, if an international student cannot do their postdoc in the US, they will do it in another country, and the public money that the US invested in their career via PhD stipends and grants will be wasted. Additionally, international students will avoid coming to the US if there is no scope for them to continue their work, meaning US researchers will not be able to benefit from the knowledge they bring in. Many subfields of science, mine included, depend on highly specialized and little-known techniques that a single-digit number of people on the planet are familiar with. When those people are lost, those techniques are lost: just look at what happened to the rare earth metal industry. In Canada, faculty viewed the US government's attacks on science with relish as they increased their hiring, poaching valuable American talent. This rule would all but guarantee that international graduate students, who make up a large fraction of all graduate students, benefit other countries rather than the US. American leadership globally is largely a consequence of US leadership in science, and without international students, American science will crash and burn and America's global influence will swiftly follow. I strongly urge the DHS to withdraw this proposed rule.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed OPT fee would devastate the US scientific enterprise and harm students.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Re: Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100 — Optional Practical Training Fees

I urge DHS to withdraw the proposed rule, particularly the fees under proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)(1)–(2). Making OPT prohibitively expensive would undermine U.S. universities’ ability to attract outstanding international students, weaken university finances, and damage the country’s long-term scientific and economic competitiveness.

The ability to recruit talented students from around the world is a foundation of American universities’ research strength. International graduate students contribute to research, collaborate with faculty and fellow students, and help translate academic discoveries into practical advances. For prospective students deciding where to pursue their education, the opportunity to gain relevant professional experience through OPT is an important part of the United States’ appeal.

Although the proposed rule would not formally eliminate OPT, fees of $70,000 for initial participation and $30,000 for subsequent participation would effectively put it out of reach for many students and institutions. Talented students with options elsewhere would have stronger reasons to choose other countries, taking their research contributions and future innovations with them. Over time, this could erode U.S. scientific leadership and weaken the talent pipeline that supports industries such as computing, biotechnology, advanced manufacturing, and engineering. The consequences would extend beyond international students to American researchers, businesses, and workers who benefit from their contributions.

The proposal also threatens an important source of university revenue: tuition from international students, particularly those enrolled in tuition-funded master’s programs. Students considering these programs weigh substantial tuition and living expenses against the educational and professional opportunities available after graduation. Making OPT financially inaccessible would make that investment less attractive and could reduce international enrollment. The resulting loss of tuition revenue could constrain universities’ ability to sustain academic programs, support faculty and staff, and provide educational resources that benefit domestic and international students alike.

DHS should fully assess these broader effects on student recruitment, tuition revenue, research capacity, and industry before proceeding. Preserving affordable access to OPT is an investment in the United States’ ability to attract talent and maintain its scientific and technological leadership. I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw the proposed rule.
comments.reason: The commenter urges DHS to withdraw the proposed rule because high OPT fees would harm U.S. competitiveness and students.

At a time when the United States faces increasing international competition for scientific talent, we cannot afford to create additional barriers for the very researchers who help sustain our academic and scientific leadership. comments.commentText:
Re: Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, Optional Practical Training Fees

I am an F-1 undergraduate student currently studying in the United States, and I write to oppose the proposed $70,000 fee for an initial OPT recommendation and the $30,000 fee for subsequent recommendations.

OPT is practical training directly related to my field of study, not a separate work visa. I came to the United States to study, I pay tuition, and I planned to use OPT after graduation to gain experience in my field before deciding my next steps. A $70,000 fee would end that plan. My university cannot reasonably pay $70,000 for every international student who seeks OPT, and the proposal itself acknowledges that schools may pass the cost on to students. I cannot pay $70,000 — an amount roughly 150 times the current $470 USCIS filing fee — for permission to work in a training position. For students like me, this fee does not regulate OPT; it eliminates it.

The fee would also harm the employers and communities that train international graduates. Employers hire OPT graduates because they have U.S. degrees and skills the employer needs; if universities stop recommending OPT because of the cost, those jobs will simply go unfilled or go to graduates educated elsewhere. The United States would lose the very talent its universities educated.

I respectfully ask DHS to withdraw this proposal. If the Department's concern is fraud, it should address fraud directly through oversight and enforcement, rather than imposing a fee that makes lawful practical training unaffordable for ordinary students.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed OPT fee is too high and asks DHS to withdraw the proposal.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I respectfully submit this comment to express my concern regarding the proposed fees for Optional Practical Training (OPT).

I understand and respect the Department’s responsibility to protect the integrity of the OPT program and address fraud or misuse. However, the proposed fee structure of $70,000 for initial OPT and $30,000 for subsequent OPT could have an extraordinary impact on international students and their families. These amounts are part of the proposed rule and are not currently effective.

I ask that you also consider the unique circumstances of children who came to the United States with their parents at a young age. Many parents came to this country legally for employment and brought their children with them. These children may have completed their elementary, middle, and high school education in the United States and then continued through an American college or university. For many of them, the United States is the only home they truly know.

Their education, family, community, friendships, professional relationships, and personal lives have been built here. Asking these young adults to pursue education or early-career opportunities in another country is not necessarily a realistic alternative. They may have little educational, professional, or social connection to another country, despite their immigration status.

Families have also made substantial financial and personal investments in their children's education in the United States, including college tuition and living expenses. After years of education, OPT provides these graduates with an opportunity to gain practical experience directly related to their field of study. Under existing rules, eligible F-1 students can generally receive up to 12 months of OPT, with eligible STEM graduates potentially qualifying for an additional 24-month extension.

A potential combined fee burden of $100,000 associated with initial and subsequent OPT would be beyond the reach of many ordinary families and could create a system in which practical training opportunities depend heavily on financial resources rather than education, merit, skills, or professional potential.

I respectfully ask DHS to carefully consider the unintended consequences of these proposed fees, particularly for students who have spent most of their formative years in the United States. I support reasonable measures to prevent fraud and misuse of the OPT program, but I believe those goals can be pursued through stronger compliance, oversight, verification, and enforcement without creating an overwhelming financial burden for legitimate students and their families.

I respectfully request that DHS reconsider the proposed fee amounts and explore a more proportionate approach that protects the integrity of the OPT program while recognizing the circumstances of students who have been educated and raised in the United States.

These students are not simply seeking an employment opportunity. For many, they are trying to begin their adult lives in the country where they grew up, studied, built relationships, and became part of their communities.

Thank you for considering the impact this proposed rule may have on these students and their families.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed OPT fees would have an extraordinary negative impact on students and their families.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Michael Walfish
comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose the proposed $70,000 initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) fee and $30,000 subsequent OPT fee. I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw this proposal entirely.

1. Excessive Financial Burden

International students already make substantial financial investments in American education, including tuition, housing, insurance, and living expenses. Many depend on education loans and family savings. Although institutions may formally bear these proposed fees, the costs could ultimately be passed to students through additional charges or reduced opportunities. A $70,000 fee is an extraordinary financial barrier for graduates who have already invested years in their education.

2. Damage to Quantitative Finance and Wall Street

This proposal could seriously damage the quantitative finance industry, including hedge funds, investment banks, proprietary trading firms, asset management companies, and financial technology startups.

Quantitative finance depends on highly specialized talent in mathematics, statistics, computer science, machine learning, artificial intelligence, financial engineering, and computational modeling. International graduates from American universities contribute valuable expertise as quantitative researchers, quantitative developers, algorithmic traders, financial engineers, and risk analysts.

A $70,000 initial fee and $30,000 subsequent fee could make hiring international graduates financially impractical. Smaller hedge funds, proprietary trading firms, and financial startups would be particularly disadvantaged because they cannot absorb such extraordinary costs.

3. Threat to American Financial Competitiveness

The United States is a global leader in financial markets partly because it attracts exceptional international talent. New York and other American financial centers depend on access to highly skilled professionals who contribute to market innovation, financial research, and technological development.

If hiring international graduates becomes prohibitively expensive, financial institutions may increasingly move recruitment, research, and development activities toward competing financial centers such as London, Singapore, and Hong Kong.

At a time when artificial intelligence, algorithmic trading, and advanced computing are transforming financial markets, restricting access to specialized talent could weaken America's competitive advantage and benefit foreign financial markets.

4. Negative Impact on American Employers and Innovation

The proposed fees would not only affect international students. They could also hurt American businesses, universities, research institutions, and employers. Companies may choose not to hire qualified graduates because of the additional financial burden. This could reduce innovation, limit employment opportunities, and weaken the talent pipeline supporting American technology and finance.

5. Disproportionate Approach to Fraud Prevention

I recognize DHS's responsibility to prevent immigration fraud and protect program integrity. However, imposing extraordinary fees on legitimate students and employers is not a proportionate solution. Fraud should be addressed through targeted investigations, institutional oversight, compliance requirements, and appropriate penalties for proven violations rather than excessive financial barriers affecting everyone.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes the proposed OPT fees and urges DHS to withdraw the proposal entirely.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Elisa Seeherman
comments.commentText:
I oppose the proposed rule imposing a $70,000 fee for initial OPT and $30,000 for subsequent OPT, including STEM extensions, for F-1 students. I submit this as a career advisor who works directly with international graduate students pursuing master's degrees in the US.

1. The fee is a de facto ban, not a cost-recovery measure. DHS's own analysis projects opportunity costs up to $8.9 billion annually and a sharply reduced participant pool, outcomes DHS describes as intentional. A fee exceeding many students' total tuition is not calibrated to processing costs; it is designed to eliminate a program Congress and DHS have authorized for decades.

2. The rule punishes the compliant majority for fraud by a few bad actors. DHS documents fraud by specific shell companies and employers. This is a problem suited to targeted enforcement (site visits, employer verification, DSO training), not a blanket fee on all 1.4 million F-1 students and every SEVP-certified school.

3. The harm extends well beyond students. OPT is how international students gain post-graduation degree-related experience, often as a precursor to H-1B sponsorship. A fee this size will force top applicants to pursue work in other countries; reduce tuition revenue and research capacity at U.S. institutions; and price out small and mid-sized employers who rely on OPT to evaluate talent at low cost. DHS offers no evidence this would meaningfully help domestic graduates.

4. DHS understates reliance interests. Calling students' expectation of OPT access "speculative" ignores that students enroll and take on debt based on the regulatory framework in place when they apply. Applying the fee to OPT recommendations issued after the effective date, with only 60 days' notice, blindsides students already mid-program.

5. DHS should withdraw the fee and pursue targeted alternatives. DHS acknowledges viable options: employer attestations, audits and risk-based site visits, but rejects them as burdensome. Administrative convenience does not justify tens of billions in costs. I urge DHS to:

•Withdraw the $70,000/$30,000 fee structure entirely.
•Direct enforcement resources toward employer verification and site visits.
•If any fee is retained, limit it to actual administrative processing costs.
•Exempt or substantially reduce fees for nonprofit and public institutions.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment. I urge DHS to reconsider this rule given its disproportionate cost, failure to target actual bad actors, and harm to U.S. graduate education and employers.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed OPT fee is a de facto ban that harms international students, universities, and employers.

comments.commentText:
I am writing to express my strong opposition to the Department of Homeland Security’s Notice of Proposed Rulemaking titled Optional Practical Training Fees (Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100). The proposed assessment of a $70,000 initial recommendation fee and a $30,000 extension fee for Optional Practical Training recommendations does not constitute a legitimate fee-for-service mechanism. Instead, this astronomical cost structure acts as a de facto prohibition that effectively dismantles the OPT program, directly undermining US higher education, international student recruitment, and national economic competitiveness.

As DHS acknowledges in its Regulatory Impact Analysis, institutions faced with a $70,000 per student requirement will be forced to either absorb insurmountable operational deficits or pass these costs directly onto international students and host employers. Passing tens of thousands of dollars in fees onto students creates an “immense new financial barrier” that restricts experiential learning exclusively to the wealthiest individuals or deep-pocketed corporate sponsors (NAFSA Comment Letter on DHS Proposed OPT Fee Rule, Nov., 3, 2026). Recent survey data from higher education leadership shows that 92% of US institutional leaders anticipate international candidates will choose competing destination countries that offer straightforward post-study work pathways (Higher Education Leadership Survey, 2026) if OPT access is effectively severed. Passing these costs to students transforms a statutory academic benefit into an inaccessible privilege.

Eviscerating OPT access poses a direct threat to the US economy:
-International students contribute $42.9 billion annually to the US economy and support over 355,700 American jobs (NAFSA International Student Economic Value Tool, 2025/2026)
-In the 2024-2025 academic year, approximately 294,000 international students used OPT to gain critical practical experience (IIE Open Doors Report on International Educational Exchange, 2025)
-Immigrant entrepreneurs, many starting as international students on OPT, have founded roughly 25% of US billion-dollar startup companies (National Foundation for American Policy, 2024)

The proposed fee structure violates the Administrative Procedure Act (APA, 5 U.S.C. § 706) by establishing arbitrary pricing that fails to consider less burdensome regulatory alternatives or account for the catastrophic opportunity costs imposed on domestic businesses and universities.

Rather than imposing punitive fees that destroy experiential learning, DHS should utilize existing SEVIS data and targeted compliance mechanisms to address administrative concerns (NAFSA Regulatory Recommendations, 2026). I strongly urge DHS to withdraw the proposed rule in its entirety.
comments.reason: The commenter strongly opposes the proposed exorbitant fees, arguing they act as a de facto prohibition on the OPT program.

comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 fee for subsequent OPT recommendations. I urge DHS to withdraw this proposal. My comments address the proposed amounts, the collection of fees through educational institutions, and the consequences for students already pursuing degrees in the United States.

I am an F-1 undergraduate student studying statistics and computer science at a U.S. university. I have invested years of effort and substantial financial resources in my education. The opportunity to pursue lawful, degree-related practical training has been an important part of my educational and professional planning.

Through internships in enterprise software and AI infrastructure, I have applied my coursework to real engineering problems. My work has included improving the reliability and efficiency of distributed computing systems and building practical AI applications. I am also pursuing research related to AI inference systems. These experiences have helped me develop skills that classroom instruction alone cannot fully provide.

As I approach graduation, I hope to continue developing those skills through authorized practical training. A $70,000 charge would be financially out of reach for me. My family has already made substantial sacrifices to support my education. We cannot simply absorb tens of thousands of dollars in additional costs.

Charging universities does not shield students from the consequences. If a university passes the fee to students, students like me would be unable to pay. If it absorbs the fee, the expense could discourage it from recommending otherwise eligible students. Either outcome could make OPT effectively unavailable regardless of a student's qualifications, academic effort, or compliance with the rules.

The additional $30,000 charge would compound the barrier for students seeking subsequent eligible training, including a STEM extension. Access would depend heavily on personal wealth or institutional resources. Neither demonstrates whether a student’s training opportunity is legitimate.

I support preventing fraud and enforcing immigration requirements. However, a large payment does not verify an employer, assess the quality of a training opportunity, or distinguish compliant participants from those violating the rules. DHS should pursue targeted employer verification, compliance reviews, and evidence-based enforcement. It should meaningfully evaluate these alternatives before imposing costs that could exclude legitimate participants.

DHS should also address the reliance interests of students already enrolled. I made substantial educational and financial commitments before this proposal. Although policies can change, introducing an unaffordable barrier near the end of a degree would fundamentally disrupt plans developed over years. Students cannot recover that time or easily transfer their educational investment to another country.

From my experience, practical training creates opportunities to contribute to engineering teams while learning from experienced colleagues. Preventing qualified graduates from participating could also disrupt employers and research groups that have invested time in training them. DHS should evaluate these consequences rather than assume that discouraging OPT necessarily benefits American workers.

Before proceeding, DHS should provide a transparent justification for the proposed amounts, explain their relationship to actual administrative costs, and assess how many otherwise eligible students would lose access. It should also examine how universities would respond and whether less burdensome measures could address documented misconduct.

I respectfully request that DHS withdraw these proposed fees and preserve financially accessible OPT. Students who follow the rules should have a meaningful opportunity to apply their education through authorized, degree-related practical training. That opportunity should not depend on the ability to pay tens of thousands of dollars.
comments.reason: The commenter strongly opposes the proposed high OPT fees and urges DHS to withdraw the proposal.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Jaison Victor Joseph Francis Xavier
comments.commentText:
Dear Sir or Madam,
I came to America as an international student to study, to learn, and to grow as a person. For me, practical training is part of that learning a chance to apply in real life what I studied in the classroom, and to learn from my American colleagues. Studying at U.S. universities provides invaluable access to modern technology and rigorous academic curricula. The OPT program serves as a critical bridge that allows students to apply theoretical knowledge to real-world environments, fostering innovation and contributing positively to the American workforce and diversified work culture.

America gave me a chance to learn from great teachers, to work alongside wonderful American colleagues, and to understand what respect, honesty, and hard work truly mean. I am deeply thankful for that. I want to say this from my heart: "we never came here to take anyone's job. We never think of encroaching on American citizens' jobs". International professionals deeply value collaboration with our American colleagues, aiming to share skills, wisdom, and mutual respect without displacing local workers. We respect every person here. We want to grow together, learn together, and build and enrich America together side by side, not apart from each other.

OPT is that chance for us. It is where what we learn in the classroom becomes real work, real service, and real contribution. If this door closes because of high fees, many honest, hardworking students will lose that chance. Introducing these fees places an undue financial burden on students who are striving to gain professional experience and contribute ethically to their employers and communities. I respectfully request that the agency reconsider these proposed fees to keep practical training accessible and support collaborative, peaceful workplace environments.

Thank you for considering my comment.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 fee for subsequent OPT recommendations. Protecting American workers and preventing fraud are legitimate policy objectives. However, these objectives require evidence-based measures that address actual misconduct. A substantial financial barrier imposed on legitimate participants is an unreasonable way to pursue them.

First, the proposal does not adequately connect the fee amounts to the services provided. Section IV.C explains that the revenue would be deposited into the Treasury as miscellaneous receipts, and ICE would not retain it for OPT oversight or enforcement. This undermines any suggestion that paying these fees would directly fund stronger program administration. DHS should provide a transparent justification for the amounts and demonstrate why less burdensome enforcement measures would be insufficient.

Second, available research challenges the assumption that restricting OPT necessarily benefits American workers. A 2024 peer-reviewed study by Xue Guo, Jing Gong, and Min-Seok Pang in MIS Quarterly, “Creation or Destruction? STEM OPT Extension and Employment of Information Technology Professionals,” found that the STEM OPT extension increased domestic employment in STEM occupations, with stronger effects in information technology. These findings warrant serious consideration before DHS adopts a policy that could sharply restrict participation. They do not establish that every OPT placement benefits every worker, but they demonstrate why a simple job-displacement narrative is inadequate.

Third, existing STEM OPT regulations already address compensation and displacement. Under 8 CFR § 214.2(f)(10)(ii)(C), duties, hours, and compensation must be commensurate with those of similarly situated U.S. workers. Employers must also attest that participating students will not replace U.S. workers. These requirements need effective verification and enforcement. A large participation fee does not verify wages, establish the quality of training, or identify a fraudulent employer.

Fourth, the broader economic consequences deserve substantial weight. NAFSA and JB International estimated that international students contributed $42.9 billion to the U.S. economy and supported more than 355,000 jobs during the 2024–2025 academic year. These figures describe international students overall, rather than OPT’s independent impact, but they show the economic interests at stake. My concern is that making practical training financially inaccessible could discourage enrollment and consequently harm universities, local businesses, and the American workers they employ.

Finally, the proposal allows institutions to pass the costs to students, other students, or employers. This creates a foreseeable risk that access will depend on personal wealth or institutional resources. Section VI should also give greater weight to currently enrolled students who committed years of study and substantial tuition under the existing framework. Applying a new charge to their future applications still disrupts decisions already made.

I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw these proposed fees. Any future changes should use transparent administrative cost estimates, targeted investigations, employer verification, and meaningful enforcement of worker protections. Program integrity should be measured by lawful conduct and educational value; the ability to produce tens of thousands of dollars is an inadequate substitute.
comments.reason: The commenter argues against the proposed high OPT fees, stating they are unreasonable and unsupported by evidence.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am writing to express my strong opposition to the proposed rule establishing fees of $70,000 for initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) and $30,000 for subsequent OPT recommendations, as described in Sections V.A and V.C and proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i).
I am an international PhD student in mathematics at a university in the United States, expecting to graduate in June 2027. Over the past several years, I have devoted myself to mathematical research and undergraduate education. In addition to pursuing my own research, I have taught undergraduate calculus courses, served as a teaching assistant, and helped organize educational programs for undergraduate mathematics students. I hope to continue my academic career in the United States after graduation, contributing to mathematical research and teaching at American universities.
OPT is an important part of this path. For international PhD students pursuing academic careers, postdoctoral positions are often the natural next step after graduation. These positions allow young researchers to develop their research programs, collaborate with other mathematicians, and contribute to university teaching. OPT provides an established way for international graduates to make this transition.
The proposed fees would create a substantial obstacle to this career path. Although the proposal requires educational institutions rather than students to pay the fees, many academic departments operate under limited budgets. A $70,000 fee for a single graduate's initial OPT recommendation would represent a significant financial burden. Universities may consequently become unwilling or unable to support OPT applications, regardless of a graduate's academic qualifications or contributions.
This concern is particularly serious in mathematics and other academic disciplines where postdoctoral researchers are hired primarily for their intellectual contributions rather than their potential to generate immediate financial returns. Academic positions are frequently funded through research grants and limited departmental resources. The proposed fee would introduce a financial consideration that is largely unrelated to a candidate's research ability, teaching experience, or academic potential.
I am also deeply concerned about the consequences for international students who have already committed years of their lives to studying in the United States. Like many international PhD students, I made long-term educational and career decisions with the understanding that OPT would offer a possible pathway to gain professional experience after graduation. The proposed rule could fundamentally change these expectations shortly before students like me complete their degrees. The proposed 60-day transition period does little to address the reliance interests of students who have spent years pursuing their education under the existing framework.
I urge DHS to distinguish between fraudulent activities and legitimate academic training and employment. A fee of this magnitude does not directly assess whether an OPT opportunity is genuine or whether a student complies with immigration regulations. Instead, it risks restricting opportunities for legitimate graduates based on their universities' willingness or ability to pay.
American universities benefit enormously from international academic exchange. In mathematics, research is an inherently international enterprise, and collaborations frequently cross national borders. International graduate students and postdoctoral researchers contribute not only to the advancement of research but also to the education of American undergraduate students. Restricting their opportunities to continue working in the United States could undermine these contributions and make American universities less attractive to future generations of talented researchers.
For these reasons, I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw the proposed OPT fee requirements in Sections V.A and V.C and proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i), and instead pursue targeted measures that address documented fraud without imposing substantial financial barriers on legitimate academic training.
Thank you for considering my comment.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed OPT fees create a substantial obstacle for international students and academic budgets.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by PANKAJ MISTRY
comments.commentText:
I oppose this proposed rule and urge DHS to withdraw it.

[Add 1–2 sentences on who you are and how OPT affects you: student, graduate, employer, faculty, school official, etc.]

**1. The fee has no relationship to the cost of the service.** The rule would charge schools $70,000 before a DSO can recommend a student for initial OPT, and $30,000 for each later recommendation, including the STEM extension. That is up to $100,000 per student. Entering an OPT recommendation in SEVIS costs the government a tiny fraction of that amount. DHS projects roughly $8.4–16.5 billion a year in collections, deposited to the Treasury. A charge designed to raise billions in general revenue, rather than recover program costs, works as a tax. The NPRM points to no clear authority from Congress to impose one. General authority under INA 214(a) to set conditions of admission is not a power to tax.

**2. The fee is not aimed at the fraud it claims to address.** If some schools, employers, or students misuse OPT, the answer is targeted enforcement against them:
- SEVP site visits and DSO oversight
- decertifying schools that misuse the program
- checking employer training plans (Form I-983)
- penalties for those who commit fraud

A flat fee on every recommendation falls equally on legitimate and fraudulent participants and cannot tell them apart. The NPRM does not explain why these narrower tools are not enough.

**3. The analysis contradicts itself.** The revenue estimate assumes OPT participation continues near current levels. Yet the rule aims to deter participation, and DHS admits schools may decline to pay at all. If participation collapses, the revenue estimate is wrong. If it doesn't, the deterrence rationale fails. Either way, the cost-benefit analysis cannot support the rule.

**4. DHS assumes the cost can be shifted without examining the harm.** The NPRM says schools may pass the fee on to F-1 students, to all students, or to employers.
- Charging F-1 students $70,000–$100,000 would put practical training out of reach for all but the wealthiest.
- Charging all students would raise tuition for U.S. students to pay an immigration fee.
- Charging employers would deter the startups, small businesses, hospitals, and research labs that rely on OPT graduates.

Many schools, especially smaller ones, will simply stop recommending OPT altogether.

**5. The rule covers pre-completion OPT.** That is training during a student's studies. A $70,000 charge on a student's first practical training has nothing to do with protecting the post-graduation job market.

**6. The rule harms U.S. schools, employers, and workers.** Students choose U.S. universities partly because OPT lets them apply what they learned. Pricing it out would lower enrollment and cut tuition revenue that supports domestic students. It would also shrink the STEM talent pipeline that U.S. employers and federally funded research depend on, and push that talent to competitor countries. The NPRM does not seriously quantify these losses.

**7. Thirty days is not enough time to comment.** DHS itself estimates the rule will move over $12 billion a year and affect about 2,478 schools. A rule of that size deserves a longer comment period.

DHS should withdraw this proposal. At a minimum, it should:
- limit any fee to the documented cost of processing OPT recommendations
- exempt pre-completion OPT and the STEM OPT extension, which already has employer training-plan requirements
- pursue enforcement against bad actors instead of a blanket charge
- reopen comment for at least 60 days with a revised economic analysis

Thank you for considering this comment.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes the proposed rule and urges DHS to withdraw it due to excessive fees.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I oppose this rule. DHS says it wants to protect American workers from "cheaper and more pliable, visa-dependent" foreign labor. That phrase comes from a source DHS quotes in footnote 106. This comment shows that the fee design makes OPT workers more dependent on employers, not less, and so works against the labor goal DHS states.

1. DHS invites employers to finance the fee
The NPRM says schools "may pass the financial obligation of this proposed fee onto F-1 nonimmigrant students, all students, or employers." It also says the rule does "not propose the imposition of specific limitations or restrictions on how the schools should collect or source the requisite funds," other than foreign gift reporting. The RIA assumes that where OPT is worth more than the fee, "affected parties could collectively cost share." So DHS expects employers to pay some fees and places no conditions on how they do it.

2. An employer who pays has a reason to lock the worker in
The fee is "not tied to a specific employer," and the NPRM says it "is not triggered by a change in employer." Once the EAD issues, the fee "will not be refunded under any circumstances." An employer that funds a $70,000 initial fee or a $30,000 STEM extension fee loses that money if the worker quits. The natural response is a repayment agreement, a training bond, or a promise to stay. Nothing in proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i) bars these terms. A worker who owes $30,000 or $70,000 on leaving cannot bargain over pay or conditions, cannot report abuse safely, and cannot take a better offer. That is the "pliable" worker DHS says it wants to remove.

3. Students who pay are pushed toward any job
If the cost falls on the student, many will borrow. Post-completion OPT allows only limited unemployment before status is at risk (90 days, or 150 with a STEM extension, under 8 CFR 214.2(f)(10)(ii)(E)). A graduate carrying a large fee-related debt and facing that clock will take the first offer at whatever wage. The fee raises the cost of saying no to a bad job.

4. DHS copied the H-1B price but not the H-1B worker protections
DHS says it set the $70,000 fee to be "comparable to the fee for H-1B visas" and to "closely align with the H-1B fees" (citing Proclamation 10973). The H-1B program, though, also forbids an employer from making the worker reimburse the ACWIA training fee (8 U.S.C. 1184(c)(9)), and Department of Labor rules bar penalties for leaving early and bar recovery of that fee from the worker (20 CFR 655.731(c)(10)). The NPRM adopts the price and leaves out the anti-recoupment rules that go with it. It never discusses the question.

5. The fee adds no wage floor
For initial OPT there is no wage or comparability requirement at all. For STEM OPT, the employer attests on Form I-983 to terms "commensurate" with similar U.S. workers, and the NPRM concedes DHS "does not generally verify the employer attestations unless and until there is a site visit." The rule changes neither. An employer that pays the fee can recover it through lower pay, which would add to the low-wage employment the RIA says the rule will reduce. The RIA never models fee recovery through wages or bonds.

6. The labor-protection claim is not supported
DHS's own footnote 103 quotes the CIS Ombudsman: OPT lacks "many of the customary protections that would have been legislated." Footnote 107 quotes testimony that OPT has "no protections for American workers or foreign workers." The fee adds none. It adds a large debt and a new reason for employers to control workers. An agency must consider an important aspect of the problem (Motor Vehicle Mfrs. Ass'n v. State Farm, 463 U.S. 29, 43 (1983)). DHS did not consider how a $70,000 charge shifts bargaining power between OPT workers and employers, or how that shift reaches the U.S. workers who compete with them.

7. Requested action
DHS should withdraw the rule. If DHS keeps any fee in a re-proposal, it should:
(a) bar any employer, school or third party from requiring a student to repay the fee, sign a training bond, or pay a penalty for leaving, modeled on 8 U.S.C. 1184(c)(9) and 20 CFR 655.731(c)(10);
(b) require the school to report in SEVIS who paid the fee and on what terms;
(c) provide a refund or credit when a worker leaves an employer because of a reported violation;
(d) analyze fee pass-through to wages, debt and job mobility in a revised RIA; and
(e) put enforcement where DHS's own evidence points: verification of employer attestations, with penalties on employers that underpay.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed OPT fee increases worker dependency and harms employers and employees.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by James Deemy
comments.commentText:
I am writing in my personal capacity as a water resources scientist, educator, and concerned citizen. The United States scientific enterprise relies on the recruitment of strong scientists from outside the nation. We train some of the brightest and best undergraduate and graduate students that other nations have to offer and then we have the chance to retain that talent to fuel our own innovation engine. Therefore, I respectfully but fundamentally oppose the proposed Optional Training Program rule because the $100,000 in total fees in the proposed rule are highly likely to prove prohibitive to the talent retention process.

Approximately, 38% of the science and engineering doctoral degrees awarded in 2024 were awarded to international students. More than half the postdoctoral positions in science, engineering, and health are also held by international scientists. The Optional Practical Training program assists in the retention of a majority of these critical scholars which greatly benefits the nation.

Much of my own training was directly influenced by extraordinarily talented scientists that chose careers in the United States. Specific but non-exhaustive examples are an organic chemist from China, a geneticist from Colombia, a genetic engineer from China, a forest resources scientist from India. All of which completed their graduate work in the United States and then were retained as part of the scientific workforce through various opportunities before subsequently contributing to the training of future scientists as university faculty at Virginia Commonwealth University or the University of Georgia.

Many of the most talented, driven, and helpful colleagues that I have had as a scientist were originally from other nations. Their contributions to the scientific workforce both in terms of scientific product as well as mentorship and collaboration would be greatly missed if we had prevented them from remaining in the U.S. post academic training.

In terms of national security, any barrier to retention of talent in science, technology, engineering and mathematics is a needless risk. Keeping talent in the U.S. is a critical step in keeping the nation secure by ensuring that we remain a top nation in scientific innovation. The current administration prioritizes attracting and retaining global talent and this rule by definition jeopardizes that priority, particularly in the fields of science, engineering, health, and technology. The current rule would all but ensure that we train strong science professionals before pipelining them out of the country instead of retaining them domestically. Please withdraw the rule to ensure the integrity of our scientific workforce pipeline.

James B. Deemy Ph. D.,
Water Resources Scientist
American Geophysical Union Member
Associate Professor of Environmental Sciences
comments.reason: The commenter argues that the $100,000 proposed fee is prohibitive and harms the retention of international scientific talent.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Missouri Baptist University
comments.commentText:
Missouri Baptist University urges DHS to withdraw the proposed OPT and STEM OPT fee rule. The structure of these fees effectively functions as a federal tax on institutions and international students. MBU is a private, tuition-dependent university with limited resources, and these mandated payments would divert funds away from academic programs, student services, and mission-driven work. The proposal would require institutions to pay large sums simply to allow students access to an educational benefit they already qualify for, creating an unfunded federal mandate that shifts federal program costs onto universities.

The rule also underestimates the administrative burden of collecting, processing, tracking, and refunding these payments. Implementing the proposal would require new staffing, expanded training, additional advising, and new financial systems—costs that would compound the financial impact of what is, in practice, a tax on participation in OPT.

International students contribute significantly to Missouri’s economy and to the St. Louis region’s workforce and innovation ecosystem. OPT provides essential practical training that complements classroom learning and supports employer needs in business, STEM-adjacent fields, and community-serving professions. Imposing a de facto tax on this educational experience would reduce access, harm students from modest backgrounds, and weaken the state’s competitiveness.

For these reasons, Missouri Baptist University strongly opposes the proposed fee structure and urges DHS to reconsider this rule.
comments.reason: The commenter urges DHS to withdraw the proposed OPT fee rule, arguing it harms students and universities.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Re: Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100 — Optional Practical Training Fees

I am a graduate worker at Yale University. I strongly oppose this proposed rule. It treats OPT as an optional benefit rather than a longstanding component of the U.S. educational system on which students, universities, and employers rely. DHS has repeatedly expanded practical training over decades, and students have made educational and financial decisions, universities have built programs and recruitment strategies, and employers have developed hiring pipelines in reliance on the availability of OPT.

DHS has not demonstrated that imposing enormous fees on every OPT participant is necessary to address the fraud it identifies. The NPRM describes fraud involving sham employers, nonexistent or staged worksites, phantom employees, false employment records, and unreported third-party placements. Those problems call for targeted enforcement, not a $70,000 charge imposed on legitimate students and educational institutions. DHS acknowledges that it considered alternatives such as expanded site visits, increased reporting, and stricter procedures, but rejects them largely because they would require additional government resources. DHS should instead evaluate risk-based employer audits, verification of worksites and payroll, and stronger penalties for employers actually engaged in fraud. The existence of enforcement costs does not justify shifting those costs indiscriminately onto the entire legitimate OPT population.

The proposed rule risks substantial harm to the economy, the higher-education system, and our international standing. The ability to gain authorized practical experience is part of the value of a U.S. education, particularly in STEM fields, and making that pathway prohibitively expensive risks sending talented students and researchers to competing countries.

DHS should withdraw the proposed rule and pursue targeted measures that punish fraudulent employment without undermining the legitimate economic, educational, and international benefits of attracting talent to the United States.
comments.reason: The commenter strongly opposes the proposed rule, arguing the fees are exorbitant and target legitimate students instead of fraud.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am writing to express my strong opposition to the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) / U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) proposed rule regarding new Optional Practical Training (OPT) fees. While regulatory cost-recovery is a legitimate agency interest, imposing punitive, unprecedented fee structures on practical training fundamentally misunderstands the role of OPT as an integral educational component. If finalized, this policy will cause irreparable harm to the U.S. higher education ecosystem, undermine domestic scientific research, and diminish America's global technological edge.

1. Catastrophic Disruption to U.S. Higher Education and Institutional Solvency
International students contribute over $40 billion annually to the U.S. economy and support hundreds of thousands of domestic jobs. Full-tuition international enrollment directly subsidizes financial aid for domestic students, faculty compensation, and campus infrastructure.

A primary driver for top global talent choosing American institutions over peer competitors (such as the UK, Canada, Australia, and the EU) is the availability of post-graduation practical training. Imposing exorbitant fees on OPT—whether levied directly on students or on sponsoring academic institutions—serves as an effective tariff on American degrees. This will inevitably redirect prospective scholars to foreign competitor nations, devastating university operating budgets and disproportionately harming mid-tier and state universities that rely heavily on international graduate enrollment.

2. Severe Blow to the U.S. Scientific Research and STEM Talent Pipeline
OPT and the STEM OPT extension are not mere employment authorizations; they are vital extensions of academic pedagogy that feed the U.S. research and development (R&D) apparatus.
- Critical Lab Operations: In fields such as artificial intelligence, advanced semiconductors, biotechnology, quantum computing, and clean energy, international graduate researchers, postdocs, and technical specialists conduct the heavy lifting on federally funded projects (supported by NSF, NIH, and DoD grants).
- Institutional Attrition: Pricing these researchers out of experiential training creates an immediate personnel cliff for university laboratories. Pushing universities to absorb massive compliance fees will force institutions to cut research assistantships and shutter groundbreaking experimental projects.

3. Erosion of National Competitiveness and Induced "Brain Drain"
The proposed fees run counter to the United States' articulated national security and industrial policy objectives, such as the CHIPS and Science Act, which explicitly require expanding the high-skilled STEM workforce. Forcing early-career scientists and engineers to exit the U.S. ecosystem immediately upon degree completion guarantees an aggressive "brain drain." Competitor economies will readily welcome this U.S.-trained intellectual capital, allowing foreign industries to commercialize breakthroughs funded by American basic research.

Conclusion:
The proposed fee structure is economically counterproductive, arbitrary, and directly harmful to the U.S. educational and scientific enterprise. I urge the agency to withdraw this proposed rule and preserve accessible, merit-driven practical training pathways that sustain American innovation.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Re: Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100 — Optional Practical Training Fees (RIN 1653-AB01)

To the Department of Homeland Security:

I am writing to strongly oppose the proposed rule imposing a $70,000 fee for initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) and a $30,000 fee for subsequent OPT participation, including STEM OPT extensions.

I am currently an international undergraduate student pursuing a degree in Computer Science at a U.S. research university. Throughout my studies, I have actively pursued opportunities to apply my technical knowledge through software engineering internships and collaborative technology projects.

My internship experiences have allowed me to contribute to real-world software development, work alongside professional engineers, and develop skills that cannot be fully acquired in a classroom. These experiences have reinforced my desire to continue working in software engineering after graduation and contribute to technological innovation in the United States.

For students like me, OPT is not simply an additional employment benefit. It is a critical opportunity to apply the knowledge gained through years of academic study, develop professionally, and contribute to the U.S. economy. The proposed fees would fundamentally undermine that opportunity.

Although the proposed fees would be charged to educational institutions, universities may have little choice but to pass these costs on to students or stop recommending OPT altogether. For most international students, an additional financial burden of this magnitude would be impossible to afford. Even academically successful students with legitimate internship experience and strong professional qualifications could effectively lose access to practical training.

I am particularly concerned about the impact on STEM graduates. The United States invests substantial educational resources in training students in computer science, engineering, and other technical fields. Preventing these graduates from gaining practical experience after completing their degrees would undermine that investment and discourage future international students from choosing American universities.

The proposed fees also appear disproportionate to the stated objective of preventing fraud. Legitimate international students who comply with immigration regulations should not face severe financial consequences because of misconduct by a small number of bad actors. If fraud prevention is the primary concern, targeted employer verification, stronger reporting requirements, and improved enforcement would be more appropriate and effective alternatives.

Beyond the immediate financial consequences, the proposal creates significant uncertainty for students who have already committed years of their lives to studying in the United States. Many of us made educational and financial decisions based on the opportunity to pursue lawful, degree-related practical training after graduation. Drastically changing the accessibility of OPT would disrupt these plans and undermine confidence in the U.S. higher education system.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am an international graduate student in a STEM field, currently on OPT, and I’m writing to oppose the proposed OPT fee rule. I ask DHS to withdraw the $70,000 initial fee and the $30,000 subsequent fee and to address fraud through targeted enforcement instead.

I understand why DHS wants to protect the program’s integrity and U.S. workers. People who abuse OPT should be investigated and penalized, and I have no objection to that. What I object to is charging a fee this large on behalf of every student and treating it as a substitute for enforcement.

My OPT position builds directly on what I studied in graduate school. It has been the part of my education where I found out how the methods I learned in class and in research actually hold up on real problems, and where I learned things no course could teach me. That is what practical training is supposed to do, and it is exactly what this rule would put out of reach for many students.

When I applied, I had to get my DSO’s recommendation, file with USCIS, pay the filing fee, submit supporting documents, complete biometrics, and wait for my EAD before I could start working. At each of those steps the government already verifies who I am, whether I’m in status, and whether my school stands behind me. If those checks need to be stronger, I’d support that. But whether my university can afford to spend $70,000 on me says nothing about whether I follow the rules. A compliant student at an underfunded school is no greater fraud risk than the same student at a wealthy one, yet under this rule their outcomes could be very different.

The fee is formally charged to schools, but DHS acknowledges that schools may pass it on to students or employers, or simply stop recommending OPT. In practice, access to OPT would come down to how much money a student’s school, employer, or family has. Small colleges, public universities under budget pressure, nonprofits, research labs, and startups would be hit hardest. DHS’s own analysis finds that 56 percent of affected institutions are small entities, that some may be unable to fund the fees at all, and that 60.5 percent of the small institutions it analyzed could face impacts above one percent of revenue (91 Fed. Reg. 64595–96). None of this separates legitimate training from fraud. It separates people by wealth.

The treatment of pre-completion OPT is especially troubling. Practical training during a degree is often where students first see how their coursework and research translate into real work. Yet a student who does pre-completion OPT and later post-completion OPT could trigger $100,000 in fees, and DHS itself expects pre-completion participation to drop. That pushes students and schools to plan training around avoiding a fee rather than around what makes sense for their education.

The costs also reach beyond students. We pay tuition, rent apartments, and spend money in our college towns; NAFSA estimates international students contributed about $42.9 billion to the U.S. economy and supported roughly 355,000 jobs in 2024–2025. The chance to gain real work experience after graduation was part of why I chose to study in the U.S., and I know the same is true for many of my classmates. DHS acknowledges the fee could reduce F-1 enrollment and that it cannot precisely quantify the lost benefits (91 Fed. Reg. 64588–89). With projected collections of roughly $8.4 to $16.5 billion per year, this is not a cost-recovery fee. It is meant to change behavior, and those effects deserve much closer scrutiny than the proposal gives them.

DHS has better tools available: risk-based audits, site visits, closer review of employers with suspicious patterns, better data sharing among SEVIS, USCIS, schools, and employers, enforcement of the field-of-study requirement, and real penalties for those who actually violate the rules. The proposal notes that DHS considered some of these alternatives. If fraud is concentrated among certain actors, enforcement should be concentrated there too.

Finally, many students chose their programs years ago under the rules in place at the time, and a 60-day transition doesn’t reflect that, especially for PhD students. Protecting only those who already have a DSO recommendation or approved OPT before the effective date leaves out students who enrolled in good faith. If DHS moves forward, it should at minimum grandfather students who were enrolled before the proposal was published.

I respectfully ask DHS to withdraw these fees. If more oversight funding is truly needed, a much lower fee tied to actual costs, paired with targeted enforcement, would serve that goal without shutting out compliant students and smaller institutions.

I came here to study and train in my field, and I have followed every rule asked of me. I respect the need for a rigorous immigration system, but rigorous oversight and a $70,000 price tag are not the same thing.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly asks DHS to withdraw the proposed OPT fee rule, arguing it harms students.

I strongly oppose the proposed $70,000 initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) fee and $30,000 subsequent OPT fee, and respectfully urge the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) to withdraw this proposal.

I am an international student pursuing a master's degree in Computer Science at a U.S. university, with an expected graduation date in 2027. I have completed a technical internship at a U.S. technology company, where I gained valuable experience applying the skills developed through my education. I hope to continue contributing to the American technology industry after graduation through OPT.

The opportunity to gain practical experience related to my degree was an important factor in my decision to pursue graduate education in the United States. Like many international students, I have invested substantial time, effort, and financial resources in my education, with the reasonable expectation that I could apply for practical training under the existing regulatory framework.

**First, the proposed fees would create an unreasonable financial barrier.** A $70,000 initial fee, followed by a potential $30,000 fee for STEM OPT extension, would make practical training financially inaccessible for many qualified graduates. Although the fees would formally be imposed on educational institutions, universities could pass these costs on to students or decline to recommend otherwise eligible students for OPT. Either outcome would effectively deny legitimate students access to opportunities for which they have spent years preparing.

**Second, the proposed fee amounts lack a sufficiently demonstrated connection to administrative costs.** The proposal does not adequately explain why charges of this magnitude are necessary to administer the OPT program. Fees should be proportionate to legitimate administrative expenses rather than function as financial barriers to lawful participation.

**Third, the proposal is poorly targeted toward its stated objective of preventing fraud.** Students who comply with immigration regulations and institutions that follow established procedures should not bear extraordinary financial burdens because of misconduct by a minority of participants. More effective alternatives would include stronger employer verification, targeted compliance audits, improved reporting mechanisms, and enforcement against fraudulent employment arrangements. These measures would address misconduct more directly without penalizing legitimate participants.

**Finally, the proposal could undermine the competitiveness of American higher education and the technology industry.** International graduates contribute valuable technical skills and practical experience to U.S. employers. Making OPT prohibitively expensive would discourage prospective students from choosing American universities and could cause U.S.-educated graduates to pursue opportunities elsewhere. This would weaken the ability of American institutions and businesses to attract and retain skilled talent.

I fully support reasonable measures to prevent fraud and ensure compliance with immigration laws. However, the proposed fees are disproportionate to these objectives and would impose severe consequences on students and universities acting in good faith.

I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw the proposed OPT fee rule and instead adopt targeted, evidence-based measures that protect program integrity while preserving accessible, lawful practical training opportunities.

I strongly oppose the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent fee. This proposal is deeply shortsighted, economically damaging, and potentially disastrous for America’s long-term competitiveness in science and technology.

I am a PhD researcher working in artificial intelligence, and I understand firsthand how rapidly this field is advancing. We are living through one of the most consequential technological transformations in history. Countries are competing aggressively for the world’s best researchers, engineers, and scientific talent. At precisely this moment, the United States is proposing extraordinary financial barriers that could drive away the very people helping it remain at the forefront of innovation.

Does the government genuinely understand the long-term consequences of what it is proposing?

American universities invest years training international researchers at the cutting edge of AI, medicine, engineering, and other critical technologies. These researchers contribute to scientific discoveries, technological breakthroughs, startups, and American industry. Imposing a $70,000 barrier on their transition from education to employment makes absolutely no strategic sense.

China and other competing nations would have every incentive to welcome the talented scientists and engineers that America pushes away. Once these researchers establish their careers, laboratories, companies, and professional networks elsewhere, bringing that expertise and investment back will not be easy. The United States cannot assume that its technological leadership is permanent.

The consequences extend far beyond international students. American workers, universities, companies, and the broader economy could all suffer.

When companies face increasing obstacles to hiring highly specialized talent in the United States, they have another option: move research, development, and employment opportunities overseas. This proposal could accelerate that shift. Instead of protecting American jobs, it risks driving investment and future job creation outside the country.

How does forcing universities to pay tens of thousands of dollars for researchers they have already trained help American innovation? How does making the United States less attractive to the world’s most talented scientists strengthen its position in the global AI race?

These are serious economic and national competitiveness questions that deserve serious answers.

I recognize the importance of preventing immigration fraud and protecting American workers. But those objectives should be addressed through targeted enforcement and evidence-based policies, not indiscriminate financial barriers that penalize legitimate students, universities, and employers.

I am increasingly concerned that the cumulative effect of restrictive immigration decisions will be to weaken the very research and technology ecosystem that has made the United States a global leader. America cannot simultaneously aspire to dominate artificial intelligence and make it extraordinarily difficult for highly trained AI researchers to contribute to its economy.

Please think carefully about the consequences before implementing a policy of this magnitude. The damage to America’s scientific competitiveness, international reputation, and ability to attract exceptional talent could persist for decades. Some opportunities, once lost to competing nations, may never return.

The United States became a global technology leader in part because it attracted brilliant minds from around the world and gave them opportunities to innovate. Undermining that advantage at this critical moment is a profound strategic mistake.

I strongly urge the Department of Homeland Security to withdraw this proposed rule in its entirety. Protecting American workers and strengthening American innovation should go hand in hand, not be placed in opposition to each other.
