comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am a graduate student worker studying neurodegeneration in the Department of Neuroscience at Yale University. I have worked in both academic and industry-based research, and I am submitting this comment on the basis of that experience. I urge DHS to withdraw the proposed rule under Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, which would charge $70,000 for an F-1 student’s first Optional Practical Training (OPT) recommendation and $30,000 for each one after that.

Neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s are diseases of aging, and they are difficult to model. No single model fully reproduces human disease, so researchers often combine several models and approaches to build a reliable picture. Mouse models are central to this work, but the pathology we study develops slowly. Mice must be bred, often across multiple genetic crosses, and then aged for many months before the disease features we want to study appear. Only then can behavioral testing, tissue analysis, and molecular experiments begin, and those need to be repeated and validated. A single well-controlled study can take well over a year from the first breeding to usable data. Because the experiments themselves are slow, training in this field takes longer. A PhD student, like me, studying neurodegeneration often reaches the point of collecting key data late in their program, and the work that follows (replication, analysis, writing, and publication) frequently extends beyond graduation. OPT is what allows an international trainee to stay and complete that work as a postdoctoral researcher. Without it, projects that took years to set up would be left unfinished, aged animal cohorts would be wasted, and the training invested in the scientist who ran them would be lost.

A fee of this size would break the link between training and employment. Few employers, whether a university lab or a small biotech startup, can justify a five-figure surcharge to hire a single early-career scientist, and no trainee can pay it out of pocket. Having worked in both academic and industry settings, I have seen how a discovery travels from the bench to the clinic. Findings typically begin in university labs and are then developed by biotech and pharmaceutical teams. The people who carry that work across are often early-career scientists who trained in one setting and were hired into the other. OPT is a major part of that handoff for international researchers. If these researchers never begin U.S. training or leave once they finish, the expertise and the public investment in their education leave with them.

Neurodegenerative diseases affect millions of American families, and the work to treat them is slow and cumulative. Narrowing the pool of people allowed to do that work will slow it further. It would also weaken the biotechnology sector and the jobs it creates, and it would encourage the strongest applicants to choose other countries that actively recruit international scientists, eroding U.S. leadership in biomedical research.

For these reasons, I urge DHS to withdraw this proposed rule.
comments.reason: The commenter urges DHS to withdraw the proposed rule imposing high OPT fees.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Barney Potter
comments.commentText: I am a postdoctoral researcher at Yale University where I study the epidemiology of diseases that greatly impact the health and well-being of millions of Americans and countless people worldwide. comments.title: Comment Submitted by Tamara Walsky
comments.commentText:
I am writing to express strong opposition to the change of the F-1 Optional Practical Training (OPT) Fees rule proposed by DHS ([DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100] RIN 1653-AB01). This change places a heavy financial burden on those applying for OPT and/or the institutions that seek to hire them, one that makes paying for OPT unaffordable for the vast majority of otherwise eligible candidates.

The assumption that increasing the fee for OPT will successfully address fraud and protect American workers is not correct. OPT provides an opportunity for international students that graduate from an American university to find work in the US, bringing their education and talent to contribute to American society, research enterprise and the economy. I am currently a graduate student pursuing a PhD, and have many peers and friends who rely on OPT to pursue their career path of choice, allowing them to utilize their passions, curiosity and intellectual talent in otherwise very competitive professional roles. Within the university setting, OPT allows for the hiring of postdoctoral associates, lecturers, fellows, etc. that lead projects tackling tough research problems and teach diverse and crucial skills to undergraduate students. Individuals applying for OPT already pay a substantial sum ($~500) and navigate a lengthy process (like taking time off work to get fingerprinted) to apply for and receive OPT. Additionally, any non-STEM professional is only eligible for 1 year of OPT before they need to find a position that will sponsor them to continue working in the US. Increasing the OPT fee will bar many of these talented individuals from further contributing to American society, research enterprise and the economy, leaving a gap in talent and education that will not automatically be filled by US citizens. An exorbitant fee like $70,000 will not ensure that honest individuals are selected for their merit, it will just allow those from wealthy backgrounds to continue their careers in the USA, destroying many’s American dream in the process.

I urge DHS to withdraw the proposed OPT fees rule.

Tamara Walsky, PhD Candidate at Cornell University
The views presented here are my own, and not of the institution I work for.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose the proposed $70,000 initial and $30,000 subsequent OPT fees [1, p. 64566] and urge DHS to withdraw this rule. It would weaken the U.S. economy, punish honest students for the fraud of a few, and hand the world's best young talent to America's competitors.

1. It harms the U.S. economy (Section VII.A). International students contributed $42.9 billion to the U.S. economy and supported about 355,000 jobs in the 2024-25 academic year [2]. Most of that money comes from abroad [3], and DHS itself acknowledges that schools could lose enrollment if students are deterred by the fees [1, p. 64588]. DHS's own primary estimate is $4.1 billion in costs every year, about $35 billion over ten years, yet DHS lists the rule's monetized benefits as "Not Estimated" [1, Tables 1 and 10]. A rule with tens of billions in costs and no quantified benefit should not be finalized.

2. It punishes honest students instead of fraudsters (Sections IV.A and IV.C). The fee is the same for every student and is not tied to any employer or fraud indicator [1, p. 64577]. DHS cites more than 10,000 students working for suspect employers [1, p. 64571]; that is a small fraction of the roughly 290,000 OPT and STEM OPT authorizations in 2024 alone [1, Table 2]. Fraud should be fought by targeting fraudulent employers and schools through site visits, E-Verify, and employer vetting. And because the fees go to the general Treasury, not to SEVP, not one dollar would fund fraud investigations [1, p. 64576].

3. It selects by wealth, not talent (Sections IV.C and VI). DHS admits schools may pass the fee on to students [1, p. 64575]. A STEM student could face $100,000 [1, p. 64583], or $130,000 with pre-completion OPT [1, p. 64577]. A brilliant young engineer from a modest family would be priced out, while a wealthier but less qualified student would not. That is the opposite of choosing "the most promising students" [1, p. 64574]. Small schools would be hit hardest: DHS estimates 98 small institutions would face costs above 20% of annual revenue [1, Table 15].

4. It gives our talent to competitors, including China. Other countries are competing hard for exactly the students this rule pushes away. In October 2025 China launched its K visa, which lets young foreign STEM graduates come and work without an employer sponsor [4]. If the United States charges $70,000 for one year of practical training, why would a top student not choose China or another competitor instead? Those graduates would then build their companies there. Today, 24% of U.S. billion-dollar startups have a founder who first came here as an international student [5]. If America wants to lead in AI, semiconductors, aerospace, and biotech, it must compete for this talent, not tax it.

5. It breaks faith with current students (Section VI). Many students already enrolled, including those in multi-year PhD programs, chose the United States expecting OPT to be available. Calling that expectation "speculative" [1, p. 64579] ignores real decisions about years of study and money already invested here.


American universities train these students with American resources. OPT lets that investment pay off here, through skilled work, research, and new companies, instead of sending it to our competitors. I urge DHS to withdraw this rule and fight fraud through targeted enforcement against the actual bad actors.

Respectfully

References
[1] DHS/ICE, "Optional Practical Training Fees," Notice of Proposed Rulemaking, 91 FR 64566 (Oct. 8, 2026).
[2] NAFSA, International Student Economic Value Tool, 2024-25 data. https://www.nafsa.org/economicvalue
[3] IIE Open Doors, "Economic Impact of International Students." https://opendoorsdata.org/services/research-special-reports-and-analyses/economic-impact-of-international-students/
[4] Caixin Global, "China to Launch New Visa to Lure Young Tech Talent Amid U.S. Curbs" (Oct. 2, 2025). https://www.caixinglobal.com/2025-10-02/china-to-launch-new-visa-to-lure-young-tech-talent-amid-us-curbs-102368491.html
[5] National Foundation for American Policy, "Immigrants and U.S. Billion-Dollar Companies" (June 2026). https://nfap.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/IMMIGRANTS-AND-US-BILLION-DOLLAR-COMPANIES.NFAP-Policy-Brief.2026.pdf
comments.reason: The commenter strongly opposes the proposed OPT fees and urges DHS to withdraw the rule.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose the Department of Homeland Security's proposed rule establishing additional fees for Optional Practical Training (OPT). I am a doctoral student at a U.S. university. American universities have established themselves as global leaders in higher education, scientific research, and innovation partly because of their ability to attract highly qualified individuals from around the world. International graduate students, particularly those pursuing advanced research degrees, are admitted to leading American institutions based on their academic qualifications, scientific merit, specialized expertise, and potential to contribute to scientific advancement. Their participation in American higher education should not be viewed simply as competition with domestic students or workers, but as an important contribution to the country's research capacity and global competitiveness.
OPT provides an essential legal pathway for international graduates to apply their advanced education and scientific training in American research institutions, universities, and STEM industries. This pathway has allowed the United States not only to attract global talent but also to retain highly skilled individuals who have already received years of advanced training within American institutions. Retaining these individuals helps strengthen scientific research, technological development, economic growth, and the long-term interests of American communities and taxpayers.
The proposed fees of $70,000 for initial OPT and $30,000 for subsequent OPT would introduce substantial financial barriers to this pathway. Although these fees would be imposed on educational institutions, their consequences could extend to international graduates, university research programs, and prospective employers. Such financial burdens could discourage institutions from supporting qualified researchers and undermine the country's ability to retain the scientific expertise it has invested in significant resources in developing.
Protecting American workers and maintaining the integrity of immigration programs are legitimate policy objectives. However, imposing exceptionally high financial barriers on qualified international graduates may not effectively address the underlying concerns of fraud or program misuse. Instead, such measures risk restricting opportunities for individuals who have followed legal educational pathways and are prepared to contribute their knowledge and expertise to the American economy.
The United States has maintained its global leadership in scientific discovery and innovation through its ability to recognize merit, attract international talent, and create opportunities for highly qualified individuals to contribute to its institutions and industries. Introducing substantial financial obstacles to retaining these individuals could weaken this competitive advantage and undermine the long-term benefits of investment in American higher education and scientific research.
I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw the proposed OPT fee requirements and consider alternative measures that strengthen program oversight and integrity without creating disproportionate financial barriers to retaining highly qualified international graduates.
Thank you for considering this comment.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed OPT fees harm international talent retention and U.S. competitiveness.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I oppose the proposed rule imposing fees of $70,000 for initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) participation and $30,000 for subsequent participation. DHS states that the rule is intended to combat fraud, strengthen program integrity, and protect U.S. workers. However, the proposal does not directly address the misconduct described in the rule and instead imposes significant burdens on compliant institutions and students.

The proposal is poorly targeted. If DHS has identified fraud involving employers, staffing firms, or improper training arrangements, enforcement efforts should focus on those actors. Instead, the rule imposes substantial costs on all participating institutions regardless of their compliance history. As a result, schools and students who follow the law would bear the costs of misconduct committed by others.

The proposed fees would likely discourage participation in OPT and reduce international student enrollment. This would have economic consequences far beyond higher education. International students contributed approximately $42.9 billion to the U.S. economy during the 2024-25 academic year and supported more than 355,000 American jobs. NAFSA reports that roughly one U.S. job is supported for every three international students.

International students support local economies through spending on housing, food, transportation, healthcare, and other services. Recent enrollment declines have already been associated with an estimated $1.1 billion reduction in economic activity and nearly 23,000 fewer jobs nationwide. The proposed rule risks worsening these losses by making the United States a less attractive destination for international students.

The rule would also undermine research, innovation, and workforce development. More than half of international students pursue STEM-related fields, and many contribute to research laboratories, graduate programs, and high-skill industries. Research has found that international researchers account for more than 30 percent of U.S. patents and approximately one-third of U.S. Nobel Prize recipients. Restricting access to OPT threatens an important pathway through which the United States attracts and retains highly skilled talent.

DHS has not demonstrated that these unprecedented fees will meaningfully reduce fraud. More targeted alternatives exist, including enhanced oversight of high-risk employers, increased penalties for proven misconduct, risk-based audits, and improved verification of training arrangements. Such measures would directly address abuse without imposing broad costs on compliant institutions and law-abiding students.

For these reasons, DHS should withdraw the proposed rule or substantially revise it to focus on enforcement against employers and entities engaged in misconduct rather than imposing sweeping financial burdens on educational institutions and students.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
To the Department of Homeland Security:

I am an international scientist working in biomedical informatics. I submit this comment anonymously because this proposal concerns my professional future and ability to continue contributing to research in the United States. I strongly oppose the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 fee for subsequent recommendations, and I urge DHS to withdraw the rule.

For scientists like me, this proposal raises a painful question: after years of specialized training, could our opportunity to continue legitimate research depend on whether an institution can afford an extraordinary payment?

The fees would create a barrier unrelated to merit or compliance.

An international scientist could be qualified for a position, needed by a research team, and fully compliant with immigration requirements, yet lose the opportunity because an institution cannot afford the fee.

Placing the payment obligation on universities does not eliminate the burden on individuals. Institutions could decline to recommend eligible participants or ration support according to departmental resources. Access to training could depend on institutional wealth and commercial earning potential rather than educational value or scientific contribution.

This places researchers in a difficult position: asking an institution to absorb the charge could mean competing with funding for colleagues, equipment, or other research needs. Being unable to secure that payment could interrupt an entire career.

Interrupted training could harm biomedical research and American collaborators.

Biomedical informatics requires more than technical proficiency. Researchers must understand how clinical data were collected, how diseases were measured, what biases affect an analysis, and which conclusions the evidence can support. Developing that knowledge takes sustained work with collaborators.

If a scientist cannot continue, a replacement may need substantial time to acquire this knowledge. American colleagues, students, clinicians, and research staff could face delayed analyses, additional workloads, and interrupted projects.

The possibility of leaving important work unfinished is personally difficult. Scientists invest years in developing the skills needed to contribute responsibly. DHS should account for the consequences of disrupting that investment.

Public-interest research may lack the resources to absorb these fees.

Research can have substantial public value without generating immediate commercial revenue. Work intended to improve disease research, clinical evidence, or health care may operate under constrained budgets.

The proposed fees could therefore disadvantage socially valuable work precisely because it cannot produce the revenue needed to justify an exceptional payment. Ability to pay should not become a substitute for evaluating the legitimacy and educational value of training.

A large payment does not establish program integrity.

I support enforcement against fraudulent employers, false records, and sham training arrangements. However, an institution’s ability to pay does not demonstrate compliance, and inability to pay does not demonstrate misconduct.

DHS should explain what evidence connects these particular amounts to preventing specific violations. It must distinguish reduced fraud from reduced lawful participation. Excluding eligible scientists because institutions cannot pay is a policy cost, not proof of successful enforcement.

Risk-based audits, verification of suspicious arrangements, and enforcement against documented misconduct deserve meaningful consideration.

DHS must address reliance interests and economic consequences.

Scientific training and research commitments develop over years. Students and researchers make substantial educational, financial, and personal decisions under the existing framework.

A short transition cannot undo those commitments or create funding that institutions never anticipated. DHS should meaningfully protect existing students and participants, including otherwise eligible extensions, if any changes proceed.

The economic analysis should also address project delays, replacement costs, lost institutional knowledge, and effects on American collaborators. It should not assume that removing an international researcher automatically creates an equivalent opportunity for an American worker.

I respectfully request that DHS withdraw the proposed fees, preserve legitimate practical training, and pursue targeted, evidence-based enforcement.

I want my future to depend on the quality of my work, responsible research, and compliance with the rules. The prospect that it could instead depend on an institution’s ability to make an extraordinary payment is deeply discouraging. Please preserve the opportunity for scientists to apply their training and contribute to research that benefits the public.

Respectfully,
Anonymous commenter

Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100: Optional Practical Training Fees

I oppose the proposed OPT fees and urge DHS to withdraw the rule entirely.

OPT is a major part of the U.S. talent pipeline. In 2024–25, 294,253 graduates of U.S. universities participated in OPT (IIE Open Doors 2025). International students, including OPT participants, contributed $42.9 billion to the U.S. economy and supported 355,736 U.S. jobs that year (NAFSA).

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am writing to express my serious concerns about the combined impact of recent restrictions on international students and the proposed OPT fees. In my view, this proposal is extreme, disproportionate, and disconnected from the realities international students face.

International students are already navigating an increasingly difficult system. Recent changes in how CPT eligibility is interpreted and administered have created uncertainty at some universities. Students who expected to participate in legitimate internships have faced restrictions, lost opportunities, or found that their institutions are no longer willing to authorize certain CPT arrangements.

Now, the proposed OPT fees could create another major barrier to lawful practical training.

OPT applications can already involve months of processing. Some students experience delays of five or six months, making it difficult to coordinate graduation, employment, and immigration deadlines. Adding a substantial payment requirement before a university can issue an OPT recommendation introduces another potential obstacle.

Has DHS adequately examined how these requirements would interact with existing processing delays, filing deadlines, employment authorization periods, and the limited time students have to maintain lawful status?

My concern is that these policies could create a harmful cycle. Students enter the United States legally, pay tuition, maintain their status, complete their degrees, and attempt to follow every requirement. Yet increasingly restrictive training opportunities, high fees, and administrative delays could leave some unable to continue their employment or maintain their intended immigration pathway.

Depending on their circumstances, students could face job loss, the expiration of employment authorization, or even the risk of falling out of status. Such consequences could also increase their exposure to immigration enforcement, despite their efforts to comply with the law.

I am not suggesting that every processing delay automatically causes a loss of lawful status. My concern is that DHS must examine these risks together rather than treating each restriction as an isolated policy.

This raises a broader question: What is the intended role of international students in American higher education if legitimate opportunities for practical training become increasingly inaccessible?

If the government's objective is to substantially reduce international student participation in practical training, that policy choice and its consequences should be explained transparently. It should not emerge through a combination of financial barriers, administrative restrictions, and uncertainty that students could not reasonably anticipate.

International students make enormous commitments to study in the United States. Many contribute to university research, support local economies, and seek to develop professional skills through lawful employment. They deserve a system with clear, consistent, and achievable requirements.

I respectfully ask DHS to evaluate the combined impact of CPT restrictions, OPT processing delays, and the proposed fees. DHS should explain what safeguards would prevent students from losing lawful employment opportunities or facing immigration consequences because of administrative barriers beyond their control.

The proposed fees should not be evaluated in isolation from the broader immigration system. A policy intended to improve compliance should not make compliance unnecessarily difficult for students who are genuinely trying to follow the rules.

I respectfully but firmly urge DHS to withdraw this proposed rule in its entirety and discontinue efforts to implement these fees.

Given the severe financial burden, potential disruption to lawful employment, existing CPT and OPT challenges, and serious consequences for international students' futures, I do not believe that minor revisions or delayed implementation would adequately address these concerns.

My request is for the complete withdrawal of this proposed rule, not merely a reduction in fees or the creation of limited exemptions.

International students who entered the United States in good faith, followed the law, and invested substantial time and financial resources in their education should not face such extreme financial barriers.

I strongly urge DHS to abandon this proposal and pursue more reasonable, evidence-based approaches that protect program integrity without unnecessarily harming law-abiding international students.

Thank you for considering my comments.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed OPT fees create major barriers and harm international students.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Amanda Bartolotta
comments.commentText:
My strong preference is for DHS to eliminate OPT and STEM OPT entirely. At an absolute minimum, the proposed rule should be implemented. These programs have evolved into a commercially exploited foreign-labor and immigration pipeline that harms American workers, undermines wages and employment opportunities, enables widespread fraud and abuse, and threatens American economic security and sovereignty.

OPT is no longer simply a training program. It is a business model. Universities profit from international enrollment, staffing intermediaries profit from recruitment and placement, and corporations gain access to foreign labor without demonstrating that qualified American workers are unavailable. Standard OPT lacks H-1B prevailing-wage certification requirements, and qualifying F-1 workers receive payroll-tax exemptions that create additional financial incentives for employers.

The consequences are far-reaching:

- American jobs and wages: OPT increases competition for jobs while American graduates struggle to enter their professions and experienced workers face layoffs, displacement, wage stagnation, and underemployment.
- Immigration pipeline: OPT and STEM OPT provide pathways into H-1B sponsorship and potentially permanent residence, extending their consequences far beyond temporary educational training.
- Fraud and abuse: Federal investigations have exposed fictitious employers, fraudulent employment records, nonexistent worksites, shell companies, and organized immigration fraud networks. Recent DHS investigations identified more than 10,000 F-1 students associated with highly suspect employers.
- Foreign-worker exploitation: Immigration-dependent employment creates opportunities for wage theft, coercive recruitment, fraudulent sponsorship, and exploitation by staffing intermediaries.
- Taxes and housing: Payroll-tax exemptions create unequal employer incentives, while additional labor supply and immigration transitions affect housing demand, affordability, infrastructure, and local economic conditions.
- National security and sovereignty: Fraudulent employment arrangements, undisclosed offshore operations, inadequate employer verification, and organized international networks expose serious weaknesses in immigration enforcement and accountability.
- Regulatory failure: DHS has acknowledged that oversight resources have not kept pace with program growth. Americans are bearing the consequences of a system the government has struggled to monitor and enforce.

Through my own investigations of interconnected, visa-dependent staffing enterprises, I have uncovered evidence of coordinated recruitment and consultant marketing, shared business infrastructure, immigration sponsorship networks, and relationships among staffing companies that raise serious concerns about labor-market manipulation, worker exploitation, and potential immigration fraud. These arrangements warrant investigation for possible antitrust violations and other coordinated misconduct. OPT and related visa programs provide opportunities for such enterprises to build and monetize immigration-dependent labor pipelines.

These are not isolated concerns. Decades of documented fraud, repeated enforcement failures, and recent federal task-force discoveries demonstrate that the vulnerabilities are longstanding and serious.

Increasing fees does not eliminate the underlying harm, but it is the absolute minimum DHS should do. The government should not continue subsidizing a system that benefits universities, staffing intermediaries, and corporations while American workers compete against immigration-based labor-cost advantages.

DHS should implement the proposed rule without weakening it, aggressively investigate participating employers and institutions, and pursue the complete termination of OPT and STEM OPT through every available lawful mechanism.

American jobs are not recruitment incentives. American workers should not be displaced to support a foreign-labor business model. American sovereignty is not for sale. End OPT and STEM OPT.
comments.reason: The commenter supports the proposed rule and prefers eliminating OPT entirely to protect American workers.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Arunkumar C Varadhan
comments.commentText:
RE: Notice of Proposed Rulemaking: Optional Practical Training Fees
Docket No.: ICEB-2026-0100 / RIN 1653-AA98
Submission Type: Public Comment opposing the proposed rule and requesting explicit exemptions for long-term U.S. residents (“Documented Dreamers”).

To Whom It May Concern,

I strongly oppose the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) proposed rule to implement a $70,000 fee for initial OPT recommendations and a $30,000 fee for subsequent recommendations. As a high-skilled professional who has lived and worked in the U.S. on an H-1B visa for 15 years, I am deeply concerned that this proposal completely ignores "Documented Dreamers"—the children of long-term, legal, tax-paying visa holders who grew up in the United States.
Applying a uniform fee structure to all F-1 visa holders is an arbitrary oversight causing severe, disproportionate economic harm to families who have perfectly maintained legal status for decades. DHS must modify the proposal to exclude students who spent their lifetimes in the U.S. and completed their schooling here.

DHS must address the following critical flaws based on our lived reality:
1. Failure to Recognize Long-Term U.S. Residents Trapped in the Green Card Backlog
Our family has maintained perfect legal status in the U.S. for 15 years, consistently paying all federal, state, and local taxes. However, due to the decades-long employment-based green card backlog for Indian nationals, our permanent residency remains delayed. Consequently, my daughter recently turned 21 and "aged out" of our green card application as a dependent, forcing her to switch to F-1 status just to remain legal. Imposing a catastrophic $70,000 fee on her to access post-graduation employment penalizes her for administrative backlogs completely outside her control.

2. Treating Culturally American Students Identically to Incoming International Students
My daughter did all her schooling in the U.S. starting from Grade 1 and is currently a senior at The Ohio State University. She knows only the U.S. as her home. It is entirely unfair to treat a student who spent her lifetime in American schools the same as a foreign national entering solely for a short-term master's enrollment.

Furthermore, my daughter should not be considered "foreign labor competition." Our family has fully paid her university tuition out-of-pocket without relying on any public aid, state subsidies, or financial support—unlike public aid programs frequently made available to undocumented immigrants.
Additionally, this rule will unfairly prevent my daughter from supporting herself to enroll in a future U.S. master's program. Many competitive graduate programs require real-time, practical work experience post-bachelor's degree. OPT is designed to provide this vital professional experience while giving her the financial ability to self-fund her future graduate studies. A $70,000 barrier completely disrupts her self-funded educational path and blocks her academic advancement.

3. Severe Economic Double-Taxation on Tax-Paying Families
Our family has already contributed significantly to the U.S. economy, including paying full tuition for my daughter’s university education. Forcing public university seniors like my daughter to absorb an additional $70,000 fee—which institutions will pass down to students—creates an insurmountable financial barrier. It forces families who have paid taxes for 15 years to buy back the right for their American-raised children to work in the only country they call home.

4. Misalignment with Fraud Prevention Goals

The proposed rule claims extreme fees are necessary to combat fraud within the OPT program. However, a student with an unblemished, 15-year record of continuous legal presence, verified through U.S. K-12 education and a degree from a major institution like The Ohio State University, presents zero fraud risk. Applying this fee to individuals with lifelong domestic histories does nothing to combat bad actors; it simply drives American-educated professionals out of the country.

Conclusion and Requested Remedy

The proposed rule fails to analyze the economic impact on long-term legal residents who aged out of the green card queue. If DHS proceeds, it must include a clear, bright-line exemption:
Any F-1 student who can demonstrate continuous legal maintenance of status in the U.S. for a minimum of ten (10) years prior to undergraduate graduation, or who has completed a majority of their K-12 education starting from primary school in the U.S., must be completely exempt from the $70,000 initial and $30,000 subsequent OPT recommendation fees.

Failing to provide this exemption makes the rule an unfair, punitive tax on young people who are culturally American and ready to contribute to the economic prosperity of the United States.

Sincerely,
[Arunkumar Varadhan / or "A Concerned 15-Year U.S. Resident, H-1B Taxpayer, and Proud Parent of an OSU Senior"]

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I respectfully oppose the proposed OPT fees and urge DHS to withdraw the fees.

1. The fee is not tailored to the fraud identified (Sections IV.A, IV.C): The NPRM's fraud evidence concerns shell employers, staged worksites, and sold job letters. Its largest cited investigation identified more than 10,000 students working for suspect employers, against approximately 360,000 OPT and STEM OPT participants in 2024 (194,554 and 165,524), roughly 3 percent. A flat per-student charge on schools does not reach the employers responsible. DHS states it considered employer-side measures, including site visits, training plans, and reporting, and chose a fee because it imposes "minimal administrative burdens on the government." Administrative convenience does not justify a $70,000 burden on the large majority of compliant students.

2. The fee does not fund oversight (Section IV.C): Receipts would be deposited in the Treasury as miscellaneous receipts and not retained by ICE. The fee therefore adds no investigative capacity, even though the NPRM attributes the problem to compliance resources that have not scaled with the program. No explanation was given on how the amount relates to any cost of administering OPT or on its authority for a charge of this size untethered from program costs.

3. The amount is not justified (Section IV.C): DHS benchmarks the fee to H-1B fees, but OPT is temporary practical training tied to a student's field of study, not a cap-subject employment classification. The statement that the fee is "on par" with one or two years of educational costs is offered without supporting data. The fee exceeds typical annual Ph.D. stipends, and the NPRM's own example of pre-completion followed by post-completion OPT totals $100,000 per student.

4. The fee selects on ability to pay, not merit (Section IV.C): DHS acknowledges schools may pass the fee to students. A charge of this size would restrict OPT to students with independent means rather than the "most promising" students DHS says it intends to retain, and would disproportionately exclude funded doctoral researchers.

5. The labor-market rationale does not match the rule's scope (Section IV.B): The cited unemployment rates of 6.1 and 7.5 percent concern computer science and computer engineering graduates aged 22 to 27. The NPRM presents no analysis by degree level, yet the fee applies identically to doctoral graduates, a population the cited data do not describe.

6. Reliance interests are inadequately addressed (Section VI): Many current students are enrolled in multi-year programs in reliance on the availability of OPT and the 24-month STEM extension. Protecting only students recommended before the effective date disregards those interests.

Here are my Recommendations: (a) withdraw the proposed fees; (b) address fraud through targeted employer-side enforcement, such as extending STEM OPT training-plan and site-visit requirements to all OPT, requiring E-Verify, and penalizing sham employers; (c) if any fee is retained, set it in proportion to documented administrative costs, exempt students enrolled as of the NPRM's publication date, and exempt doctoral students.
comments.reason: The commenter opposes the proposed OPT fees and urges DHS to withdraw them due to lack of justification and burden on students.

comments.commentText:
I am an international PhD graduate writing in my individual capacity to oppose this proposed rule.

1. The fee amount is disconnected from actual administrative costs. DHS’s own preamble states the $70,000 figure was selected to be “comparable to the fee for H-1B visas” and to deter participation, not calculated from the cost of adjudicating an OPT recommendation. A fee set to suppress program use, rather than to recover processing costs, functions as a tax, which courts have already held DHS lacks authority to impose unilaterally in the H-1B context (State of California v. Mullin; Global Nurse Force v. Trump).

2. DHS has not adequately considered reliance interests. Thousands of students shape multi-year academic and career plans — including choice of degree program, dissertation timeline, and job search strategy — around the existing OPT framework. The proposed rule’s reliance-interest analysis dismisses these as speculative, but OPT eligibility is a foreseeable and relied-upon feature of F-1 status that predates these students’ enrollment decisions.

3. The rule would functionally eliminate OPT access for students at under-resourced and public institutions. DHS’s own analysis estimates that 56% of affected SEVP-certified institutions are small entities. A $70,000 per-student fee is not a marginal cost adjustment; it would force many schools to stop recommending OPT altogether, regardless of a student’s qualifications, which contradicts DHS’s stated goal of preserving OPT for “high-achieving” students.

4. The fee undermines, rather than serves, DHS’s stated fraud-prevention rationale. The proposed rule does not add any fraud-screening mechanism, site-visit requirement, or verification step beyond what STEM OPT already requires. A flat fee paid by the institution does nothing to identify fraudulent employers or sham worksites; it simply prices out legitimate students and schools that lack the funds to pay it, while leaving the underlying fraud vulnerabilities DHS describes in Section IV.is unaddressed by any new enforcement tool.

I urge DHS to withdraw this proposal or, at minimum, substantially reduce the fee to reflect actual administrative cost and to exempt students who have already begun a course of study in reliance on current OPT rules.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes the proposed rule, arguing the fee is excessive, punitive, and harms students and institutions.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Comment on the Proposed OPT Fees

I am an international PhD student currently pursuing my doctoral degree in the United States, and I strongly oppose the proposed $70,000 initial and $30,000 subsequent Optional Practical Training (OPT) fees. I respectfully urge the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) to withdraw this proposal.

As an international doctoral student, I have dedicated years of my life to advanced education, research, and developing specialized skills in the United States. Like many other international students, I view OPT as an important opportunity to apply my academic training, contribute to the U.S. workforce, and continue participating in research and innovation after graduation.

1. Disproportionate financial burden on international students

A $70,000 OPT fee would create an extraordinary financial barrier for students like me. PhD students often spend several years completing their degrees while living on limited stipends or research assistantships. Even students who have demonstrated academic excellence, contributed to scientific research, and followed all immigration requirements may be unable to afford such a fee.

Access to professional opportunities should be based on qualifications, skills, and compliance with immigration regulations, not on an individual's financial resources.

2. Negative consequences for research and innovation

International PhD students contribute to American universities through research, teaching, publications, and scientific advancement. Many pursue doctoral degrees with the expectation that they may have an opportunity to gain practical experience in their fields after graduation.

Making OPT financially inaccessible could discourage talented researchers from continuing their careers in the United States. This could negatively affect universities, research institutions, employers, and the country's ability to attract and retain highly skilled talent.

3. High fees do not necessarily prevent fraud

I understand the importance of maintaining the integrity of immigration programs and preventing fraudulent employment arrangements. However, imposing extremely high fees on all international students does not directly address misconduct by fraudulent employers.

A student's ability to pay $70,000 does not demonstrate honesty, qualifications, or compliance with immigration rules. Instead of creating financial barriers for legitimate students, DHS should prioritize targeted employer verification, stronger oversight, and enforcement against individuals or organizations involved in fraud.

4. Inadequate consideration of economic and personal consequences

The proposed fees could have consequences beyond the immediate financial burden on students. International students make significant investments in American education and often plan their academic and professional futures years in advance.

For doctoral students in particular, completing a PhD requires a long-term commitment. Dramatically changing access to post-graduation employment opportunities could undermine those plans and create substantial uncertainty for students who have already invested years in their education.

I am also concerned that the proposed rule may not adequately account for the broader economic benefits of international graduates, including their contributions to research, innovation, taxes, and local communities.

5. Need for more reasonable alternatives

I respectfully encourage DHS to consider less burdensome and more targeted alternatives, including enhanced employer oversight, improved compliance monitoring, and stronger enforcement against fraudulent activities.

These measures would more directly address program integrity concerns without unfairly restricting opportunities for students who have complied with the law and invested in their education.

Conclusion

As an international PhD student, I am deeply concerned that this proposal would make years of academic dedication and research less meaningful by placing an unreasonable financial barrier between graduation and professional development.

International doctoral students come to the United States to learn, conduct research, contribute to their fields, and participate in the country's scientific and economic progress. Policies should protect the integrity of immigration programs without unnecessarily excluding talented and law-abiding students.

I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw the proposed OPT fee rule and pursue fair, evidence-based alternatives that address fraud while preserving legitimate educational and professional opportunities.

Thank you for considering my comment.
comments.reason: The commenter strongly opposes the proposed OPT fees and urges DHS to withdraw the proposal.

comments.commentText:
Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, Optional Practical Training Fees, 91 FR 64566 (Oct. 8, 2026)

I am writing on behalf of myself and my friends, international graduates who came to this country to study, worked hard through our degrees, and are now on Optional Practical Training, trying to build honest lives doing the work we trained for.

We left our homes and families behind. We paid our tuition. We followed every rule. OPT is the one bridge that lets us use what we studied in real jobs, while we search for a longer future here. It is not a shortcut. It is the reward for years of sacrifice, and for many of us, it is the only hope we have of staying close to the life we have worked so hard to build.

I respectfully ask DHS to withdraw the proposed fees of $70,000 for a first OPT recommendation and $30,000 for each later recommendation, including a STEM extension. Even though the fees would be paid by schools, DHS itself notes that schools could pass the cost to students, to all students, or to employers. At this level, many schools could simply stop recommending OPT. Employers could simply stop considering us.

That would not just raise a cost. It would shut the door on graduates who did everything right, and it would tell thousands of young people who believed in this country that their dreams are no longer welcome here. Please do not take that bridge away. Please keep OPT accessible for every graduate who earned it.

Thank you for considering this comment.
comments.reason: The commenter asks DHS to withdraw the proposed OPT fees, arguing they harm students and shut doors for graduates.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am an F-1 international student pursuing a doctoral degree in the United States. I write to oppose the proposed fees for Optional Practical Training recommendations under Docket ICEB-2026-0100: $70,000 for an initial OPT recommendation and $30,000 for each subsequent recommendation, including STEM OPT extensions.

OPT is not a bonus or a loophole. It is the only structured bridge between completing a US degree and beginning lawful professional employment, and it already operates under strict reporting, employment, and time-limit rules. A $70,000 charge at the point of recommendation would not regulate that bridge — it would price it out of existence for nearly every student, and for the universities asked to collect it.

Fees of this size would not fall on the wealthy alone; they would end OPT for the ordinary students who make up most of the international population, while doing nothing to address program integrity, which existing SEVP reporting already covers. The predictable result is fewer international students choosing US universities, and more US-trained graduates taking their skills to countries that compete directly with the United States.

For these reasons, I urge DHS to withdraw the proposal.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed fees are prohibitive and urges DHS to withdraw the proposal.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Izabelle Viana Costa
comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose this proposed increase in OPT and STEM OPT fees. I believe this policy could actually hurt the U.S. labor market rather than strengthen it. International students spend years studying and training at American universities, contributing to research, innovation, and the development of knowledge. Many of us are already part of the workforce, even before graduation, helping advance projects and institutions that benefit the United States.

Making it extremely expensive for international graduates to stay and work here could push talented people to take their skills elsewhere. This would be a loss not only for students, but also for American universities, research institutions, companies, and the economy as a whole. Other countries would be more than willing to welcome the scientists, engineers, and professionals that the United States has invested years in educating. In other words, this policy could accelerate a brain drain that ultimately benefits America's competitors.

As a Ph.D. student at an American university, I see firsthand how much international students contribute to the academic and research community. We are not just coming here to receive an education; we are actively helping build the scientific and technological future of this country. It makes little sense to invest in educating talented people and then create financial barriers that force them to leave. The United States should be making it easier to retain the talent it helps develop, not pushing that talent away.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed fee increase harms the U.S. labor market and causes brain drain.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText: I am a professor at a four-year college. Many of my students are international, and they bring so much to our campus community: varied perspectives, new languages, intelligence, enthusiasm, warmth, work ethic, and, crucially, tuition dollars that allow us to subsidize the cost of attendance for poorer American students. Requiring them to pay $70,000--a 15,000% increase!--to stay for a year after graduation for Optional Practical Training is absurd. International students are an asset to our country, not competition and not a drain. Their presence in our workforce for a mere year sows the seeds of international cooperation and healthy foreign policy for our country. I urge you: reject this vindictive legislation, and stop pillaging US higher ed.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the high OPT fee is absurd and urges DHS to reject the rule.

I am respectfully submitting this comment in opposition to the proposed rule, which would require SEVP-enrolled schools to pay $70,000 before an F-1 student's first OPT authorization and another $30,000 for each subsequent extension. I am a student at a mid-sized Northeastern university that has a large population of international students. While I am an American citizen myself, many of my friends, coworkers, classmates, and professors are all here on F-1 visas or in the case of my professors, would not be here if it was not for their OPT. Nothing has benefitted my education more than learning from and with people from all over the world. My concern is that the rule's fee levels are not supported by the evidence in the record, impose large costs on people that have followed the rules, and do not match the fraud problem that the DHS describes. I want the DHS to consider three questions before finalizing any rule.

1. What is the evidence that OPT causes displacement of US workers?
The proposed rule justifies the fees as protection for US workers but it should identify evidence that OPT participation causes displacement and on what scale this displacement happens. A study of ICE data on STEM OPT participants from 2008 to 2016, by a former Federal Reserve economist found no evidence that OPT reduces job opportunities for U.S. workers. It found that US workers are more likely to turn to international student workers when US workers were scarce. Additionally, the number of international students approved for STEM OPT is negatively correlated with measures of unemployment rate among US STEM workers (i.e. if there are less STEM US workers to be hired, more international students will be approved for OPT to fill that gap). The number of STEM international students approved for OPT is extremely low, ranging as low as one half of one percent (Zavodny). DHS's own figures show the scale of the program: around 194,554 OPT and 95,384 STEM OPT authorizations with 2024 start dates. That is a very small share of a U.S. labor force of around 170 million. I am curious where DHS is finding studies that show that OPT is causing job displacement, and how large that affect is for American workers and why $70,000 fee per student is the amount that was come to to offset that affect.

2. Has DHS weighed the US jobs that international students support?
An analysis should count the jobs and economic activity that international students create, not only the jobs they are assumed to take. International students contributed $55 billion to the US economy in 2024 according to the US department of commerce, mainly through tuition and living expenses(Open Doors,US Department of State). Their spending supported 355,000 jobs in 2024-2025(Marketplace). These contributions are dependent on OPT. In a survey, 54% of current international graduate students and postdocs said that they would not have come to the U.S. if OPT did not exist (STAT). Since we know how high the number is if OPT completely did not exist, before going through with these added fees, DHS should quantify how many fewer students would enroll if OPT carried these fees, and the resulting loss of tuition, spending, and supported jobs and then weigh those losses against any measured benefit to US workers.

3. Why not target fraud directly through verification, site visits, and compliance reporting?
The fraud that DHS describes is real and deserves action. I understand that 10,000 OPT students were found to be working for highly suspect employers. However, 10,000 is roughly 3-4% of 2024 OPT and STEM OPT authorizations, and a fee charged to schools for every student does not distinguish the majority from that minority. The fee also doesn't fund enforcement. As the rule is currently proposed, collections would go to the general treasury rather than to fraud detection. DHS already has tools to target the fraud problem. Including the STEM OPT training plan, the E-Verify requirement for STEM OPT employers, and the authority to conduct employer site visits. I am curious why DHS rejcted easier and less burdensome alternatives before deciding to impose a fee on students that have proved to be following the rules.

While OPT fraud should be found and stopped, the current proposed fees are not tied to any evidence of displacement nor do they fund enforcement and would fall the hardest on students. I ask the DHS to
1. Withdraw the proposed fees.
2. Publish evidence on worker displacement and a full account of the economic contributions at stake
3, Pursue targeted fraud-prevention measures instead
4. At a bare minimum, fully protect students who are enrolled under the current rules and allow them to not pay the fee.

Thank you for considering this comment.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes the proposed rule because the excessive fees harm international students and lack evidence.

Submitted via: www.regulations.gov
To: U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, U.S. Department of Homeland Security
Re: DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, RIN 1653-AB01, Optional Practical Training Fees, 91 FR 64566 (October 8, 2026)
Date: November 6, 2026
Submitted by: An individual staff member at a large public R1 research university in the southern United States

I am a staff member at a large public R1 research university in the South, and I submit this comment in my individual capacity. The views expressed are my own. My work gives me direct knowledge of the offices that would have to make the proposed Optional Practical Training (OPT) fee function in practice: international student services, student billing, financial management, sponsored projects administration, procurement, compliance, and legal counsel. My institution recommends thousands of OPT each year, more than 4,000 over the past two fiscal years.

I urge DHS to withdraw the proposed rule in its entirety and to preserve the Optional Practical Training program. The evidence in this comment shows that the rule:
•imposes administrative costs far larger than DHS's analysis acknowledges;
•cannot be implemented through the financial controls that govern a public university; and
•does nothing to address the employer fraud DHS cites as its justification.

DHS estimates that each payment would take 30 minutes of Designated School Official (DSO) time and 30 minutes of administrator time, plus a one-time 65 hours of rule familiarization (91 FR 64584–85). That estimate is fundamentally wrong. It treats each fee as a single payment. In reality, each fee is a multi-party financial transaction that must be collected, screened, held, approved, remitted, and reconciled across at least five university offices, under deadlines the university does not control.

The proposal requires a university to pay $70,000 before recommending a student for initial OPT and $30,000 before each subsequent recommendation (proposed 8 CFR 214.2(f)(11)(ii), 214.13(i)). DHS invites schools to collect that money from F-1 students, from all students, from employers, or from other parties (91 FR 64575, 64578). A university that does so becomes a collection agent for the federal government, with all of the cost and none of the control.
Research universities know exactly what that work costs, because they perform a version of it every day in sponsored projects administration. Measured against that benchmark, two conclusions are unavoidable:

•The required infrastructure is substantial, and DHS has not counted any of it. Managing multi-party outside money under audit demands routing and approval, written agreements, restricted accounts, compliance screening, reconciliation, collections, correction procedures, and closeout. DHS's analysis accounts for none of this work.
•The OPT fee would be harder to administer than sponsored projects, not easier. Every feature that makes sponsored funding manageable (a deliverable the university controls, cost recovery that pays for the administration, and predictable refund and closeout rules) is absent from the fee.
ached file(s)

DHS's analysis treats the OPT fee as a one-hour transaction. For a public research university, it would be a new, permanent, unfunded financial operation: multi-party collections, restricted accounting, foreign-source compliance, legal agreements, high-dollar disbursement approvals, and discretionary refunds, all run against regulatory deadlines the university does not control. Experience administering sponsored projects shows exactly what that work costs. The OPT fee would demand all of it, without the deliverable, the cost recovery, or the predictable rules that make sponsored projects administration workable.

I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw the proposed rule in its entirety and to work with institutions on targeted measures that address actual misconduct while preserving Optional Practical Training.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
This is a comment in opposition to the proposed rule from the Department of Homeland Security “Optional Practical Training Fees” (Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100).

Fee Amounts and Legal Authority:
This proposed rule disguises a tax as a fee. This is much like the H-1B “fee” that has been blocked by multiple judges (source: https://www.reuters.com/legal/government/second-judge-blocks-trumps-100000-fee-new-h-1b-worker-visas-2026-10-01/). The USCIS Policy Manual describes how a fee may be set and what it may be used for, such as “to recover the full cost” of a service, but this proposed rule does not explain how the $70,000 and $30,000 fees are connected to the cost of the I-765 service, particularly when the regular filing fee incurred by the petitioner is still in place (see: https://www.uscis.gov/policy-manual/volume-1-part-b-chapter-3). A fee goes toward recuperating the cost of the process and to fund the department that collects the fee, yet these “fees” are to be deposited in the U.S. Treasury as a miscellaneous receipt. Thus, this is a tax and not a fee, which means it could only be implemented by Congress and not through the rulemaking process. The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) does not have the legal authority to implement these optional practical training (OPT) “fees.”

There is also a question of whether it would be legal for Designated School Officials (DSO) to not recommend a student for OPT if the "fee" could not be paid. Per the Code of Federal Regulations (CFR), "practical training may be authorized to an F-1 student who has been lawfully enrolled on a full -time basis, in an approved SEVP-certified college, university, conservatory, or seminary for one full academic year" and " may apply to USCIS for authorization for temporary employment for optional practical training directly related to the student's major area of study" (see: 8 CFR 214.2(f)(10)). When a DSO recommends OPT in SEVIS, they are confirming that a student meets these basic qualifications. If a student meets these qualifications but cannot pay the fee, and does not have an employer willing to pay the fee, would the student's school be required to pay the fee so that they can recommend the qualified student for OPT? Such a requirement would quickly bankrupt a large swath of the U.S. higher education system and is an unreasonable burden to place on the American public, particularly through rulemaking.

Economic Impacts:
If implemented, this "fee" would negatively impact the financial health of higher education institutions and their communities. Not only will the "fee" itself impact higher education institutions, but also it is highly likely that fewer international students will attend school in the United States if the pathway to training opportunities is limited in this way. Thus, enrollment at U.S. higher education institutions will fall, decreasing revenue in a time when schools are already struggling to maintain enrollment and revenue. I work as a DSO at an institution where over half of our international students, who make up over one third of our student body, apply for post-completion OPT. These students tell me the opportunity to train in their field of study after graduation is a one of the major factors in choosing to study at my institution. This trend is not unique to my institution (see: https://ifp.org/wp-content/uploads/26-10-06-International-Student-Survey-on-OPT-and-Experiential-Learning.pdf). If these students were to choose other destinations over our school, the school itself may be unable to survive.

Effectiveness in Addressing Fraud:
The supposed purpose of implementing these “fees” is to combat fraud, and yet the details of how the two are connected is vague at best. The idea seems to be that legitimate students will be rich enough to afford this fee, but I see no evidence that the only legitimate students are the rich ones. Furthermore, the “fee” money does not go to USCIS, the department responsible for investigating immigration fraud. "Fee" money deposited into the Treasury as a miscellaneous receipt, and there are no details about oversight for how the funds would be used.

Less Burdensome Alternatives Exist That Would Address DHS’s Concerns:
F-1 students on pre-completion, post-completion, or STEM OPT must report their employment information through the Student and Exchange Visitor Information System (SEVIS), providing DHS with timely and detailed information about where and for whom students are working. To address concerns about fraud, DHS could make better use of this system such as conducting site visits, improving SEVIS to collect information on remote employment to avoid confusion about work addresses, or perform other investigations or updates.

I recommend that DHS rescind the proposed rule "“Optional Practical Training Fees" in its entirety.

To: U.S. Department of Homeland Security, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, Student and Exchange Visitor Program (SEVP)
Re: Comment on the Notice of Proposed Rulemaking, “Optional Practical Training Fees,” published October 8, 2026 (Federal Register document 2026-20660)
Submitted by: University of Lynchburg, Lynchburg, Virginia
The University of Lynchburg respectfully submits this comment on the Notice of Proposed Rulemaking published by the U.S. Department of Homeland Security (DHS) on October 8, 2026, which would require SEVP-certified schools to pay a fee of $70,000 before recommending an F-1 student for initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) and $30,000 for each subsequent recommendation, including the STEM OPT extension. For a single student who completes both, the total reaches $100,000.
The University of Lynchburg is a private university in central Virginia enrolling about 2,360 undergraduate and graduate students. International students are a growing and valued part of our community. We share DHS’s stated goals of preventing fraud and abuse, protecting the integrity of the immigration system and protecting U.S. workers. However, we believe the proposed fees are disproportionate to those goals and would, in practice, close OPT to most students at institutions like ours. We urge DHS to reconsider the proposed fee schedule in favor of targeted oversight measures that preserve the educational purpose of practical training.
The University of Lynchburg respectfully requests that DHS:
Withdraw or substantially revise the fee schedule. Any fee should reflect the actual administrative cost of reviewing and overseeing OPT, consistent with other immigration benefit fees.
Address fraud and abuse through targeted oversight. Strengthen employer verification, SEVIS reporting checks, and SEVP compliance reviews, focused on the bad actors DHS has identified, rather than imposing a cost on every student and school.
Conduct a full economic and educational impact analysis. Assess the effects on international enrollment, small and tuition-dependent institutions, research, employers and regional economies before finalizing any rule.
Protect small institutions and students with financial need. If a fee is retained, adopt reduced or tiered fees for small institutions, need-based waivers, and exemptions for public-interest, educational, health care and research fields.
Protect currently enrolled students. Exempt students who enrolled before any final rule takes effect, since they made their decisions based on the rules in place at the time.
Conclusion
The University of Lynchburg supports a secure, well-administered F-1 program and stands ready to work with DHS on measures that protect its integrity. We urge DHS to pursue those goals in a way that keeps Optional Practical Training open to qualified students, sustains the institutions that educate them, and preserves the benefits they bring to U.S. communities. Thank you for considering our comment.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose this proposed rule and request its withdrawal in full. OPT participation should be free of charge. I request a $0 participation fee for initial OPT, subsequent OPT, and STEM OPT extensions, with no charge shifted to students, educational institutions, or employers. This comment concerns the proposed new participation fees; existing USCIS filing fees are separate.

1. Ability to pay does not establish compliance (sections IV.A-C and V.A).

The proposed $70,000 initial fee and $30,000 subsequent fee would make access depend on financial resources. A compliant student at an institution with a limited budget could lose access, while a well-funded participant presenting greater compliance risks could remain eligible. DHS should provide evidence that these amounts distinguish legitimate training from fraud. Reducing participation alone does not demonstrate improved program integrity.

2. The payments would not directly fund oversight (section IV.C).

The notice states that receipts would enter the Treasury and would not be retained by ICE or earmarked for OPT oversight. Payment therefore would not automatically provide additional investigators or compliance resources. Because DHS relies on deterrence, it should demonstrate why these amounts are necessary, how legitimate participation would be protected, and why targeted enforcement without a participation charge would be inadequate.

3. Charging institutions still burdens students and education (sections V.A and VII).

Schools may ration recommendations, pass costs to students or employers, increase other charges, or redirect resources from teaching and research. For illustration, 100 initial recommendations would require $7 million at the proposed rate. Identifying the school as the formal payer does not remove the economic burden. DHS should assess the effects across institutions with different budgets and students with different financial circumstances. Educational access should depend on eligibility and compliance, rather than wealth.

4. Fraud should be addressed through targeted enforcement (sections IV.A and IV.C).

DHS should evaluate employer verification, risk-based audits, checks for fabricated employment or implausible worksites, clearer guidance for designated school officials, and enforcement against proven violations with appropriate procedural protections. Existing SEVP guidance already addresses documenting the relationship between employment and a student's field of study. Improving verification would address misconduct more directly than charging every legitimate participant. Oversight should use existing legally available resources and, where necessary, additional congressional appropriations.

5. Worker protection requires analysis of actual employment practices (sections IV.B and VII.A).

DHS should assess wage violations, displacement, discriminatory recruitment, and sham training arrangements. STEM OPT already includes compensation safeguards and employer attestations concerning replacement of U.S. workers. The agency should evaluate compliance and identify specific gaps. It should also assess whether employer-financed participation fees could increase graduates' dependence on employers or discourage reporting abuse.

A complete economic analysis should examine lost training, disrupted research, recruitment difficulties, financing burdens, and opportunities moving abroad. DHS should not assume that eliminating one OPT opportunity necessarily creates an equivalent opportunity for a U.S. worker.

6. Existing commitments deserve meaningful consideration (sections V.C and VI).

Students and institutions may have made multiyear educational and financial commitments under the existing framework. A proposed 60-day transition cannot necessarily allow them to recover those commitments or make alternative arrangements. DHS should meaningfully assess reliance interests, including those of enrolled students and participants planning eligible extensions.

7. DHS should explain its authority and respond to alternatives (section III.A).

DHS should identify the specific statutory delegation authorizing this deterrent payment and explain how its amounts and conditions fit that authority. Under 5 U.S.C. 553(c) and 706(2)(A), (C), relevant public submissions and the requirements of lawful, reasoned agency action matter. DHS should provide a reasoned response to fee-free enforcement alternatives and the concerns raised here.

I request withdrawal of proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i) and the related payment conditions in 8 CFR 214.2(f)(11). I also oppose a smaller substitute participation fee or a fresh initial charge at each higher educational level. Preserve legitimate OPT participation without a new charge and fund necessary oversight through lawful public resources.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Laura Georgi
comments.commentText:
Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100
I am a retired US-born STEM worker. I am acutely aware of the potential reduction in salaries and job opportunities with competition from international students. You need to provide a proper quantitative analysis of the impact. What you have provided is almost completely worthless. The “source” for your employment numbers is a Presidential proclamation, which provides no citations for its numbers, no agency reports, no independent third party analysis. The President is a liar and has surrounded himself with liars. The administration has no credibility. If a student had turned in something like this I would have asked them to fix it and resubmit if not failed them outright.
Please provide properly sourced data on the impact of immigrants on STEM employment opportunities and salaries. While it is facile to conclude that every position an immigrant takes is one less job for a US worker, it is also a fact that immigrants increased the size and vigor of our scientific enterprise. It isn’t necessarily a zero-sum situation; we might all have pie if we make a bigger pie. Sound data could show which of, and to what extent, the two alternatives prevail.
Regardless, I do not approve of the proposed massively inflated OPT fee, for a number of reasons.
First, I question whether you have the authority to impose them. This fee goes beyond prescribing “conditions” for alien admission. Congress has the power to tax. At least one judge has ruled that your similarly gargantuan H-1B visa fee amounts to an illegal tax. This is no different. Speaking of which, you justify the size of the proposed OPT fee based on your proposed massive H-1B fee. If the H-1B fee increase fails (and I believe it currently is blocked) then the OPT fee would be massively disproportionate.
In another filing you attempted to justify the proposed H-1B visa fee as offsetting administrative costs by incorporating some fairly tangential expenses, so I was surprised that here you state that the OPT fees will go into the Treasury’s general fund and you won’t have any claim to them because you lack the legal authority. On the other hand, you repeatedly state that “ without the fees proposed in this rule, (ICE) cannot operate OPT consistent with its focus on preventing fraud and may shut down the program entirely.”
Your justifications for your proposed OPT fees make very little sense. The only likely consequence of the fee increase, and I suspect your true reason for it, is fewer students participating in the program. A smaller program would of course be easier for you to administer and simplify enforcement.
Your stated expectations of what the schools “would” do in response to the fee increase make no sense to me (and I notice that later in the document you say schools merely “may” take those actions). HOW does the higher fee “ensure that only highly qualified eligible F-1 students participate”? HOW does the fee “ensure that schools, students, and employers participate in OPT for its intended purpose” and why is it “necessary” for achieving that purpose? is there really no other way? HOW does the fee “encourage schools to ensure that OPT opportunities provide genuine educational value”? WHY do you “anticipate that schools will consider adopting internal policies and procedures that prioritize quality and compliance over quantity of participants”? It’s likely to reduce quantity, but wouldn’t schools prioritize participants whose defining quality lies in ability to pay? you explicitly say you aren’t restricting how the schools source the funds as long as it’s legal.
Your goal is to reduce fraud, and you propose this fee increase as a quick and easy way to do so, in lieu of actually enforcing current regulations. How does this reduce fraud? Apart from reducing the supply of OPT participants, how does this fee ensure that employers aren’t using them to replace US workers, and that conditions of employment are comparable? How does this prevent bypassing of prevailing wage determinations? How does the fee prevent false employment documents? The fraud examples you cite were revealed by making site visits to employers.
The fee cannot possibly eliminate the need for enforcement activity. You really need to police the employers. You have an obscenely huge budget that you are wasting on for-profit detention centers, robot dogs, crowd-control weapons, and illegal political campaign ads. The funds could be better spent.
Is the fee increase even needed today to reduce participation in OPT? Given how your agents have abused international students and visitors and the damage this administration has done to our scientific research enterprise, foreign students are already avoiding us. Even native born scientists are bailing, and the ones who can find billets in other countries are of course our very best. The damage to our country’s future prosperity and strength are incalculable.
