comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am an F-1 student in my last year of a PhD program in applied mathematics. I respectfully oppose the proposed fee and ask DHS
to withdraw it, for the reasons below.

First, Each fraud example in Section IV.A of the proposed rule concerns employers: fabricated offer letters, shell companies, "staged worksites" at IT services firms, and "phantom employees" at residential addresses (91 FR 64570-64571). None describes an accredited university knowingly recommending an ineligible student, yet the school is the only party the rule regulates. DHS already runs employer-side safeguards for STEM OPT (E-Verify, a signed training plan, site visits) and admits it declined to extend them to all OPT because they "may require substantial time and resources" (64576). Agency convenience does not make a fee better targeted. DHS should withdraw the fee and instead extend the STEM OPT employer safeguards to all post-completion OPT, a program it already administers for roughly 95,000 STEM authorizations a year (64583).

Second, DHS states the rule "does not need to define which OPT experiences provide genuine educational value" and expects schools to recommend only "the most promising students" (64574-64575). Nothing in current regulations lets a DSO rank students by promise; the DSO confirms eligibility. The rule creates a merit gate, hands it to more than 2,000 institutions, and supplies no standard. The criterion that will fill that vacuum is money: a school deciding whom to fund will favor students who can repay the fee or whose employers will, which means the highest-paid industry placements. Students headed to research, nonprofits, public agencies, clinics or startups lose first. That selection has nothing to do with fraud risk and everything to do with wealth and field, and because every student the rule reaches is a foreign national, it falls entirely along national-origin lines, a consequence the proposal does not analyze. Any school-side measure must come with published eligibility standards, a written decision and an administrative appeal; a fee with none of those is arbitrary and should be withdrawn.

The rule contradicts itself on cost, federalism and its own numbers. The UMRA section says the rule "would not result in" a $100 million expenditure and, in the next paragraph, that it "exceeds the $100 million expenditure threshold" (64597). The federalism section finds no "substantial direct compliance costs on State and local governments" (64598) while 1,044 of the 2,478 affected schools are state-run (64592), and DHS "did not consult with elected representatives of
the affected State, local, and tribal governments" (64597). The Paperwork Reduction Act section counts 226,200 annual responses (64598); footnote 143 counts 289,938. Section IV.B cites 165,524 STEM OPT participants for 2024 (64573); the economic analysis uses 95,384 (64583). The reliance section says "only about 20 percent of F-1 nonimmigrants participated in OPT in 2024" to show students do not depend on it (64578), counting every enrolled student rather than graduates, while the same rule says OPT growth has "exponentially outpaced" DHS's capacity (64571) and the program is "flooded with participants" (64570); it cannot be both marginal and a flood. DHS should reconcile these statements, conduct the state consultation it admits it skipped, and publish a corrected analysis with the underlying data before proceeding.

Every example in Section IV.A is an IT consulting or staffing worksite. DHS offers no instance of a PhD graduate, a postdoctoral researcher or a research university involved in OPT fraud. A fee that does not distinguish a national-laboratory postdoc from a "phantom employee" at a residential address (64571) is not "targeted" (64576). At minimum, DHS should exempt doctoral graduates, pre-completion OPT and employment with H-1B cap-exempt institutions, and grandfather every student enrolled on the effective date.

Alternative solutions exist apart for the ones suggested. For example, Match SEVIS employer names and EINs against IRS and state business registrations and hold any employer with no filings. Shell companies with "no employees present" and "missing
employment records" (64571) fail this check at no cost to students or schools. Pilot any new measure first in the sector DHS identifies (IT services and staffing firms), publish results after one year, and expand only with data. DHS calls the fee a "first step" and a "measured approach" that will produce "valuable data" (64576); a pilot is what that language describes.

I ask DHS to publish the underlying data for Tables 2-17, which appear only as images, and the per-institution fee analysis the rule says it ran in Python, so that the public can check the figures.

I request that DHS withdraw the proposed fee. Any integrity measure that follows should act on employers, where the evidence of abuse lies. Thank you for considering this comment.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Re: Optional Practical Training Fees — Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100

I am an international student enrolled in a graduate program in the United States. I am writing to express my opposition to the proposed Optional Practical Training fees and to respectfully request that DHS withdraw this proposal.

First, the fees proposed in Section V.A would create a substantial financial barrier to legitimate practical training. Requiring schools to pay $70,000 for an initial OPT recommendation and $30,000 for subsequent OPT recommendations could make participation inaccessible even to students who satisfy every eligibility requirement. A school may decline to recommend a qualified student simply because it cannot afford the fee. If schools pass these costs on to students, access could depend on personal financial resources. Neither a university’s budget nor a student’s ability to pay reliably measures academic merit, compliance, or the educational value of a training opportunity.

Second, I am concerned that the transition provisions and reliance analysis in Sections V.C and VI do not adequately account for currently enrolled students. Graduate education requires substantial commitments of time, resources, and planning. Students may reasonably consider the availability of lawful, degree-related practical training when choosing their educational programs. OPT does not need to be the sole reason for that decision to be an important consideration. A 60-day transition after publication of a final rule would provide little opportunity for students already pursuing their degrees to adjust their plans. DHS should give greater weight to these existing commitments and preserve access under the current framework for students already enrolled.

Third, I support efforts to prevent fraud and ensure that OPT serves its intended purpose. However, the approach described in Sections IV.A and IV.C does not establish why a substantial financial requirement would reliably distinguish legitimate participation from abuse. An institution’s ability to pay does not demonstrate that a training opportunity is genuine, and an inability to pay does not indicate misconduct. DHS should prioritize measures directly connected to compliance, including verification of employers and training activities, targeted investigations, and enforcement against documented violations. The agency should also explain why those approaches would be insufficient before imposing such substantial costs on compliant participants.

Fourth, the proposal gives insufficient weight to the educational value of practical training. For graduate students, opportunities to apply advanced coursework and research methods in professional settings can deepen understanding and develop skills that classroom instruction alone cannot fully provide. The value of such training cannot reasonably be measured only by whether a student, school, or employer can afford the proposed fee. Making these opportunities financially inaccessible would weaken an important connection between academic study and practical experience.

I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw the proposed fees and pursue targeted, evidence-based measures that address misconduct while preserving access to legitimate practical training. Any further proposal should meaningfully account for currently enrolled students and the educational consequences of restricting their opportunities.

Thank you for considering my comment.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes the proposed OPT fees, stating they create financial barriers for students and universities.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Dear Department of Homeland Security Officials,
As a current STEM OPT beneficiary, I am writing to submit formal comments strongly opposing the proposed rule titled Optional Practical Training Fees, published on October 8, 2026. The proposal to establish a $70,000 fee for initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) recommendations alongside an additional $30,000 fee for subsequent authorizations (such as the 24-month STEM OPT extension), totaling up to $100,000 per student, is economically punitive, arbitrary, and directly contrary to the national economic and technological interests of the United States.
While DHS suggests that higher education institutions are nominal payees, the agency explicitly acknowledges that colleges and universities will inevitably pass these obligations onto international students or prospective employers. Imposing $100,000 in regulatory fees on recent graduates, individuals who have already contributed substantial out-of-pocket tuition to American universities, places an impossible financial burden on early-career professionals.
Most entry-level roles across STEM, business, and humanities do not offer compensation packages capable of absorbing a $70,000 to $100,000 administrative surcharge in addition to baseline living expenses and educational debt.
Tying basic post-graduation training authorization to six-figure fees effectively transforms OPT into a program accessible exclusively to personal wealth, eliminating merit-based career mobility.
A $70,000–$100,000 fee bears no statutory or rational relationship to the actual administrative cost incurred by the Student and Exchange Visitor Program (SEVP) to issue an automated I-20 recommendation in the SEVIS database. Under federal fee-setting statutes, fees must reflect reasonable agency service costs rather than serving as a prohibitive tax designed to suppress lawful participation.
The proposed fees will dismantle the U.S. Higher Education global advantage since international students contribute tens of millions of dollars annually to the U.S. economy, cross-subsidizing domestic research facilities, laboratories, and financial aid. Surveys consistently indicate that practical training pathways (OPT and STEM OPT) are a primary reason global talent chooses U.S. universities over competitors in countries such as the UK, Canada, Australia, and the EU.
Enacting a $100,000 surcharge signals to international scholars that U.S. academic degrees lead into a closed professional door. The resulting collapse in international enrollment will destabilize university operating budgets, impair graduate-level research departments, and compel the elimination of academic programs across both public and private institutions.
OPT functions as the primary bridge connecting U.S.-trained engineers, scientists, medical researchers, and software architects to the domestic workforce. Thus, this proposal will have catastrophic harms to the American innovation ecosystem and labor market.
Critical domestic industries, including artificial intelligence, semiconductors, biotechnology, clean energy, and sustainability, already experience structural technical talent shortages. Imposing prohibitive surcharges will sever this vital pipeline. Employers, particularly startups, mid-sized companies, and academic labs, cannot pay hundreds of thousands of dollars in entry-level visa costs, forcing companies to outsource technical roles abroad or relocate R&D operations to countries with coherent skilled immigration policies.
Far from protecting domestic workers, expelling U.S.- educated high-skilled graduates shrinks the overall economic pie, depresses tax revenues, and decreases entrepreneurship activities that create secondary employment for Americans.
The proposed $70,000 and $30,000 fee structure does not represent a good-faith cost recovery for government services; it operates as a de facto ban on post-completion practical training. For these reasons, I urge the Department of Homeland Security to immediately withdraw this proposed rule in its entirety.

Sincerely,

ACC
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed OPT fees are economically punitive, financially burdensome, and harm international students.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Claudia Sandoval
comments.commentText:
**RE: Public Comment on Proposed Rule – Optional Practical Training Fees**
**Docket No.: ICEB-2026-0100**

To the Department of Homeland Security:

I respectfully oppose the proposed $70,000 initial fee and $30,000 subsequent fee for Optional Practical Training (OPT).

I understand the government's responsibility to prevent immigration fraud, protect American workers, and maintain the integrity of the immigration system. However, I believe the proposed fees are excessively high, disproportionate, and likely to produce consequences that conflict with the educational and economic purposes of the F-1 student visa program.

**1. Disproportionate financial burden on international students and their families**

Many international students come to the United States with limited financial resources. Their families make substantial sacrifices to finance tuition, housing, insurance, and other educational expenses.

A $70,000 OPT fee could make practical training financially inaccessible, particularly for students who depend on employment after graduation to begin their professional careers and recover their educational investments.

Although the proposed fee is technically payable by educational institutions, DHS explicitly acknowledges that institutions may transfer this financial burden to students or employers. This creates a substantial risk that students will effectively be required to pay an amount that many cannot afford.

**2. Negative consequences for American universities**

Universities could face difficult choices between absorbing enormous additional expenses, transferring costs to students, or limiting their willingness to recommend international students for OPT.

This could make American higher education less attractive to talented international students and undermine the competitiveness of American universities in attracting global talent.

**3. Negative consequences for American employers and the economy**

OPT provides employers with access to graduates who have received education and training in the United States.

An exceptionally high fee could discourage employers from hiring international graduates, including highly qualified individuals who could contribute to American businesses, research institutions, and innovation.

This could result in the loss of valuable talent that American universities have already invested years in educating.

**4. The proposed fee is not sufficiently connected to the individual student's circumstances**

A flat $70,000 fee is imposed regardless of the student's university, field of study, employer, compensation, or individual circumstances.

I respectfully question whether such a substantial financial requirement is reasonably necessary to accomplish the government's stated objectives, particularly when less restrictive and less financially burdensome alternatives could be considered.

Fraud prevention should focus on identifying fraudulent institutions, employers, and applications rather than imposing an enormous financial barrier on legitimate students.

**5. Request for reconsideration and alternative solutions**

I respectfully request that DHS:

- Withdraw the proposed $70,000 and $30,000 fees.
- Consider a substantially lower fee that is reasonably related to actual administrative and enforcement costs.
- Establish exemptions or reduced fees for legitimate students with demonstrated financial hardship.
- Protect students who are already enrolled in degree programs and have made educational and financial commitments based on the existing OPT framework.
- Prevent educational institutions from transferring excessive regulatory costs to individual students.
- Establish clear transition protections for students approaching graduation and those who have already completed their studies.

International students contribute to American universities, research, businesses, and communities. Policies intended to protect the American workforce should not unnecessarily undermine legitimate education, professional development, and economic participation.

I respectfully ask DHS to reconsider this proposal and pursue alternatives that protect American workers while preserving fair and reasonable opportunities for legitimate international students.

Thank you for considering my comments.

Respectfully,

A Concerned Member of the Public

Comment on DHS Proposed Rule: Optional Practical Training Fees
Docket No.: ICEB-2026-0100 | RIN: 1653-AB01

I respectfully request that DHS reconsider the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent OPT fee. I am submitting this anonymous comment as a parent whose family has built its life in the United States and whose older child may be directly affected by this proposal as he moves from college to employment.

My older son was born outside the United States and came here when he was approximately four years old. He has completed essentially his entire school education in the United States. This is the country where he has grown up, attended school, developed friendships, and built his academic future. He is now preparing to enter college.

Although he has spent nearly his entire childhood and education here, his immigration circumstances may make his transition to college and eventually to employment more complicated than that of many of his classmates. Because of the long employment-based immigration backlog affecting our family, we must carefully plan his future immigration status as he approaches the age limit for dependent H-4 status.

If he needs to pursue F-1 status for college, his ability to obtain practical training after graduation may become an important part of his pathway from education into professional employment. Even under the existing system, international students can face additional challenges finding employers willing and able to navigate immigration requirements and employment authorization. Students may have to compete for jobs while employers consider sponsorship requirements, timing, and immigration-related uncertainty.

The proposed OPT fees could make this transition substantially harder. A $70,000 fee for a school's first OPT recommendation and $30,000 for a subsequent recommendation could discourage schools from recommending students for OPT, increase education-related costs, or make employers less willing to consider graduates who need practical training. Even though the proposed fee is payable by the educational institution, the financial burden could ultimately be passed to students, other students, or employers.

For a young person who has studied in the United States for practically his entire life, it is difficult to understand why the opportunity to gain practical experience related to his college education could become subject to such a significant additional financial barrier. He would be investing years in education here, preparing for a professional career, and trying to contribute his skills to the U.S. workforce. The proposed fee could make that path less accessible before he even has an opportunity to demonstrate his abilities.

Our family has also made long-term commitments in the United States. I have worked here for many years, paid taxes, and pursued employment-based permanent residence. My spouse has also rebuilt her professional career after years when her dependent immigration status restricted her ability to work. Our younger child was born in the United States and is a U.S. citizen. Both children have grown up here and consider this their home.

Our older son's situation illustrates the impact that immigration rules can have on children who have spent nearly all their formative years in this country. He did not choose the immigration category under which our family lives, nor did he choose the lengthy employment-based immigration backlog. Yet those circumstances may affect his ability to continue his education and enter the workforce.

I understand DHS's stated objectives of preventing fraud, maintaining program integrity, and protecting U.S. workers. Those objectives are important. However, I respectfully ask DHS to consider whether a fee of this magnitude is a proportionate way to achieve them, particularly when it may restrict legitimate students who have completed their education and want to gain professional experience in their fields.

I request that DHS reconsider the proposed fees and evaluate less burdensome alternatives, such as stronger institutional oversight, targeted compliance reviews, and reasonable administrative fees. If additional fees are considered necessary, they should not be so high that schools become reluctant to recommend legitimate students for OPT or that students and families face costs that make the opportunity practically inaccessible.

Students who have invested years in U.S. education should have a reasonable opportunity to apply what they learned, gain professional experience, and contribute to the U.S. economy. I respectfully request that DHS preserve a practical and financially accessible OPT pathway for legitimate international students.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Patrick Morrison
comments.commentText:
Good evening,

I am writing today to express my deep concern with the proposed rule to require universities to pay $70,000+ to recommend students for Optional Practical Training (OPT). I serve as the Senior International Officer at the University of South Dakota (though please note I am writing in my private capacity as a citizen only), and I can speak firsthand to the devastating impact this will have on US universities' ability to recruit international applicants.

First, it is absurd on its face to expect universities to pay $70,000 to recommend students for OPT. Universities - especially public universities - are in a very tight spot financially right now and I cannot imagine a situation where a public university in South Dakota, for instance, would pay five times a yearly non-resident tuition fee to recommend a single student for OPT. I know many universities whose international offices have an operating budget of less than $70,000 as well, so the idea that this fee would be paid is laughable. Even if one were to find a university willing to pay this amount for a single student, they would only be the most elite of the elite, which would gate-keep a program designed to be available to all students.

Second, even if students were somehow allowed to pay this fee to the university, I can imagine this being very difficult to implement logistically. Public universities, especially, are not set up to facilitate this sort of thing from an accounting and record-keeping perspective. Additionally, if students were able to pay this fee, only the extremely wealthy students from extremely wealthy parts of the world would benefit from this program. In essence, only those that could afford to participate in the program would do so versus those who actually have the merit and the intellect and the drive. If companies were somehow able to pay the fee, very few would, and only the wealthiest companies.

Second, if this rule is implemented, it would have a devastating impact on our ability to recruit talented students to the United States and to our universities. I can point to many studies showing that a significantly large percentage of students would not study in the US if they did not have the chance to participate in OPT. This tracks with the hundreds of conversations I have on this topic every year with students and families. Simply put, a key factor in calculating return on investment of a US degree is the ability for students to understand the American workplace and gain hands-on experience before returning home. If we cut off this opportunity, the ROI simply isn't there for most students and we will lose them to countries like Australia with a stay back option or lose them to low cost of attendance countries like China.

In South Dakota, we have been able to offset declining domestic enrollment with qualified international students that pay out-of-state tuition. These students bring vital revenue to our campuses to maintain high-quality and low-cost public education for the citizens of South Dakota. I would estimate that we would see a 60-70% decline in international enrollment, which would not be able to be made up through the domestic population in South Dakota. Since these students are concentrated in STEM fields, we would likely see program and job cuts across our public education system and certainly within the international offices themselves. In short, our public education system in South Dakota would become poorer, smaller, less cutting-edge, and Americans would lose their jobs.

I strongly recommend that this rule be withdrawn. There are ways to address the concerns of Homeland Security regarding OPT "fraud" - which while a very, very small percentage of overall program does exist - without destroying this program, and by extension international education in the United States.

Sincerely,

Patrick Morrison
Vermillion, South Dakota
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed OPT fees are absurdly high and will devastate university recruitment and operations.

Prospective students may also choose other countries if they cannot reasonably anticipate access to practical training after completing their degrees.

I recognize the importance of preventing fraud and protecting U.S. workers. However, a high, broadly applied fee does not itself distinguish legitimate training from abusive arrangements. A compliant student and institution would face the same financial barrier regardless of the quality of the training opportunity. DHS should explain, with evidence, why these particular fee amounts are necessary and how they would address misconduct more effectively than targeted oversight and enforcement.

Before proceeding, DHS should examine how the proposal would affect participation across income levels, institution types, and employment sectors. Its analysis should account for opportunities that disappear because a school, student, or employer cannot pay, rather than focusing only on fees collected. It should also evaluate potential consequences for university research, international enrollment, and employers that collaborate with U.S. institutions.
The proposal raises particular concerns for students already enrolled. These students have committed years to their education under an existing framework for practical training. Even if a new fee applies only to future recommendations, it could substantially disrupt the educational and professional plans of students who are already well into their degrees.

I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw the proposed fee structure. If additional resources are needed to administer and oversee OPT, DHS should consider proportionate fees supported by a transparent accounting of program costs, alongside targeted measures addressing documented misconduct. Any changes should include meaningful protections for currently enrolled students and avoid making legitimate practical training available only to those with substantial financial resources.

The United States benefits when researchers educated here can apply their training and contribute to its scientific and technological progress. OPT policy should preserve that opportunity while addressing specific, demonstrated problems.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed OPT fees will make practical training inaccessible and harm students and research.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I oppose the proposed OPT fees and request that DHS withdraw proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i) and the related payment requirements in 8 CFR 214.2(f)(11). The fees could harm American research, employers, workers, and investments in U.S. education.

1. Proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)(1)–(2) would reduce the return on American investment in education and research.

The proposed $70,000 initial fee and $30,000 subsequent fee could prevent qualified graduates from applying their U.S. education through practical training. American universities and research institutions invest faculty time, laboratory resources, and institutional support in developing these graduates. Making practical training financially inaccessible risks reducing the domestic return on that investment and encouraging graduates to contribute their skills to competing countries.

DHS should evaluate the consequences for research continuity, commercialization, and access to specialized expertise. This assessment should address fields such as biomedical research and engineering that require lengthy training and sustained collaboration.

2. Proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)(1)–(2) could harm American workers on collaborative research and development teams.

Research and development often depends on teams whose members contribute complementary technical skills. Preventing a qualified graduate from participating in practical training could leave a skills gap that delays projects and reduces the productivity of American colleagues. In biomedical research, expertise in experimental models, data analysis, and disease mechanisms may develop over years and be difficult to replace during an ongoing project.

DHS should assess whether reduced access to specialized graduates would delay research, weaken business expansion, or limit opportunities for American workers on the same teams. Before assuming that excluding an OPT participant creates a corresponding opportunity for a U.S. worker, the agency should examine the availability of candidates with equivalent expertise and the consequences of leaving a position unfilled.

3. The fees in proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)(1)–(2) require a stronger connection to fraud prevention and worker protection.

Ability to finance a substantial fee is a poor measure of whether a training arrangement is legitimate or whether an employer complies with labor protections. A blanket charge could exclude compliant participants while allowing well-financed abusive arrangements to continue.

DHS should explain, with evidence, why these fee amounts would address identified misconduct more effectively than targeted audits, verification of training arrangements, investigation of fraudulent employers, and enforcement against wage violations. These alternatives would focus resources on misconduct while supporting legitimate training and protecting American workers. DHS should explain its fee calculations and assess less burdensome alternatives.

4. Proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)(3), Section V.C, and Section VI inadequately protect existing investments and planning.

Implementation after 60 days, based on recommendation dates, could disrupt university budgets, recruitment plans, and research staffing arranged well before publication of a final rule. DHS should examine these concrete reliance interests and the costs of interrupted projects.

If DHS proceeds with any new fee, it should exempt currently enrolled students and existing OPT participants for their associated OPT and STEM extensions. It should also provide adequate time for institutions and employers to plan.

5. If DHS retains a fee requirement, proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i) should exempt advanced STEM and doctoral graduates.

At a minimum, DHS should exempt graduates of U.S. institutions who have earned a master's or doctoral degree in a STEM field, as well as other doctoral graduates, from both initial and subsequent OPT fees. These exemptions should cover their eligible post-completion OPT and STEM OPT extensions.

Advanced research training requires sustained investment in specialized facilities, mentorship, and expertise. Imposing substantial barriers when graduates can apply that training could weaken U.S. research capacity and competitiveness. Doctoral graduates may also contribute through teaching, mentoring, and developing methods that support American colleagues.

DHS should explicitly evaluate these exemptions as alternatives to a blanket fee, while continuing to enforce eligibility requirements and address fraud through targeted oversight.

I urge DHS to withdraw this proposal. If it proceeds, DHS should adopt these exemptions and explain its statutory authority, fee methodology, effects on American workers and institutions, and consideration of less burdensome alternatives. Program integrity should support America's ability to benefit from its investments in education and research.

Re: Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, RIN 1653-AB01 — "Optional Practical Training Fees," 91 FR 64566 (Oct. 8, 2026)

I am an F-1 international student at Arizona State University, enrolled in the M.S. in Public Health Technology program at the Downtown Phoenix campus. I expect to complete my degree in Summer 2027 and plan to apply for post-completion Optional Practical Training. I write to respectfully urge the Department to withdraw the proposed fees of $70,000 for an initial OPT recommendation and $30,000 for each subsequent recommendation, including the STEM OPT extension.

First, the amounts are so large that they would act as a barrier, not a fee. For a student like me, the initial recommendation plus a STEM extension would total $100,000. Few public universities can absorb that cost for every international student, and the proposal leaves schools free to pass the cost on to students. Either way, many students would effectively lose access to OPT — not because their applications lack merit, but because the price is out of reach.

Second, the fee does not distinguish legitimate use from fraud. It charges every student the same amount whether or not any fraud is involved, so it cannot be described as a targeted anti-fraud measure. A flat charge of this size punishes the many students who follow the rules in order to reach the few who do not.

Third, the practical result would be fewer trained graduates entering the U.S. workforce. My field, public health technology, serves hospitals, health departments, and communities that already face staffing shortages. OPT is the pathway through which international graduates contribute that training here. If schools stop recommending OPT because of the cost, the United States loses those workers, and the students who invested in a U.S. education lose the training the program was designed to provide.

I understand the Department's interest in the integrity of the OPT program, and I support measures that address fraud directly. But a fee of this magnitude is not proportionate to that goal. I respectfully ask the Department to withdraw the proposed fees, or at minimum to set any fee at a level tied to the actual administrative cost of processing an OPT recommendation.

Thank you for considering my comment.

Sincerely,
An F-1 international student

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Isabella Steele
comments.commentText:
Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100
RIN 1653-AB01

I am a financial technology and fraud prevention writer. I am also a member of the School of Visual Arts. My strong opposition to the DHS’s OTP fee proposal is a result of my experience in these communities.

I have structured my argument around the three goals stated by the DHS: to combat fraud, strengthen the integrity of the immigration system, and protect US workers. My full comment, with sources, is attached.

I. Combat fraud

DHS says it "cannot confidently predict" the fees' effect (91 Federal Register 64582) and cites no evidence that fees deter fraud. The government's own record suggests they do not. H-1B visa employers began paying a $500 fraud fee in 2005, yet US Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) still found a 13.4 percent fraud rate. Fraud declined only after USCIS began site visits. The OPT fees would go to the Treasury and fund no enforcement (91 FR 64576).

The Government Accountability Office (GAO) found that 38 percent of OPT records lacked an employer name or start date (GAO-14-356), showing inadequacy of oversight. A later GAO report recommended fraud risk profiles, data analytics, network analysis, and fraud training for school officials to identify patterns of abuse (GAO-19-297). These tools can help uncover shell employers, fraudulent job offers, and document-selling networks. The proposed fees do none of this: schools must pay before students are required to have an employer (91 FR 64569), leaving the employer relationships and networks DHS is concerned about unexamined.

II. Strengthen the integrity of the immigration system

DHS's figure that only 20 percent of F-1 student visa holders use OPT counts every enrolled student. Among graduates, 54 percent use OPT, including 64 percent in Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics (STEM) fields. Canada, the United Kingdom, Australia, and Germany offer post-study work for fees ranging from 98 euros to 5,750 Australian dollars. The US would charge $70,000 to $100,000—a fee that would be absorbed by US educational institutions.

Importantly, DHS acknowledges that schools may pass the fees on to “all students” (91 FR 64575, Sec.IV.C; 91 FR 64575, Sec IV.C;91 FR 64579, Sec VI), resulting in a more costly education for US citizens. The suggested fees may also steer international students toward Curricular Practical Training (CPT), which DHS itself identifies as a source of fraud and national security threats (91 FR 64577). The current proposal does nothing to address this.

Alternative models exist for maintaining the integrity of US systems: for example, the United Kingdom gives graduates of high-compliance universities a longer post-study work period, targeting oversight according to institutional compliance rather than imposing a uniform burden.

III. Protect US workers

International students supported 355,736 US jobs in 2024–25. NAFSA: Association of International Educators projects that fall 2026 enrollment declines could put up to 40,000 jobs at risk. At the School of Visual Arts, for example, falling international enrollment has contributed to a $22 million deficit—its largest ever—and the closure of four graduate programs.

Nearly one in four billion-dollar startups in the US has a founder who came to the United States as an international student. These companies have created an average of 1,123 jobs each, according to the National Foundation for American Policy. Restricting the ability of international graduates to remain and work in the United States threatens a talent pipeline that has helped build American companies and employ American workers.

The DHS proposal does not require employers to substantiate their attestations, provide payroll records, verify wages, or assume additional responsibility for ensuring that OPT employment meets program requirements. It leaves the financial incentive DHS identifies untouched while placing a $70,000 initial fee on schools and students before a specific employer relationship even exists.

IV. Conclusion

In conclusion, DHS should withdraw the proposed fees. It should invest instead in activities that will move the needle on fraud in a direct, measurable way. As it stands right now, the DHS proposal overlooks clear opportunities like risk technologies specialized in business verification as well as and oversight based on compliance records.
comments.reason: The commenter expresses strong opposition to the DHS OPT fee proposal, arguing it does not combat fraud or protect U.S. workers.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
EXECUTIVE SUMMARY OF PUBLIC COMMENT
I am writing to express strong logical and regulatory disagreements with the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) proposed rule to establish a $70,000 fee per F-1 student for initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) recommendations and a $30,000 fee for subsequent extensions.
While securing program integrity is a critical objective, the proposed blanket fee structure relies on flawed economic assumptions, imposes wildly disproportionate financial burdens, and misdirects enforcement away from actual bad actors.
KEY SUMMARY POINTS (FULL ANALYSIS IN ATTACHED FILE)
Flaws in the "Cheap Labor" Rationale:
F-1 students on post-completion OPT enter competitive, skilled labor markets directly related to their academic majors. By regulatory definition, OPT is not unskilled labor. Official SEVP data shows that 61.5% of international students in U.S. higher education are in Master’s or Doctoral programs, and top OPT employers consist of major technology firms, financial institutions, and research universities paying market-rate wages. Employers still maintain a natural preference for domestic candidates due to nonimmigrant administrative requirements; international graduates hold no unfair advantage.
Context of Declining International Enrollment:
According to NAFSA and higher education data for the 2025–2026 cycle, new international enrollment fell 17%, total enrollment (excl. OPT) dropped 7%, Common App international undergraduate applicants fell 10%, doctoral applications dropped 21%, and student visas issued fell 23% (India -57%, China -28%). In this climate of declining enrollment, matriculating students are highly vetted and less likely to game the system. Prohibitive fees misdiagnose current enrollment trends.
Disproportionality & Exacerbation of "Pay-to-Stay":
The proposed fees represent an increase of over 13,000% compared to USCIS Form I-765 filing fees ($470 online / $520 paper) and bear no relationship to administrative cost recovery. Furthermore, requiring $70,000–$100,000 does not eradicate pay-to-stay schemes; rather, it exacerbates them by incentivizing ultra-wealthy applicants or fraudulent entities to arrange illicit side deals to buy access to post-completion work.
Direct Targeted Enforcement Over Blanket Penalties:
Regulatory abuse identified by SEVP should be combated through targeted entity enforcement. SEVP already possesses statutory authority to decertify non-compliant institutions (withdrawing certification for 183 schools in 2024 alone). DHS should levy civil monetary fines on bad-actor businesses and decertify fraudulent schools rather than penalizing compliant universities and students nationwide.
Two-Tiered Student Status Resolution Framework:
Tier 1 (Willful Participants): Students individually proven to have knowingly engaged in fraudulent schemes face immediate SEVIS termination under 8 CFR § 214.2(f) and inadmissibility under INA § 212(a)(6)(C)(i).
Tier 2 (Innocent Students): Non-complicit, compliant students at a decertified school should be granted a 60-to-90-day safe-harbor transfer window to move to another SEVP-certified institution without accruing unlawful presence or forfeiting earned OPT eligibility.
SUMMARY RECOMMENDATIONS
DHS should withdraw the proposed $70,000 / $30,000 institutional fee schedule and instead implement targeted administrative fines on bad-actor entities, streamline SEVP decertification procedures, and establish safe-harbor protections for innocent students.
Please refer to the attached PDF document for the full public comment submission, complete with references.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100 | RIN 1653-AB01
Comment on the proposed Optional Practical Training Fees, 91 Fed. Reg. 64566 (Oct. 8, 2026)

I respectfully oppose the proposed $70,000 initial and $30,000 subsequent OPT fees (proposed 8 CFR 214.2(f)(11)(ii)-(iii), 214.13(i)). I share DHS's goal of preventing fraud, but this fee is the wrong tool.

I am a former international student who studied in the United States on an F-1 visa and worked on OPT. I've returned and now work in a European Union country. My study and work in the US exposed me to a culture of innovation, democratic values, hard work, and respect for private property. Those experiences shaped my values, and I bring them to my work every day. I believe the world needs more people who think innovatively and value hard work and technological progress, rather than relying on regulation alone. OPT is one of the ways the United States helps produce them.

The attached PDF sets out my full comment and supporting sources. In summary:

1. DHS does not have the legal authority to impose this fee (NPRM III.A).
INA 214(a)(1) lets DHS set the "time" and "conditions" of admission. It does not mention fees or revenue. In Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump (U.S. Feb. 20, 2026), the Supreme Court held that a power to "regulate" does not include the power to tax. When Congress wants students or schools to pay, it writes the payment into law and ties it to cost (8 U.S.C. 1184(m), 1356(m), 1372(e)). DHS acknowledges ICE cannot keep the money, which goes to the general Treasury (NPRM IV.C). A charge that is not based on cost, is meant to discourage lawful participation, and funds nothing related to OPT is in substance a tax. NCTA v. United States, 415 U.S. 336 (1974); United States v. Sperry Corp., 493 U.S. 52 (1989). Only Congress may impose a tax, and a decision of this size, about $12.4 billion a year, belongs to Congress.

2. The fee punishes all participants instead of ending fraud (NPRM IV, V).
DHS's evidence describes fraudulent employers: shell companies, empty worksites, and sold job letters. Yet the fee is charged to schools for every student, before any employer is identified, and DHS expects the cost to be passed on to students. Honest students and schools would pay, while the shell companies would pay nothing. The ability to pay $70,000 measures money, not merit. DHS lists the rule's benefits as "Not Estimated," and it set aside targeted tools, such as employer verification, site visits, and penalties for proven violations, mainly because a fee is easier to administer. Motor Vehicle Mfrs. Ass'n v. State Farm, 463 U.S. 29 (1983).

3. The rule ignores what international students do for the United States (NPRM VI, VII.A).
Students who study and train here carry American values and goodwill home. Research shows that people educated in democracies help advance democracy in their home countries (Spilimbergo, 99 Am. Econ. Rev. 528 (2009)), and that US-hosted exchanges help spread liberal values (Atkinson, 6 Foreign Pol'y Analysis 1 (2010)). As of 2024, 70 serving world leaders had been educated in the United States (HEPI Soft-Power Index 2024). OPT lets graduates work alongside Americans and build lasting ties. It is also a major reason students choose America: past OPT expansions raised international enrollment by 18% at the bachelor's level and 30% at the master's level (Amuedo-Dorantes, Shih & Xu, 61 Econ. Inquiry 253 (2023)). DHS's analysis does not consider any of this.

I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw the proposed rule and to address fraud through targeted enforcement against the employers and institutions responsible.

Thank you for considering this comment.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I respectfully oppose the proposed OPT fees of $70,000 for initial OPT and $30,000 for subsequent OPT. Although preventing fraud and protecting U.S. workers are legitimate objectives, the proposed fee structure is overly broad and may discourage legitimate practical training.

I would like to highlight four concerns:

**1. The fee structure unfairly penalizes pre-completion OPT.**

A student who uses 12 months of OPT after graduation would trigger a $70,000 fee. However, a student who uses part of the same authorized OPT period before graduation and the remainder afterward could trigger $100,000 in total fees. Both students receive the same total OPT duration, yet one faces an additional $30,000 charge simply because of the timing of participation. This discourages students from pursuing legitimate practical training during their studies. DHS should reconsider this distinction.

**2. Existing STEM OPT safeguards are not adequately considered.**

STEM OPT already requires Form I-983 training plans, employer attestations, and compliance with additional oversight requirements. DHS also has authority to conduct employer site visits. Before imposing an additional $30,000 fee, DHS should explain why these existing safeguards are insufficient and demonstrate why a substantial financial barrier is more effective than targeted verification and enforcement.

**3. Educational institutions bear financial risks they cannot fully control.**

The proposed fee is paid by the educational institution, rather than being directly tied to a specific employer. However, schools cannot fully control or independently investigate employers' ongoing business operations and workplace compliance. This could discourage schools from recommending otherwise qualified students simply because of the financial exposure. DHS should reconsider whether institutions are the appropriate parties to bear this substantial financial responsibility.

**4. The refund process lacks adequate procedural protections.**

The proposal gives SEVP discretion over refund requests, prohibits refunds after an EAD is issued, and does not provide an administrative appeal process. DHS should establish clear refund criteria, require written explanations for denials, and provide a reasonable review process to address erroneous or unfair decisions.

More broadly, DHS should provide transparent evidence supporting the proposed fee amounts and their relationship to actual administrative and enforcement costs. Fraud involving fictitious employers or noncompliant training should be addressed through targeted investigations and employer accountability, rather than imposing substantial uniform costs on legitimate students and institutions.

I urge DHS to reconsider the proposed fee structure, evaluate its effects on different OPT categories, and prioritize targeted enforcement over broad financial barriers to legitimate practical training.

Thank you for considering my comments.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes the proposed OPT fees, arguing they create unfair financial burdens and discourage legitimate training.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Re: Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, RIN 1653-AB01 - Optional Practical Training Fees

I am an F-1 international student at a U.S. university. I strongly oppose the proposed $70,000 initial and $30,000 subsequent OPT fees, which could cost a STEM student up to $100,000. I urge DHS to withdraw the rule.

The fee would cost the U.S. far more than it collects.
DHS reports 194,554 F-1 students held OPT authorization and reported employment in 2024. Using SEVIS’s 2024 degree mix, that is roughly 80,000 bachelor’s and 115,000 master’s graduates per year. At many universities, international tuition alone is about $50,000-$85,000 per year, before housing, cars, insurance, food, and daily expenses. At a conservative $70,000 per year, one cohort spends about $38 billion in the U.S. over a four-year bachelor’s or two-year master’s program; at $100,000 per year, about $55 billion. Even if no student were deterred, the fee would raise at most about $13.6 billion, largely paid by the same students. In reality, many students would choose other countries, so the government would collect little while the U.S. loses tens of billions in tuition, rent, and consumer spending. 92% of U.S. institutions told IIE that without OPT, international students would likely study elsewhere.
The rule undermines American leadership in science and technology.
The U.S. leads the world in innovation because talented people from everywhere come here to study, research, and work. About 24% of U.S. billion-dollar companies have a founder who first came as an international student. Pricing OPT out of reach sends top talent to Canada, the U.K., Australia, and Germany. Blocking foreign students from studying and working here directly conflicts with technological leadership.
The rule would harm U.S. universities and research.
International tuition helps fund faculty, labs, and aid for domestic students. Losses are already visible: DePaul University cut spending after a 30% drop in international enrollment, reducing nearly 8% of its staff to close a $12.6 million budget gap. In a May 2026 survey, new international undergraduate enrollment fell 20% and graduate enrollment 24% from spring 2025, and over a third of institutions expected budget cuts. This rule would deepen those losses and weaken U.S. academic competitiveness.
OPT benefits U.S. workers; isolated fraud does not justify a universal penalty.
OPT participants work for U.S. companies and pay federal and state income taxes. Their skills help employers grow and expand, creating more jobs, including for Americans. DHS cites about 10,000 students linked to suspect employers, against roughly 195,000 OPT and 165,000 STEM OPT participants in 2024. Isolated cases cannot prove that hiring international graduates harms U.S. workers across all industries. The proper response is targeted enforcement against fraudulent employers and schools, not a blanket charge on every legitimate student. DHS also gives no reasoned basis for the $70,000 and $30,000 amounts. Because the fee goes to the Treasury as general revenue and is unrelated to any cost of service, it functions as a tax that INA 214(a) does not authorize DHS to impose.
My own experience.
I pay high international tuition. I have bought a car, rent housing, buy insurance, and spend money in my local community. I have never evaded taxes. I study hard, passed my exams, and earned an internship at a U.S. company through my own ability, creating value for that company. Nothing I have done is fraudulent or unfair to anyone. This rule would treat me and hundreds of thousands of students like me as suspects and charge a price most families cannot pay.
Reliance interests.
Current students enrolled and paid tuition relying on OPT as part of their F-1 program. Applying the fee to students already mid-study unfairly changes the terms.

Requested action: Withdraw the proposed rule. Address fraud through targeted enforcement against bad-actor employers and schools. At a minimum, exempt all students enrolled before any final rule takes effect.

Respectfully,
An F-1 international student
comments.reason: The commenter strongly opposes the proposed OPT fees and urges DHS to withdraw the rule.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I'm an international graduate student in a STEM field at a U.S. university, graduating next year, and I'm writing to ask DHS to express my opposition about this proposed rule.

I understand the concerns behind it. The fraud cases described in Section IV.A are real, and nobody benefits when shell companies sell fake jobs or list empty buildings as worksites. But almost every example in the rule is a problem with a specific employer: staged worksites, residential addresses, phantom employees. Those are things DHS can find and punish through site visits, E-Verify, and checking that employers actually exist. A flat $70,000 fee does none of that. It charges the same amount for a student going to a well-established company as for one going to a shell company, so it doesn't separate fraud from legitimate training. It just makes OPT too expensive for almost everyone.

The fee also doesn't pay for oversight. Section IV.C says the money would go to the Treasury as a miscellaneous receipt, not to SEVP or enforcement, and that the amount was chosen to match H-1B fees rather than any cost of running the program. DHS also acknowledges that schools can pass the cost on to international students, to all students, or to employers. In practice that means either students pay a sum close to a full year of tuition, American students see higher tuition, or employers stop hiring graduates who need OPT. None of those outcomes targets fraud.

I also don't think cutting off OPT this way serves the United States. Universities and the federal government invest heavily in training graduate students in fields like computer science. OPT is how a share of that investment stays here, as engineers and researchers who pay taxes, build products, and sometimes start companies that end up hiring Americans. Canada, the United Kingdom, and Australia all offer post-study work options to international graduates. If OPT becomes unaffordable, strong students will choose those countries instead, and the skills they would have built here will go to competitors. The rule notes that only about 20 percent of F-1 students used OPT in 2024, which suggests OPT is not the reason most students come. For those who do use it, though, it is often the step that turns a U.S. degree into U.S. work and innovation. This is not a small effect. NAFSA estimates that international students contributed about $43 billion to the U.S. economy and supported over 350,000 jobs in the 2024-2025 academic year, and new international enrollment is already falling. Congress has also recognized OPT's value: the Keep Innovators in America Act (H.R. 8013) would write OPT into statute. A fee that effectively ends OPT for most students moves in the opposite direction.

The timing matters for students like me, too. I've already accepted a full-time job offer in my field that starts after graduation, and it depends on post-completion OPT. Section VI says reliance interests are speculative and that students who apply before the effective date are protected. But under Section V.C, the fee applies to any DSO recommendation dated after the effective date. If the final rule comes out in early 2027, students who chose their programs, paid tuition, and accepted jobs under current rules could still be caught by it. If DHS goes forward, I ask that it at least exempt students who were already enrolled before the effective date, and that it reject the alternative in Section V.A of charging the $70,000 fee again when a student moves on to a master's or doctoral degree.

If the goal is protecting American workers and cutting fraud, targeted tools would do that better: wage requirements, employer verification, and enforcement against the companies abusing the system. I hope DHS will pursue those instead of a fee that falls on everyone.

Thank you for considering my comment.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed fee is too expensive, does not target fraud, and harms students and employers.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Re: Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100 — Optional Practical Training Fees

I strongly oppose the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 fee for each subsequent OPT recommendation.

I support effective enforcement against fraud. However, this fee is a blunt instrument that would burden legitimate students and institutions while failing to target the specific actors responsible for fraud. Because a school must pay before making an OPT recommendation, the practical effect will be to deny or sharply limit lawful, field-related training for qualified F-1 students. Schools may pass the cost to students, restrict OPT recommendations, or reduce enrollment of international students altogether.

The scale of the proposed financial burden is extraordinary. DHS estimates annual fee transfers of $8.4 billion to $16.5 billion, with a primary estimate of $12.4 billion. DHS also recognizes that OPT availability can contribute to international enrollment and associated institutional revenue. Therefore, schools unable or unwilling to fund these fees may lose both OPT participants and enrollment revenue. This is especially harmful to smaller schools: DHS estimates that, in the transition year, 116 small entities—8.4 percent of affected small entities—would face impacts greater than 20 percent of annual revenue. A rule with that level of impact is not a narrowly tailored integrity measure.

The proposed structure also produces arbitrary results. A student who uses pre-completion OPT and later post-completion OPT could trigger $100,000 in fees, even though the total authorized OPT period, excluding a STEM extension, is limited to 12 months. DHS itself anticipates that schools and students would shift away from pre-completion OPT to avoid that fee differential. Thus, the rule would distort educational and career decisions rather than evaluate whether a particular training opportunity is legitimate.

The rule would also affect U.S. employers and the American economy. DHS acknowledges that employers benefit from OPT participation and may face productivity losses if they cannot replace OPT participants with other qualified workers. DHS further describes the loss of OPT participation as a loss of societal benefits, including the value of participants’ labor to employers, their contribution to the U.S. economy, and the educational value of practical experience. Under DHS’s low-participation scenario, it estimates annual opportunity costs of approximately $8.92 billion during the transition period and $8.07 billion after the transition period. Those costs are borne across schools, workers, employers, students, and communities—not simply by the people alleged to be engaged in fraud.

The proposal also does not demonstrate why an institution-wide fee will meaningfully protect American workers. The fee is paid by schools before an OPT recommendation, not by employers based on documented misconduct. It therefore penalizes compliant schools and students regardless of whether an employer presents any fraud or labor-market concern. DHS should not impose multi-billion-dollar costs on legitimate educational institutions, employers, and students without demonstrating that this mechanism directly addresses the identified misconduct.

I respectfully request that DHS withdraw the proposed OPT fee rule.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes the proposed OPT fees, arguing they impose an extraordinary financial burden on students and schools.

comments.commentText:
Comment on DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100 — Optional Practical Training Fees

I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw this proposed rule. I’m writing not only out of concern for international students, but because I believe it would quietly hurt the United States itself: its universities, its workers, its economy, and the trust the rest of the world has long placed in it.

The fee does not address the problem it names. DHS says the rule is meant to combat fraud. But the money would go into the general Treasury, not into investigating fraud. The rule also openly says one of its main goals is to discourage participation in OPT. A $70,000 charge for every student doesn’t separate honest students from bad actors. It shuts out everyone who can’t pay, and fraud continues wherever someone can. If fraud is the concern, the answer is targeted enforcement: auditing suspicious employers, checking the records of schools that misuse the program, and penalizing actual violators. Charging every law-abiding graduate for the misconduct of a few doesn’t fix fraud.

American universities, and American students, would pay the price. Schools would owe these fees to recommend a student for OPT. In practice, many would stop recommending students, or pass the cost on. The opportunity to train in the U.S. after graduation is one of the main reasons talented students choose American schools. Take it away and many will go elsewhere. International tuition helps keep classes running, keeps graduate programs open, and holds down costs for domestic students. Independent economists estimate that fees at this scale could cost U.S. universities billions of dollars a year. When enrollment falls, American students lose programs, faculty, and financial aid. College towns lose jobs and local businesses. Smaller and regional institutions, with less margin to absorb the shock, would be hit hardest.

The talent won’t disappear. It will go to our competitors. The UK, Canada, Australia, and others actively welcome international graduates through post-study work pathways. Students who once would have built their early careers here, in American labs, firms, and startups, would build them in Toronto, London, or Sydney instead. Many of the people who founded American companies and led American research started out on student visas and practical training. Shutting that door doesn’t protect American innovation. It hands that innovation to other countries.

OPT does not displace American workers. Research suggests that where OPT participation is higher, job opportunities for American college graduates rise as well. Skilled graduates help companies grow, open new teams, and keep work in the United States instead of offshoring it. If Congress believes the payroll tax treatment of student workers creates an unfair cost advantage, it can address that directly. A fee that functions as a ban is the wrong tool.

The rule’s own analysis is not adequate. By DHS’s own estimate, the public cost ranges from about $32 million to over $8 billion a year. A range that wide is not a reasonable basis for a decision of this size. The public deserves a real accounting of what this rule would cost American universities, employers, and communities before it is finalized.

Finally, there is a cost that won’t show up in any budget table. Generations of international graduates have left the United States with real affection for it: for the mentors who trained them, the colleagues they worked beside, and the idea that hard work here would be met with fair opportunity. That goodwill has been one of America’s quiet strengths. A rule designed to make these students feel unwelcome would erode it, and it is far easier to lose than to rebuild.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
An exaction of this scale requires clear congressional authorization. Under the major questions doctrine, an agency action of this economic and political magnitude requires a clear statement of congressional authorization (Biden v. Nebraska, 600 U.S. 477 (2023); West Virginia v. EPA, 597 U.S. 697 (2022)). DHS's own estimates put annual transfers at $8.4–16.5 billion, with a primary estimate of $12.4 billion per year across 2,478 affected institutions (91 FR at 64584). INA § 214(a)'s general authority to prescribe the "time and conditions" of admission has never before been read to authorize multi-billion-dollar per-student exactions. The closest precedent has already been struck down: in June 2026, a federal court vacated the administration's $100,000 H-1B charge as an unauthorized tax, and courts have since declined to stay or have separately enjoined it. The OPT fee shares these identical defects.
The rule is arbitrary and capricious.
• No reasoned basis for the amounts: The NPRM offers no explanation of why $70,000 and $30,000 are the correct figures rather than any others.
• Circular cost-benefit analysis: DHS "assumes these opportunity costs are equal to or less than the proposed fee per OPT instance" (91 FR at 64585), effectively valuing a lost year of skilled professional work at exactly the arbitrary fee amount DHS invented.
• Gross mismatch of means and ends: DHS's own evidence shows fraud concentrated among a small minority of bad actors. Even its 2026 probe identified roughly 10,000 suspect participants out of about 194,554 OPT employment authorizations in 2024—only around 5%. Yet, this fee punishes the other 95% of compliant students across every field and treats compliant universities identically to bad actors. While targeted tools like site visits, training plans, and employer verification were considered, they were rejected simply as too administratively burdensome (91 FR at 64577). Administrative convenience is not a reasoned basis for a blanket punitive fee.
• Irrational compounding: A student who uses pre-completion OPT followed by post-completion OPT triggers a combined $100,000 fee ($70,000 + $30,000) for a single individual, even though any purported fraud risk is per person rather than per recommendation.
It punishes the wrong people. The fraud DHS describes concerns fake employers and shell companies falsifying employment, not a university's recommendation. Taxing the school's recommendation does nothing to catch fraudulent employers; it only deters compliant universities from recommending legitimate students. The mechanism is fundamentally mismatched to the stated purpose.
OPT is not "optional" for many graduates. For many F-1 students, OPT is the degree-related practical training that completes their education. It represents the supervised, field-related work experience their degree program is designed to lead into, and in many fields, it is the only lawful pathway to gain that experience after graduation. As a graduate student transitioning to specialized post-graduation work, my planned OPT period is an indispensable extension of my academic training, allowing me to apply complex technical research to real-world innovation. Facing an effective unavailability of OPT would disrupt my post-graduation work authorization, derailing my career trajectory and halting the contributions I can bring to advanced research and technical development in the United States.
Skilled immigration complements, rather than displaces, U.S. workers. DHS frames the fee as a mechanism for protecting American workers, but the evidence points the other way. The Information Technology and Innovation Foundation (ITIF) notes research finding that H-1B immigration raised native non-STEM workers' incomes by about 15 percent in computer systems design, demonstrating that skilled immigration grows the economic pie rather than taking slices from American workers. Consequently, a fee that drives away U.S.-trained graduates harms, rather than helps, the domestic workers DHS claims to protect.
comments.reason: Argues the rule lacks congressional authorization, is arbitrary and capricious, and relies on circular cost-benefit analysis.

comments.commentText:
I oppose the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 fee for subsequent OPT. DHS should withdraw these provisions and pursue evidence-based, targeted safeguards instead.

**1. A financial barrier is not a fraud-detection system.**

Sections IV and V.A identify real concerns about OPT abuse. Fraud should be investigated and punished. But requiring $70,000 for a legitimate student's OPT does not establish that a placement is fraudulent; nor does the ability of a university, student, or employer to pay establish that a placement is legitimate.

The proposed fee measures financial capacity, not program integrity. DHS should publish evidence showing how these particular dollar amounts would reduce fraud relative to targeted employer verification, risk-based audits, stronger reporting, and enforcement against sham placements.

**2. The proposal would undermine an American competitive advantage built over generations.**

The United States became a world leader in research, semiconductors, computing, biotechnology, and artificial intelligence in part by making its universities and laboratories destinations for talent from around the world. International graduates do not merely consume educational resources: they collaborate with American students, contribute to research, and help American companies create technology and jobs.

The National Science Board's 2026 Science and Engineering Indicators report found that temporary visa holders earned 61% of U.S. computer and information sciences doctorates and 54% of engineering doctorates in 2024. These are degrees awarded by American universities, yet this proposal could make the transition from American education to American practical training prohibitively expensive.

Research by Bernstein and coauthors (NBER Working Paper 30797, revised 2025) found that immigrants accounted for approximately 16% of U.S. inventors but authored 23% of patents in the study sample, with substantial positive knowledge spillovers to collaborators. That evidence does not mean every OPT participant will become an inventor; it demonstrates why cutting off pathways for emerging talent deserves serious economic scrutiny.

**3. A $70,000 entrance charge favors wealth, not merit—and can disadvantage American startups.**

Under proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i), the institution must pay before recommending a student; the proposal also contemplates shifting this cost to students or employers. A well-funded technology company might absorb the cost. A small American startup, university lab, nonprofit, or early-stage research team often cannot.

This is a fee that can distort hiring away from the strongest candidate and toward whoever can finance access. It threatens precisely the entrepreneurship and competition that keep Big Tech innovative.

A STEM graduate needing both initial OPT and an extension could be associated with $100,000 in these fees. This is not a modest compliance adjustment. It could function as a financial prohibition for otherwise eligible students and small institutions.

**4. DHS's own analysis identifies major costs and uncertainties.**

Section VII.B estimates annualized costs of approximately $4.1 billion in its primary scenario (at a 3% discount rate). DHS also acknowledges it cannot precisely quantify the opportunity cost of lost OPT participation and uses unpaid fees as a proxy.

That leaves a crucial question unanswered: what is the full cost to American research, startup formation, productivity, and future innovation if U.S.-trained graduates cannot gain practical experience here?

Protecting U.S. workers is a legitimate goal. But a proposal of this magnitude should demonstrate that its benefits outweigh its harms, rather than assuming that a price barrier is an effective substitute for enforcement.

I urge DHS to withdraw the proposed OPT fees, publish a stronger analysis of their impacts on U.S. education and innovation, and consider narrower tools: risk-based site visits, verified training plans, transparent employment reporting, and penalties aimed at proven misconduct.

**America's technological leadership has never been sustained by making opportunity available only to the wealthiest. The relevant question is not how much money a graduate can pay, but what that graduate can contribute to the United States.**

Sources: DHS NPRM, 91 FR 64566, Sections V.A and VII.B (Oct. 8, 2026); National Science Board, The State of U.S. Science and Engineering 2026; Bernstein et al., NBER Working Paper 30797 (revised Aug. 2025).
