Re: Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, Optional Practical Training Fees (RIN 1653-AA99)

I strongly oppose this proposed rule and urge DHS to withdraw it in its entirety.

A $70,000 fee for initial OPT and $30,000 for each subsequent period is not a "fee." It is a prohibition dressed up as a cost-recovery measure. DHS's own analysis concedes this: the rule estimates annualized costs of up to $8.2 billion, admits it "cannot confidently predict the extent of any reduction in participation," and states twice that without these fees the agency "may shut down the program entirely." No institution will pay $70,000 per student for a 12-month work authorization. The predictable and intended result is the end of OPT in practice, without Congress ever voting on it.

1. This is an attack on American multiculturalism and on what makes America exceptional.
America's strength has always been that the most talented people in the world want to come here, study here, and build here. OPT is the bridge between an American education and an American career. Pricing it out of existence sends a clear message to the roughly one million international students on our campuses: you are welcome to pay tuition, but you are not welcome to stay and contribute. That is a betrayal of the pluralism and openness that built this country's universities, laboratories, and industries. Other countries (Canada, the UK, Germany, Australia) are actively recruiting the students we would be turning away.

2. America's innovators, scientists, and entrepreneurs are disproportionately foreign-born, and most of them arrived as students.
- More than half of America's billion-dollar startups were founded by immigrants, and a large share of those founders first came to the U.S. as international students.
- Nearly half of Fortune 500 companies were founded by immigrants or their children.
- Immigrants have won roughly 40 percent of the Nobel Prizes awarded to Americans in physics, chemistry, and medicine since 2000.
- International students earn the majority of U.S. doctoral degrees in computer science, electrical engineering, and several other STEM fields. Our graduate programs in these fields cannot function without them.
- Immigrants account for a disproportionate share of U.S. patents and roughly a quarter of the STEM workforce.
OPT is the single most common pathway by which these students become American scientists, founders, and employees. Cutting it off does not "protect American workers." It cuts off the pipeline that produces American jobs.

3. This rule would hurt Americans the most.
- American workers: Every immigrant-founded company employs overwhelmingly American workers. The research DHS cites on wage effects is contested; the evidence that high-skilled immigrants create jobs, raise productivity, and expand the overall labor market is extensive and consistent.
- American universities and college towns: International students contribute over $40 billion a year to the U.S. economy and support hundreds of thousands of American jobs. OPT is a primary reason students choose the U.S. over competitors. Enrollment declines will mean program closures, layoffs, and higher tuition for American students.
- American employers, hospitals, and state and local governments: DHS's answer to staffing losses is that employers "can minimize this impact by recruiting U.S. citizens." Employers already do. The shortage of engineers, researchers, and clinicians is real, and this rule makes it worse.
- American competitiveness: Ceding talent to China, Canada, and Europe in AI, semiconductors, and biotech is a national security cost that the rule does not even attempt to quantify.

4. The rule's justifications do not support its scale.
DHS cites fraud by a small number of bad actors, yet proposes a fee that would eliminate the program for everyone. Fraud is addressed through enforcement, site visits, and SEVP decertification, which DHS already has authority to do. A fee that is orders of magnitude above any plausible administrative cost is not reasonably related to fraud prevention and is arbitrary and capricious. Nor does the rule weigh the enormous reliance interests of students who enrolled in multi-year degree programs with OPT as a lawful and longstanding part of the F-1 framework.

5. Request.
DHS should withdraw this proposed rule. If the agency believes a fee is warranted, it should propose one that reflects actual processing costs, is paid by the applicant, and is accompanied by a real regulatory impact analysis of its effects on American research, American employers, and American workers.

America did not become the world's leader in science and innovation by closing its doors to the people who wanted to help build it. This rule would do exactly that, and Americans would pay the price.

I oppose the proposed rule to impose additional fees on Optional Practical Training (OPT). This proposed rule is 1) legally flawed, and 2) instead of protecting US students and workers, it will actually cause severe, lasting harm to American universities, students, and ultimately, the US economy and healthcare system.

1) Technical and legal issues

a) It is a disguised tax

Under the Independent Offices Appropriations Act (31 U.S.C. 9701), federal agency user fees must reflect the actual cost of providing a regulatory service. Students already pay SEVIS I-901 and USCIS Form I-765 filing fees to cover adjudication and oversight. Because the proposed $70,000 and $30,000 fees go directly to the general US Treasury rather than funding SEVP administration, this fee is a de facto unauthorized tax, which only Congress is constitutionally authorized to levy.

b) The proposed amount is arbitrary and unjustified

Under the Administrative Procedure Act (5 U.S.C. 706), agency rules cannot be arbitrary. Charging $70,000 for an entry-level training period alone exceeds the entire annual salary of many new graduates, not counting the additional $30,000 for the extensions. From the proposed rule, this amount is arbitrary and not clearly calculated or justified. It will most likely be challenged in court should it become effective.

c) It does not help with the intended objective

DHS claims these fees will deter fraudulent employers and "pay-to-stay" schemes, which is an understandable objective. Yet, instead of penalizing the fraudulent employers, the rule shifts the entire financial and legal burden to SEVP-certified universities. That does not include additional hidden infrastructure and staffing costs to implement such a rule.

Furthermore, under 8 CFR 214.2(f)(10)(ii), initial post-completion OPT does not require a job offer at the time a Designated School Official (DSO) makes a recommendation in SEVIS. Billing a school $70,000 before an employer is even involved cannot logically police employer fraud.

2) Negative impact on the US

Gaining work experience is a standard component of studying. The possibility of gaining work experience in the US is a big part of making the US an attractive destination for international students. Losing such attraction will ultimately discourage international students from coming to the US and lead them to instead seek opportunities in competing countries like Canada, Europe, or Australia. The actual impact is much wider than intended and can actually harm the US in different ways.

a) To higher education

International students generally pay full, unsubsidized tuition with restricted access to financial aid that domestic students may be eligible for. Their enrollment heavily cross-subsidizes financial aid, facilities, and departmental budgets for domestic students ( https://doi.org/10.3386/w22981 ). Losing this revenue will worsen existing financial struggles across US universities and colleges, forcing schools to close academic programs or even entire campuses, raise tuition on domestic students, and reduce educational opportunities.

b) To research capability

According to the National Science Foundation’s "Survey of Earned Doctorates" ( https://ncses.nsf.gov/surveys/earned-doctorates/ ), temporary visa holders earn roughly one-third of all US science and engineering doctorates (and over 50% in engineering, computer science, and mathematics). US universities rely heavily on these F-1 graduates and OPT/STEM OPT postdoctoral researchers to staff laboratories and execute federally funded grants (such as NSF, NIH, and DoD projects). University lab budgets and federal grants cannot absorb a $70,000 to $100,000 surcharge per researcher, which will cripple research output and surrender the US's lead in critical STEM fields.

c) To the economy

Instead of being pure "competition" to the local workforce, according to NAFSA’s "International Student Economic Value Tool" ( https://www.nafsa.org/policy-and-advocacy/policy-resources/nafsa-international-student-economic-value-tool-v2 ), international students actually contributed $42.9 billion to the US economy and supported over 355,000 US jobs in the 2024-2025 academic year. Moreover, SEVIS employment data shows the vast majority of OPT graduates work for small and mid-sized US businesses, regional manufacturers, and community organizations, which are not large corporations that can absorb a $70,000 to $100,000 fee. Pricing OPT out of existence will starve small American businesses of critically needed talent and export innovators we trained directly to foreign competitors.

d) To the healthcare system

The US faces a severe healthcare worker crisis...

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am an F-1 international student pursuing a J.D. and an M.S. in Cybersecurity Risk Management at Indiana University, with an expected graduation date of December 2026. My education has included legal research, community legal services, and practical experience in data privacy, cybersecurity, and environmental compliance. These opportunities have shown me that applying academic knowledge in professional settings is an essential part of legal and technical education. I hope to continue developing these skills through lawful, degree-related post-completion practical training.

First, the proposed fees would make access to professional training depend on financial resources rather than academic achievement, compliance, or professional merit. Under the proposal, educational institutions must pay $70,000 for an initial OPT recommendation and $30,000 for subsequent recommendations. Section VI expressly acknowledges that schools may pass these costs on to international students or employers. As a student who has invested years in American higher education and received scholarship support, I am deeply concerned that my academic preparation and professional qualifications could become irrelevant if neither my university nor a prospective employer can reasonably absorb such an extraordinary expense. This burden would be especially severe for graduates pursuing public-interest law, legal aid, academic research, and positions with smaller organizations, where limited financial resources do not necessarily reflect the social value of the work performed.

Second, Section VI inadequately addresses the legitimate reliance interests of students already enrolled in American universities. I am approaching graduation in December 2026. My decisions about where to study, which degrees to pursue, and how to finance my education were made long before this proposal was published. The fact that OPT was not my sole motivation for pursuing an American education does not mean that the longstanding availability of practical training was irrelevant to those decisions. Applying an unprecedented financial requirement based on the date of a DSO recommendation would create sharply different consequences for students who made substantially similar educational commitments. A 60-day transition period cannot undo years of financial and academic planning. At a minimum, students already enrolled before the final rule should receive meaningful transitional protection.

Third, the proposal does not adequately establish that imposing extraordinary fees would prevent fraud more effectively than targeted oversight. Section IV.C identifies deterrence as a central justification, while acknowledging that the collected revenue would be deposited into the U.S. Treasury rather than retained by ICE for OPT oversight or enforcement. Legitimate students and institutions would face the same financial requirement regardless of their compliance histories. The ability to pay $70,000 is not evidence of regulatory compliance, just as an inability to pay is not evidence of fraud. More targeted measures, including risk-based audits, verification of employment and training, investigations of fraudulent employers, and improved institutional reporting, would address identifiable misconduct more directly.

I also oppose the alternative discussed in Section V.A that would impose another $70,000 initial fee when a student advances to a higher educational level. Such an approach would further discourage advanced and interdisciplinary education without establishing that pursuing an additional degree increases the risk of fraud.

I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw the proposed fee requirements and pursue alternatives proportionate to documented administrative costs and identifiable compliance risks. If DHS proceeds with any additional OPT fee, it should provide a transparent justification for the amount, assess the economic consequences for students and employers, protect students who enrolled under the existing framework, and consider reasonable hardship exemptions.

As someone preparing to enter the legal profession, I recognize the government’s responsibility to enforce immigration law, prevent fraud, and protect American workers. These objectives are important. But a policy that makes legitimate practical training effectively inaccessible to qualified students solely because of financial constraints risks undermining the very educational and professional opportunities that make American higher education internationally respected.

I chose to invest in an American education because I value its academic rigor, professional standards, and commitment to the rule of law. I hope that the regulatory system will likewise recognize the distinction between preventing abuse and imposing disproportionate barriers on students who seek to comply with the law.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed OPT fees create an extreme financial burden that harms students and limits career opportunities.

Re: Public Comment on Optional Practical Training Fees (DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100)

I am an international graduate and a predoctoral researcher at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. I respectfully oppose the proposed OPT fees and urge DHS to substantially revise the rule.

I have personally navigated the STEM OPT extension process, including premium processing, to maintain continuous employment authorization and avoid interruptions to my research work. The proposed $70,000 initial fee and $30,000 subsequent fee, although formally imposed on educational institutions, could be passed on to students or employers. I am particularly concerned about the reliance interests of current F-1 students. Many students made substantial educational and financial commitments to U.S. institutions under an established regulatory framework that included OPT and STEM OPT. I urge DHS to withdraw the proposed per-student fees. If additional funding is necessary, DHS should instead adopt reasonable, cost-based administrative fees and targeted anti-fraud measures. At a minimum, students already enrolled before the final rule’s effective date should be grandfathered in, and previously approved OPT participants should not face new fees for subsequent STEM OPT extensions. comments.title: Comment Submitted by Harish Parthasarathy
comments.commentText:
To the Department of Homeland Security and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement,

I am writing as a prospective international graduate student planning to pursue higher education in Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence in the United States. I respectfully oppose the proposed Optional Practical Training (OPT) fees of $70,000 for initial authorization and $30,000 for subsequent authorization.

I urge DHS to reconsider this proposal because of its potential consequences for international students, American universities, and the nation’s technological competitiveness.

1. Financial Burden on International Students

International students already make substantial financial sacrifices to study in the United States. Many depend on education loans, family savings, and years of financial planning to afford tuition and living expenses.

Although the proposed fees would be imposed on universities, institutions may be unable to absorb these costs. This could restrict OPT opportunities or indirectly increase financial burdens on students.

Access to practical training should depend on academic qualifications and compliance with immigration regulations, not financial circumstances.

2. Importance of OPT for STEM Graduates

OPT provides an essential connection between academic education and professional experience. Students in Computer Science, Artificial Intelligence, engineering, and other STEM fields benefit from applying their knowledge to real-world problems.

International graduates contribute to areas such as healthcare technology, cybersecurity, artificial intelligence, and advanced computing. Restricting practical training could limit these contributions to American industries.

3. Impact on American Universities and Innovation

The United States attracts international students because of its academic excellence, research opportunities, and strong technology industry.

Excessive OPT fees could discourage talented students from choosing American universities and encourage them to pursue education in countries offering more accessible practical training opportunities.

Reduced international enrollment could affect university finances, research collaboration, and America’s ability to attract skilled graduates.

4. Better Alternatives to Prevent Fraud

I support protecting American workers, preventing immigration fraud, and maintaining the integrity of student visa programs.

However, imposing extraordinary fees on universities does not necessarily prevent misuse of OPT.

DHS should instead strengthen employer verification, improve employment reporting, conduct targeted audits, and impose meaningful penalties on organizations violating immigration regulations.

These measures would address misconduct without disproportionately affecting legitimate international students.

5. Request for Reconsideration

I respectfully request that DHS withdraw the proposed fee structure and evaluate less burdensome, evidence-based alternatives.

Any additional fees should be reasonable, transparent, and supported by documented administrative costs.

DHS should also evaluate the potential effects on international enrollment, university finances, STEM employment opportunities, and American innovation before implementing significant changes.

Conclusion

As a prospective international student, I view the United States as a global leader in education, research, and technological innovation.

International students invest substantial financial resources and years of preparation to pursue American higher education. Legitimate practical training is an important part of that educational experience.

Protecting American workers and preventing fraud are important objectives, but these goals should be achieved through effective enforcement rather than excessive financial barriers.

I respectfully urge DHS to reconsider this proposal and preserve fair, accessible, and properly regulated OPT opportunities.

Thank you for considering my comments.

Section V.A would require schools to pay $70,000 before a student’s initial OPT recommendation and $30,000 for subsequent recommendations, potentially including STEM OPT extensions. The proposal permits schools to pass these costs to students or employers. For graduates beginning their careers, such charges could exceed what they can reasonably finance. For smaller employers, they could make hiring otherwise qualified graduates impracticable. Schools might decline to recommend eligible students for financial reasons unrelated to program integrity.

I recognize DHS’s interest in preventing fraud and protecting U.S. workers. But a student’s or school’s ability to pay a substantial fee is not a reliable measure of whether employment is genuinely related to a degree. DHS should explain, with evidence, why this fee level would address documented violations more effectively than targeted audits, stronger employer verification, and enforcement against fraudulent arrangements.

Section VI also gives insufficient weight to current students’ reliance interests. Students commit years to degrees and plan their transition to professional training under established rules. A 60-day implementation period does little for those already enrolled but not yet recommended, or planning a STEM extension.

I urge DHS to withdraw the proposed fee schedule. At minimum, adopt evidence-based, cost-proportionate measures, protect students already enrolled or on OPT, and assess the consequences for universities and smaller employers before finalization.

comments.title: MM32 Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
To the Department of Homeland Security:

I respectfully oppose the proposed $70,000 initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) fee and $30,000 fee for subsequent OPT recommendations. I urge DHS to withdraw this fee structure and preserve reasonable access to legitimate, degree-related practical training.

My principal concern is that these fees would make access to practical training depend on financial resources rather than educational merit, professional qualifications, or compliance with immigration requirements. Although the proposal places payment responsibility on educational institutions, it acknowledges that those institutions may pass the financial burden to students or employers. Shifting responsibility for payment does not eliminate the burden. I am concerned that institutions could decline to recommend otherwise qualified students, employers could withdraw legitimate training opportunities, and students could lose access to practical experience despite meeting all other eligibility requirements.

I support protecting American workers, preventing fraud, and maintaining the integrity of the immigration system. However, the ability to pay a substantial fee is not evidence of compliance, and the inability to pay is not evidence of misconduct. DHS should demonstrate why these particular amounts would effectively distinguish legitimate educational training from abuse. A reduction in participation should not, by itself, be treated as evidence that fraud has been prevented.

The proposal states that the fees would be deposited in the U.S. Treasury and would not be retained by ICE or specifically earmarked for immigration enforcement activities. I therefore ask DHS to explain how these fees would improve oversight beyond creating a financial deterrent. The agency should evaluate less burdensome alternatives, including targeted compliance reviews, verification of degree-related training, employer accountability, and enforcement of applicable worker protections. Measures directed at demonstrated misconduct would be preferable to a financial barrier affecting compliant participants.

I am also concerned about the proposed effective date of 60 days after publication of a final rule. DHS should meaningfully consider students who have already committed to educational programs, incurred substantial expenses, or accepted future training opportunities under the existing framework. Describing a requirement as prospective does not resolve its potential impact on decisions made years earlier. I request explicit protections for currently enrolled students and existing OPT participants, including those who would need a later recommendation or extension.

Before proceeding, DHS should assess the potential consequences for universities, teaching hospitals, veterinary services, scientific research, small employers, and underserved communities. The analysis should examine whether these fees could discourage legitimate clinical training, interrupt research, reduce educational opportunities, or limit access to essential services. It should also consider whether smaller institutions and modestly funded training programs would face disproportionate barriers compared with organizations possessing greater financial resources.

DHS should also evaluate whether shifting substantial costs to students could increase debt or dependence on employers willing to finance participation. A policy intended to protect workers should be examined carefully for the possibility that it could make participants more financially vulnerable.

For these reasons, I request that DHS withdraw the proposed fee structure. Any alternative should be supported by transparent evidence, proportionate to its stated objectives, and designed to address demonstrated problems without making legitimate training financially unattainable. At a minimum, DHS should evaluate substantially lower fees, meaningful exemptions or waivers, and transition protections for students with existing educational commitments.

Protecting American workers and preserving immigration integrity are important goals. They should be pursued through effective oversight and evidence-based enforcement, not by making lawful, education-related practical training accessible only to those with exceptional financial resources.

Thank you for considering this comment.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes the proposed OPT fees and urges DHS to withdraw the fee structure.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Isaiah Williams
comments.commentText:
Dear Secretary Mullin,

I am writing to register my strong opposition to the proposed rule regarding Optional Practical Training (OPT) fee adjustments.

The United States has long maintained its edge as a global hub for research and higher education precisely because it draws top talent from around the world. International graduates utilizing OPT are vital drivers of domestic progress, contributing directly to critical advancements in medicine, clean energy, agriculture, and high-tech industries. These contributions do not just benefit academia—they fuel local economies, foster entrepreneurship, and create employment opportunities across the country.

Imposing exorbitant fees—such as $70,000 for initial OPT authorizations and $30,000 for extensions—is both prohibitive and counterproductive. Rather than strengthening labor standards, this steep financial barrier effectively locks out promising scholars who lack personal wealth, turning a merit-based training pipeline into a pay-to-play system. Workplace regulations should focus on ensuring fair wages, protecting worker rights, and discouraging exploitative labor practices for domestic and foreign professionals alike. This measure does none of that; it simply penalizes early-career researchers and workers.

If enacted, this rule will compromise our ability to retain top-tier talent, drive skilled graduates to competing nations, and weaken the collaborative environment within American universities and research institutions.

For the continued vitality of the American economy and our leadership in global innovation, I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule.

Sincerely,

Isaiah Williams
comments.reason: The commenter strongly opposes the proposed OPT fees, arguing they create prohibitive financial barriers and harm the economy.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by William Keyes
comments.commentText:
Docket ICEB-2026-0100: Optional Practical Training Fees (91 FR 64566)

I strongly oppose the proposed fees and urge their removal. As Executive Director of International House Philadelphia, I work to attract, support and retain international students and scholars in Greater Philadelphia. This proposal would undermine that mission and our region's economic prospects.

Institutional burden (Sections IV.C, V.A, VII.A): Charging $70,000 for initial OPT and $30,000 for subsequent recommendations risks effectively ending OPT. Just 100 initial recommendations would cost $7 million. Many institutions could not sustain payments for any students. SHEEO's FY2025 finance report shows falling real public-college education revenue per student in 36 states and D.C. Passing fees to students or employers would merely shift an often prohibitive burden.

DSO responsibilities (Sections III.D.1, IV.C): Under 8 CFR 214.2(f) and 214.3(l), designated school officials assess eligibility, advise students, maintain records and review STEM training plans. They lack investigative powers and resources to uncover employer fraud nationwide. Students need not even have an employer when requesting initial OPT. A large payment supplies no investigative expertise.

Enrollment and economic harm (Section VII.A): IDP's 2024 Emerging Futures 6 survey found 62% of surveyed international students would change destination for access to a post-study visa. International students contributed $42.9 billion and supported over 355,000 U.S. jobs in 2024-25 (NAFSA). The U.S. Commercial Service ranked education sixth among U.S. services exports in 2020. Curtailing OPT jeopardizes this export industry and American jobs.

WICHE's Knocking at the College Door (11th edition) projects 17% fewer Pennsylvania high-school graduates in 2041 than in 2023, with declines in 38 states. Pennsylvania's Independent Fiscal Office (2026 Demographic Outlook) projects 141,000 fewer residents aged 20-64 in 2035 than in 2025, alongside rapid aging. The report cites CBO projections that the U.S. ratio of working-age residents to those 65+ falls from 3.1 to 2.7 over that decade. Discouraging international enrollment would deepen these education and workforce challenges.

The George W. Bush administration expanded STEM OPT in 2008 to address employers' talent needs and strengthen U.S. competitiveness (73 FR 18944). NSF's 2026 Science and Engineering Indicators reports that temporary-visa holders earned over 40% of U.S. science and engineering master's degrees and 38% of doctorates in 2024. Driving this talent elsewhere would damage research, entrepreneurship and innovation.

Fee authority (Sections III.A, IV.C): The deterrent purpose, lack of a demonstrated service-cost basis, and deposit into general Treasury receipts raise serious unauthorized-tax concerns. These revenues are not earmarked for OPT enforcement. General authority over admission conditions does not by itself establish congressional authorization for this levy. DHS should explain its authority in light of the tax/fee distinction in National Cable Television Ass'n v. United States, 415 U.S. 336 (1974).

Fraud and proportionality (Sections IV.A, VII.A): ICE recorded over one million OPT/STEM authorizations in 2020-24 (SEVIS By the Numbers 2024). Yet the rule establishes no reliable fraud rate. The cited 2020 fraud conviction concerned at least 2,693 F-1/H-1B customers, not a count of proven OPT fraud since 2020. Arrests and employment at "highly suspect" firms do not prove individual fraud. The limited proven evidence does not justify a burden that could effectively end OPT. DHS should model near-zero participation and the resulting enrollment, research and workforce losses, and compare these costs with demonstrated benefits and targeted enforcement.

Alternatives (Section IV.C): Remove institutional fees and:

- Require employer tax ID numbers in SEVIS's existing optional field for ordinary OPT.

- Require named supervisor contact details in the existing optional fields.

- Offer incentives for curricula and OPT training aligned with critical workforce needs.

- Replace routine in-person visits to established, compliant schools with remote reviews; reserve travel for new campuses and identified risks, and redirect field-representative capacity to OPT reporting audits.

- Consider extending STEM OPT's E-Verify requirement to other OPT employers to strengthen employment-eligibility checks alongside Form I-9.

- Comment period (Sections I, VI): Thirty days is inadequate for institutions, employers and students to assemble considered evidence on consequences this substantial. Extend the period to at least 60 days, consistent with ACUS Recommendation 2011-2 for significant rules.

Protect program integrity through targeted oversight, remove these prohibitive fees, and preserve OPT's educational and economic benefits.

Bill Keyes
Executive Director
International House Philadelphia
comments.reason: The commenter strongly opposes the proposed OPT fees, arguing they create prohibitive institutional and student burdens.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I understand DHS’s responsibility to protect U.S. workers, prevent fraud, and ensure that OPT remains connected to its educational purpose. Students who follow the rules also benefit from a program that schools, employers, and the public can trust.

I hope DHS will reconsider the proposed OPT fees, taking into account the educational value of legitimate practical training and the contributions international students can make to U.S. teams and businesses.

I am an international graduate student studying product development in the United States. My studies involve understanding customer needs, evaluating technical possibilities, and turning research into product requirements and design decisions. Practical training would help me understand how to apply these methods within real teams, budgets, and development processes while learning from experienced professionals.

I also hope to contribute during that training. For example, I could help a team investigate why users struggle with a product, organize the findings into clearer requirements, and test whether a proposed improvement addresses the problem. My experience working across languages and cultural contexts could offer another perspective when considering different users’ needs. These are practical ways I hope to apply my education while supporting the work of a U.S. team.

My purpose in seeking OPT is to gain supervised, degree-related experience. I understand that OPT is temporary, requires authorization, and comes with conditions I must follow.

My concern with the fees proposed in Section V.A is that they could prevent these legitimate opportunities alongside any misuse they might discourage. Even if higher costs deter some abuse, they could also exclude students and organizations that follow the rules but cannot afford the additional expense.

Although schools would make the payments, they may reduce OPT recommendations or pass costs to students or employers. If that happens, a student could lose access to relevant training even when the student is eligible and the opportunity has genuine educational value. A smaller organization could also lose the opportunity to host a student despite being able to provide useful experience and appropriate supervision.

In these situations, the loss would extend beyond the student. U.S. teams could lose contributions to research, product development, and other projects from people whose skills were developed at American universities. International graduates can also bring knowledge of overseas customers and markets that may help American businesses serve a broader range of users. Keeping legitimate training accessible allows the United States to benefit from this exchange of skills and knowledge.

Over time, making practical training financially inaccessible could also lead some prospective students to choose other countries for their education. I hope DHS will consider the potential loss of future talent and professional connections, alongside its goals of protecting American workers and preventing abuse.

I am also concerned about students who are already enrolled. We have committed time and resources to our education and are planning how to apply what we learn. I understand that OPT is not guaranteed, but a substantial new financial requirement during our studies would make those plans more difficult to carry out.

Before imposing these fees, I ask DHS to compare their likely effects on legitimate participation with their expected benefits in reducing misuse. Please also further evaluate whether focused compliance checks and enforcement against documented violations could address the identified problems with less disruption to lawful training.

For these reasons, I respectfully ask DHS to withdraw the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent OPT fee, and pursue measures that address abuse while preserving meaningful access to legitimate practical training and its benefits to the United States.
comments.reason: The commenter asks DHS to reconsider the proposed OPT fees due to their impact on students and businesses.

My concern with the fees proposed in Section V.A is that they could prevent these legitimate opportunities alongside any misuse they might discourage. Even if higher costs deter some abuse, they could also exclude students and organizations that follow the rules but cannot afford the additional expense.

Although schools would make the payments, they may reduce OPT recommendations or pass costs to students or employers. If that happens, a student could lose access to relevant training even when the student is eligible and the opportunity has genuine educational value. A smaller organization could also lose the opportunity to host a student despite being able to provide useful experience and appropriate supervision.

In these situations, the loss would extend beyond the student. U.S. teams could lose contributions to research, product development, and other projects from people whose skills were developed at American universities. International graduates can also bring knowledge of overseas customers and markets that may help American businesses serve a broader range of users. Keeping legitimate training accessible allows the United States to benefit from this exchange of skills and knowledge.

Over time, making practical training financially inaccessible could also lead some prospective students to choose other countries for their education. I hope DHS will consider the potential loss of future talent and professional connections, alongside its goals of protecting American workers and preventing abuse.

I am also concerned about students who are already enrolled. We have committed time and resources to our education and are planning how to apply what we learn. I understand that OPT is not guaranteed, but a substantial new financial requirement during our studies would make those plans more difficult to carry out.

Before imposing these fees, I ask DHS to compare their likely effects on legitimate participation with their expected benefits in reducing misuse. Please also further evaluate whether focused compliance checks and enforcement against documented violations could address the identified problems with less disruption to lawful training.

For these reasons, I respectfully ask DHS to withdraw the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent OPT fee, and pursue measures that address abuse while preserving meaningful access to legitimate practical training and its benefits to the United States.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose the proposed rule imposing a $70,000 fee for initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) and a $30,000 fee for subsequent OPT. These extraordinary fees are economically unjustifiable, disproportionate, and harmful to American higher education, scientific innovation, and economic competitiveness. I urge the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) to withdraw this proposal entirely.

1. The proposed fees would effectively eliminate OPT for most qualified graduates.

A $70,000 fee is not a reasonable administrative charge. It is a prohibitive financial barrier that would make OPT inaccessible to most graduates, regardless of their qualifications or legitimate employment opportunities. Access to practical training would depend on personal wealth rather than merit. The burden would be especially severe for graduates entering academic research, public health, education, and nonprofit organizations, where salaries and institutional budgets cannot support such expenses.

2. The proposal would undermine American scientific leadership and economic competitiveness.

U.S. universities and research institutions depend on highly trained graduates to advance biomedical research, technological innovation, and public health. OPT enables graduates to apply their specialized training and contribute to American institutions. These fees would drive qualified researchers away, disrupt scientific projects, and weaken America's ability to attract global talent.

Research institutions could face staffing shortages, delayed discoveries, and reduced productivity. Prospective students would increasingly choose countries offering more accessible post-graduation opportunities, weakening American universities and the broader economy.

3. Excessive fees are not an evidence-based solution to fraud.

Preventing immigration fraud is legitimate, but imposing enormous fees on compliant participants does not directly address fraudulent employment or institutional misconduct. Financial barriers cannot verify whether employment is genuine or whether employers follow regulations.

DHS should instead strengthen employer verification, conduct targeted investigations, improve oversight, and penalize proven violators. These approaches would address misconduct without indiscriminately punishing legitimate students, universities, and employers.

4. The proposal fails to establish benefits for American workers.

Restricting OPT does not necessarily protect American jobs. Highly skilled graduates complement domestic workers, support research, contribute to innovation, and generate economic activity. Eliminating access to qualified researchers does not guarantee their positions will be filled by American workers. Instead, positions may remain vacant, projects may be canceled, and economic opportunities may move overseas.

DHS should provide empirical evidence that these fees would improve wages or employment outcomes rather than diminish America's ability to retain talent.

5. The economic justification is inadequate.

Projected government fee collections are not equivalent to net economic benefits. These fees would divert resources from universities, employers, and research institutions while discouraging enrollment, employment, and innovation.

A credible regulatory analysis must account for lost tuition revenue, reduced research productivity, diminished competitiveness, and the long-term costs of driving highly skilled graduates away from the United States.

6. The proposal raises serious concerns about proportionality and reasoned decision-making.

DHS must adequately justify why fees of $70,000 and $30,000 are necessary and why less burdensome alternatives would be insufficient. Under the Administrative Procedure Act, agencies must engage in reasoned decision-making, consider significant consequences, and evaluate reasonable alternatives. The extraordinary burden imposed by this proposal warrants rigorous justification.

Conclusion

This proposal would penalize legitimate participants, weaken American universities, discourage scientific innovation, and damage national competitiveness without demonstrating that such severe financial barriers are necessary to prevent fraud or protect American workers.

America's strength depends on attracting, educating, and retaining exceptional talent. Creating prohibitive barriers to practical training undermines that national interest.

I strongly urge DHS to withdraw this proposed rule in its entirety and pursue targeted, proportionate, evidence-based measures to address documented abuses.
comments.reason: The commenter strongly opposes the proposed high OPT fees and urges DHS to withdraw the proposal entirely.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Richard Spicer
comments.commentText:
I write as the founder of OPT Global, an international career coaching consultancy — and I should start by saying plainly that this rule would be good for my business. If OPT disappeared, students would need my help more, not less, and I would probably make a lot of money. I am opposing the rule anyway, because the value of OPT to the United States, to our competitiveness, and to the students we invited here is worth far more than what my company would gain. I also work at a large research university, but these comments are my own, not my employer's.

DHS says this rule targets fraud and protects American workers. Take that at face value, then do the math: the current I-765 filing fee for OPT is $470. This proposal sets it at $70,000. Is fraud really 150 times more expensive to prevent than to commit?

And be clear about who pays: the university does. This is a fee on the school for recommending a student for practical training — $70,000 per initial recommendation, $100,000 for a student who uses post-completion OPT and then a STEM extension. It is not a fee on a student, and it is not a fee on fraud. It is a fee on the institution that educated the student and is asked to vouch for them.

American universities are the engine of scientific progress, and that has been America's leading strength. This rule taxes that engine directly. A university facing $70,000 per recommendation will recommend fewer students, ration access, or cut elsewhere to absorb the cost. In every version, the university does less of what made it valuable, and the student loses the training that was part of why they came.

That is how American competitiveness falls behind. In 2024, 165,524 foreign students participated in STEM OPT, according to ICE's 2024 SEVIS by the Numbers report. Those are the engineers, researchers, and technologists American employers hire because the domestic pipeline does not yet produce enough of them. Every recommendation a university cannot afford is one fewer STEM graduate working here — and the countries competing with us for the same talent will take the ones we turn away.

DHS also expects schools to "steer students toward post-completion OPT only" under the fee structure. The agency's own proposal predicts it will distort student decision-making away from pre-completion OPT, which exists because early work experience helps students land. When your rule needs a disclaimer about the behavior it will cause, that is the rule telling you what it costs.

There is a promise at stake, too. We brought these students to this country, and in doing so we entered into a social contract with them: an American education came with practical training attached. That was the value of our education to the world — not just the degree, but the chance to do the work. A $70,000 price on the university's recommendation breaks that promise after students have already invested years and tuition. The world notices when America's word on its own education does not hold.

Here is what $70,000 buys the American economy under this rule: nothing. The fees go to the general Treasury, not to the SEVP system that administers OPT. American workers, whose protection is the stated goal, gain no jobs from a rule that makes universities poorer and hiring new graduates more expensive.

If fraud is the problem, price the enforcement at the fraud. At $70,000, this isn't enforcement. It's a velvet rope — hung across the university door.

Withdraw the proposal.

Respectfully submitted,
Richard Spicer
Founder & CEO, OPT Global

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am an international student pursuing my bachelor's degree at a public university in the United States. Like many international students, I left behind my family, friends, and everything familiar to pursue an education and build a better professional future.

Studying in the United States has been one of the most rewarding experiences of my life, but also one of the most emotionally and financially challenging. My family has made countless sacrifices to give me this opportunity, and every day I carry the responsibility of making those sacrifices worth it.

International students contribute to the American economy throughout our education. We pay tuition, rent, utilities, transportation, and everyday living expenses. We support local businesses and contribute to our university communities. Our families invest years of savings into an American education, believing in the value of the knowledge and professional experience we can gain here.

For students like me, Optional Practical Training (OPT) is much more than work authorization. It represents the opportunity to apply years of education, dedication, and sacrifice in a professional environment. It allows us to gain practical experience directly related to our degrees, understand the American workforce, and develop skills that will benefit our future careers.

Throughout my education, I have worked incredibly hard to succeed academically, gain professional experience through internships, and become involved in my university community. I have followed the rules, maintained my legal status, and done everything expected of me as an international student.

The possibility of a $70,000 OPT fee is heartbreaking. Even if this fee is imposed on universities rather than directly on students, its consequences would ultimately affect students like me. I attend a public university, and I worry that institutions simply would not have the resources to pay such an extraordinary amount for every international student seeking OPT.

My family has already invested so much in my education. They have supported me financially and emotionally through years of living far away from home. It is devastating to think that after years of hard work, the opportunity to use my degree could be taken away, not because I lack qualifications, dedication, or ambition, but because the institution I attend may not be able to afford such an enormous fee.

What hurts the most is knowing that so many international students have spent years preparing for the opportunity to gain practical experience after graduation. We have built friendships, professional relationships, and dreams here. We have contributed to our universities and communities, and we genuinely want to contribute through practical training related to everything we have studied.

I am approaching graduation in 2027, and instead of feeling only excitement and pride about everything I have accomplished, I find myself feeling anxious and uncertain about whether I will even have the opportunity to pursue the professional experience I have spent years preparing for.

I think about my family back home, how proud they are of me, and everything they have sacrificed to help me get here. The thought of telling them that years of dedication and financial investment may not lead to the practical training opportunity we had planned for is heartbreaking.

I understand that studying and working through authorized practical training in the United States is a privilege, and I have never taken that privilege for granted. I respect the temporary nature of my F-1 status and the importance of following immigration regulations. But I sincerely believe that access to practical training should be based on academic eligibility, qualifications, and compliance with the rules, not on whether a university can afford an extraordinary additional fee.

I respectfully ask you to consider the real people and families behind this proposal. Behind every international student is a story of sacrifice, courage, hope, and a family that believed in a dream. We are not just immigration statistics or sources of revenue. We are students and future professionals who have invested years in an American education.

Please consider how this financial barrier could prevent qualified students from accessing the temporary practical training opportunity they have worked so hard to prepare for. All we are asking for is a fair chance to apply the education we have earned.

Thank you for considering my perspective and the voices of international students whose futures may be affected by this proposal.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Legal Critique: Statutory Overreach and Unconstitutional Taxation
The proposed fee faces substantial vulnerability in federal court under administrative and constitutional law.
Violation of the Administrative Procedure Act (APA). Under the APA, agency actions cannot be "arbitrary and capricious." DHS has not demonstrated how a $70,000 charge—more than 130 times the existing $520 USCIS filing fee—is rationally connected to the actual administrative cost of adjudicating an application or investigating fraud.
Unlawful "Tax" vs. Permissible "User Fee." Under the Independent Offices Appropriations Act (IOAA) and established Supreme Court precedent, executive agencies may charge user fees only to recover the cost of providing a specific benefit or service. Because the proposed revenue is routed directly to the general U.S. Treasury for unspecified purposes rather than earmarked for SEVP or USCIS processing, legal scholars and groups like NAFSA argue the charge functions as an unconstitutional revenue-raising tax, a power reserved exclusively for Congress.
De Facto Repeal of a Statutory Program. By setting a financial barrier that few universities or students can afford, DHS is effectively terminating the OPT program through executive fiat rather than through congressional legislation or transparent rulemaking.
Economic Critique: Self-Inflicted Harm to U.S. Innovation and Higher Education
Rather than protecting the domestic economy, the proposal risks triggering severe financial contraction across U.S. universities and key industries.
Collapse of International Enrollment. International students contribute tens of billions of dollars annually to the U.S. economy and frequently pay full out-of-state tuition, which subsidizes financial aid and research programs for domestic students. According to the American Immigration Council, the fee could trigger a 35% drop in international graduate applicants, resulting in billions in lost university revenue and potential tuition hikes for American students.
Loss of Global STEM Competitiveness. OPT—and particularly the two-year STEM OPT extension—serves as the primary talent pipeline for U.S. research labs, healthcare systems, and technology startups. Pricing graduates out of post-completion training pushes U.S.-educated scientists and engineers directly into competing economies like Canada, the United Kingdom, and the European Union.
Disproportionate Impact on Small Businesses and Nonprofits. While mega-cap corporations might occasionally absorb exorbitant sponsorship costs for select hires, public universities, rural hospitals, non-profit research institutes, and early-stage startups cannot pay $70,000 to $100,000 per graduate, consolidating talent exclusively among the wealthiest corporate employers.
Humanitarian and Equity Critique: Socioeconomic Exclusion and Precarity
From a human impact perspective, the rule undermines educational equity and destabilizes the lives of compliant students.
Wealth-Based Gatekeeping. Practical training is designed to be an experiential extension of a student's academic curriculum, evaluated on merit and academic alignment. Attaching a $70,000 price tag transforms educational opportunity into an auction, ensuring that only students from ultra-wealthy backgrounds—or those backed by affluent institutions—can access hands-on training in their fields.
Punishing Compliant Students for Institutional Oversight Gaps. DHS justifies the fee as a mechanism to force universities to police fraud. However, shifting a massive financial penalty onto the recommendation process punishes hundreds of thousands of law-abiding students who have already invested life savings and years of hard work into accredited U.S. degrees under existing rules.
Sudden Disruption of Life Plans. F-1 students make multi-year financial and personal commitments to study in the United States with the legitimate expectation of gaining practical experience before returning home or pursuing further sponsorship. Abruptly erecting an insurmountable financial wall mid-degree leaves students stranded with heavy educational debt and no viable pathway to apply their training.
Having supervised students on OPT, I can attest to the value this program generates for employers and students alike.
Thank you for your consideration.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose the proposed OPT fee structure of $70,000/$30,000. While I recognize DHS's responsibility to protect program integrity and prevent fraud, this proposal creates disproportionate financial, operational, and educational consequences for American universities, international students, and the broader U.S. economy.

1. Misalignment with Statutory Intent and Administrative Overreach

These fees are not reasonable cost-recovery measures; they are prohibitive financial barriers that could effectively eliminate OPT opportunities for many students and institutions. The proposed amounts are disproportionate to the administrative purpose they serve. Furthermore, directing collected revenue into general Treasury funds rather than dedicated OPT oversight raises questions about the connection between these fees and their stated anti-fraud objectives.

2. Severe Financial and Operational Impact on Higher Education

Placing this financial responsibility on colleges and universities creates an unfunded institutional mandate. Nonprofit, faith-based, and mid-sized institutions cannot reasonably absorb tens of thousands of dollars in additional expenses. The impact would disproportionately affect education, nonprofit, religious, humanitarian, and early-stage research sectors, which often lack the financial resources of large corporations but provide tremendous value to American communities.

3. Misunderstanding of Institutional Oversight and DSO Responsibilities

Designated School Officials (DSOs) already fulfill significant regulatory responsibilities through SEVIS record management, required reporting, and employment verification. Universities are active partners in ensuring compliance. Imposing extraordinary financial liability does not inherently improve oversight or reporting accuracy; it penalizes institutions for fulfilling their existing regulatory duties.

Practical training is also a natural extension of higher education. The opportunity to apply academic knowledge professionally strengthens the value of a degree. Disconnecting post-graduate training from the educational mission disregards the relationship between academic preparation and real-world application.

4. Broad Economic and U.S. Workforce Consequences

OPT strengthens America's talent pipeline by allowing international graduates to contribute to U.S. businesses, research, education, and nonprofits. These contributions address workforce needs, advance research, and drive innovation.

The United States is competing globally for talented students and professionals. Prohibitive OPT fees risk driving exceptional talent toward countries such as Canada, the United Kingdom, and Australia, weakening America's competitiveness in higher education and the global workforce.

My Request

I respectfully urge DHS to reconsider and withdraw this proposed fee structure. Protecting program integrity is important, but enforcement measures must be reasonable, proportionate, transparent, and aligned with actual administrative costs. Higher education institutions and DSOs must be included in developing practical solutions.

International students are more than temporary participants in our educational system. They are students, researchers, professionals, and contributors to American communities. We can strengthen program integrity without undermining the institutions that make American higher education globally respected.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly states strong opposition to the proposed prohibitive OPT fee structure.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose the proposed fees of $70,000 for initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) and $30,000 for subsequent OPT. These fees are excessive, financially prohibitive, and counterproductive to the interests of American universities, employers, and the U.S. economy.

1. Unreasonable Financial Burden on International Students

A $70,000 fee for initial OPT is an extraordinary financial burden for international students, many of whom have already invested substantial personal and family resources in pursuing higher education in the United States. Most students do not have the financial means to pay such an amount, particularly when transitioning from student status to their first professional employment.

This proposal would effectively make OPT accessible only to individuals with significant financial resources rather than those with strong educational qualifications and professional merit. It would disproportionately disadvantage students from lower- and middle-income backgrounds and undermine the accessibility and fairness of American higher education.

2. Harm to American Universities, Research, and Employers

International students are essential contributors to the U.S. academic and research community. They participate in scientific discoveries, laboratory research, technological advancement, and innovation. Many graduate students spend years conducting research at American universities, contributing to research projects and advancing knowledge in critical fields.

Preventing these graduates from participating in OPT would disrupt the transition from academic research to professional employment. American universities, research institutions, and companies would lose access to a substantial pool of highly educated and trained talent. This would ultimately weaken the country’s research capacity and economic competitiveness.

3. Disproportionate and Ineffective Fraud Prevention

Preventing immigration fraud and protecting the integrity of the immigration system are legitimate government objectives. However, imposing fees of $70,000 and $30,000 on students is neither a reasonable nor a targeted solution.

An individual’s financial resources have no meaningful relationship to whether they comply with OPT requirements. High fees do not establish the legitimacy of employment or prevent fraudulent reporting. If fraud prevention is the objective, the government should strengthen employer verification, conduct targeted compliance audits, improve oversight of participating institutions, and enforce existing regulations against fraudulent employment arrangements. These measures would address potential abuse without indiscriminately penalizing legitimate students.

4. Undermining America’s Global Competitiveness

International students choose the United States because of its world-class universities, research opportunities, and professional development prospects. The opportunity to gain practical experience after graduation is an important consideration when deciding where to pursue higher education.

A $70,000 OPT fee would send a message that international graduates are no longer welcome to contribute their expertise unless they can afford an extraordinary financial payment. Other countries actively compete to attract international graduates and skilled professionals. This proposal risks driving talented scientists, engineers, researchers, and entrepreneurs elsewhere, resulting in lost innovation, research capacity, and economic opportunities for the United States.

5. Unfair Treatment of Law-Abiding Students

International students have made significant commitments to their education in the United States. They have complied with visa requirements, maintained their legal status, paid substantial tuition, and contributed to their universities and communities. They should not be collectively subjected to financially prohibitive fees based on generalized concerns about potential fraud. Immigration enforcement should target actual violations rather than penalize students who have consistently followed the rules.

Conclusion and Request

I urge the Department to withdraw this proposal and reject the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent OPT fee.

If the government identifies weaknesses in the OPT program, it should pursue evidence-based, narrowly tailored enforcement measures that target fraudulent actors rather than impose financially prohibitive fees on all international students.

OPT is an important bridge between American higher education and the U.S. workforce. Preserving this opportunity benefits international students, American universities, employers, research institutions, and the broader U.S. economy. The United States should remain a country that attracts exceptional global talent and enables educated individuals to contribute to its scientific, technological, and economic advancement. This proposal would undermine those goals.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes the excessive proposed OPT fees, arguing they burden students and harm the U.S. economy.

Architecture programs (often STEM-designated) foster global perspectives essential for addressing the country’s policy priorities, including efficient design of cities and buildings, resilience against disasters, and robust infrastructure supporting American business interests. comments.commentText:
I am writing in avid support of the new OPT changes due to the reasons provided in the description of the change. However, there’s a few areas I’d like to focus on.

The first, and arguably most important factor, is how OPT has affected the job market for Americans, particularly those looking to start their careers. As stated in the description, “according to the Presidential Proclamation, Restriction on Entry of Certain Nonimmigrant Workers, “among college graduates ages 22 to 27, computer science and computer engineering majors face some of the highest unemployment rates in the country at 6.1 percent and 7.5 percent, respectively—more than double the unemployment rates of recent biology and art history graduates.”” These early career years are oftentimes the most difficult in obtaining and keeping employment due to the need to gain experience to provide value. And while some claim that OPT helps fill a theoretical gap of knowledge workers (which is not the actual intent), the numbers indicate that this gap does not exist and actually adversely impacts the early careers of Americans. I see hundreds of applications for early career STEM related roles, indicting an oversupply of candidates. And when those looking to start their careers see the numbers of applications, the stories of layoffs in STEM, and the hardships to get back on their feet, whether in that same STEM field or in a completely different field unrelated to STEM due to the job market struggles, those early career Americans often move away from pursuing those STEM related roles, resulting in America itself losing the ability to generate its own knowledge workers. Sadly, as someone in an early career STEM role, I’ve seen these hardships first hand and have had to advise my younger family members, those in rural and poor parts of America looking to make a better life for themselves, to avoid STEM at this time due to the unpredictability of the job market.

Secondly, the description also calls out the costs associated with monitoring OPT for the purposes of preventing fraud and other misuse. As stated, “DHS notes that without the fees proposed in this rule, it cannot operate OPT consistent with its focus on preventing fraud.” These additional fees help ensure that the costs associated with the program are helped to be funded by the program itself. This prevents an imbalance where costs are incurred without a clear, direct supporting source and ensures that funding to prevent misuse of OPT is not taken from other programs that are already struggling with tight budgets and cutbacks. While the fees will naturally decrease the number of those pursuing OPT, this will actually support a fairer and more cost effective OPT as the description also states that “a reduction in the pool of OPT applicants, along with the stabilization of participant numbers, would alleviate DHS's resource burden tied to enforcement activities related to OPT and enable the agency to conduct more focused and efficient oversight of SEVP programs.”

Overall, due to the need to protect American workers (both from worker fraud and an increased tightness in the labor market) along with better, more direct funding of said programs, I am in avid support of this change.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly states avid support for the new OPT changes due to impacts on the US job market.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Alfred Tang
comments.commentText:
Dear Secretary Mullin,

I got my BS in physics from MIT in 1987, received two masters in theology from Biola University in 1991 and 1997 and received my PhD in physics from University of Wisconsin in Milwaukee in 2002. I was a foreign student in US and deeply appreciate the opportunities that I had in the home of my heart--i.e. USA--even though I live in Hong Kong now. During my foreign student days, I benefited from gaining physics experience through OPT. As a poor student, I did not have any financial resources. The money earned during OPT was helpful to pay the bills but it was the hands-on experience that was priceless. I would not be able to afford OPT if it costed a lot of money upfront. As a former foreign student, I continue to contribute to US interests while living in Hong Kong because I want to pay back what I received from US.

I'm writing to express my opposition to the excessive OPT fees proposed in DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, "Optional Practical Training Fees". As explained in the American Physical Society's public comment (ICEB-2026-0100-2924), the proposed $70,000 initial recommendation fee and subsequent $30,000 extension fee to be levied on universities would likely put OPT out of reach for essentially all international students. Such fees would shatter the U.S. STEM talent pipeline, forcing international, high-skilled students and graduates trained at U.S. institutions to leave the U.S. for competing nations.

Increased fees in OPT may not directly impact my decision to study in US. But it may impact my decision to stay in US after my education. There are a lot of opportunities for highly skilled workers in other countries such as China. OPT is a good way to retain talents in US.

There are not enough Americans to take up high skilled tech jobs. The international tech talents pool remain pretty constant. The percentage of intelligent and hard working tech workers in any population is about same throughout time. Every country is competing for same talent pool worldwide--either US, China, India or Europe. If US fails to retain the high skilled foreign students, other countries (notably China) will welcome them. In that case, US loses out.

Once again, I ask you to withdraw this proposed rule. Our economy, national security, and international influence depend on it.

Sincerely,
Alfred Tang
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed OPT fees are excessive and would harm the U.S. STEM talent pipeline.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am writing to express my concerns about the proposed OPT fees and to recommend substantial revisions, particularly to Sections V.A, V.C, and VI.

As someone who studied in the United States and subsequently entered the U.S. workforce, I have experienced firsthand the importance of opportunities to apply academic knowledge in professional settings. OPT provides a valuable bridge between education and employment, benefiting both international graduates and American employers.

The proposed $70,000 initial fee and $30,000 subsequent fee would create substantial financial barriers. Although institutions would formally pay these fees, the costs could ultimately be passed on to students or lead universities to limit OPT recommendations. This would disproportionately disadvantage students with fewer financial resources, making access to practical training depend more on institutional funding and personal wealth than academic qualifications or professional potential.

I recognize DHS's legitimate interests in preventing fraud and protecting U.S. workers. However, imposing such substantial fees on institutions recommending eligible students does not necessarily distinguish fraudulent participation from legitimate training. More targeted compliance monitoring, verification, and enforcement could address these concerns without broadly restricting opportunities for qualified graduates.

The proposal also raises serious reliance concerns. Many current students chose U.S. universities and made significant financial commitments under an established framework that included OPT opportunities. Although the proposed rule provides a transition period, students who have not yet received OPT recommendations could still face unexpected barriers after years of investment.

Beyond individual students, these fees could reduce the international competitiveness of American universities and discourage talented graduates from contributing their skills to the U.S. economy.

I respectfully urge DHS to reconsider the proposed fee amounts, evaluate less burdensome fraud-prevention alternatives, and provide meaningful protections for students already enrolled in U.S. institutions. Any revised fee structure should be proportionate, evidence-based, and designed to preserve legitimate educational and professional opportunities.

Thank you for considering my comments.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed OPT fees create substantial financial barriers and recommends substantial revisions.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Jessica Winderweedle
comments.commentText:
To Whom It May Concern,

I write today as a faculty member of the Theological School at Drew University and as a member of the clergy in the United Methodist Church to voice my unequivocal opposition to the recent proposal by the Department of Homeland Security establishing exorbitant fees for those students and recent graduates on F-1 visas wishing to take part in Optional Practical Training employment. I would like to strongly urge the Department of Homeland Security to withdraw this proposal.

These fees–$70,000 for an initial authorization and $30,000 for subsequent authorizations–will serve as a barrier to the vast majority of international students who not only wish to engage in internships during their studies, which provide essential hands-on vocational training, but it will also prevent graduates from garnering entry-level professional experience in the crucial months following their graduation. For theological school students, most of whom are seeking to be ordained as clergy, these pre-completion and post-completion OPT positions make possible the kind of service required of many ordination processes, including in the United Methodist Church. They are also vital experiences where ordination candidates and other emerging religious leaders are able to strengthen their language skills, grow in intercultural competencies, and build important, life-giving relationships with congregations and communities, who in turn, enable the students to support themselves financially during their studies. These relationships are also critically important for the organizations where these students and recent graduates serve; often, OPT participants provide expanded leadership to churches and non-profits that could otherwise not afford such support.

These unreasonable fees are out of the realm of what any student, recent graduate, church, non-profit, or institution of higher education can possibly afford. This is surely not an unknown fact to the government officials who have attempted to institute these fees, which means that the desired result of this rule is to eliminate the possibility of F-1 visa holders from gaining this type of professional training and employment. However, instead of simply eliminating the program, this fee mechanism communicates that only those with extravagant wealth are deserving of opportunities for advancement and betterment. This runs absolutely counter to the message of God’s unconditional love that our theological students have staked their lives and careers on. They are more than worthy of these opportunities, and our churches and non-profits stand to benefit greatly from the kind of passionate, capable leaders who participate in OPT programs.

I respectfully request that this rule, which is harmful and unjust, be withdrawn.

Sincerely,

The Rev. Dr. Jess Winderweedle
Assistant Teaching Professor of Preaching
Interim Director of Vocational Placement
The Theological School at Drew University
comments.reason: The commenter strongly urges DHS to withdraw the proposal, arguing the exorbitant fees create barriers for students.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am a small business owner that has greatly benefitted from the Optional Practical Training (OPT) program. A few months ago, a member of my staff who had done accounts payable processing for over 30 years abruptly left. I reached out to the local county college who introduced me to a talented, straight A student finishing up her associates degree and eager to begin learning the hands on nature of the accounting profession on the OPT program. She started with us, and has since blossomed into a highly valuable team member who has assisted in streamlining our processes. Had it not been for the OPT program, I would not have been introduced to top talent with fantastic growth potential. The OPT program allows small businesses like mine to meet top talent while also being introduced to a more global way of thinking. Her bilingual skills have been an added bonus I did not know I needed!

The currently proposed OPT fees would have prevented me from bringing this individual onto our team. These fees should not be applied to businesses 25 employees or under. A carve out to exempt those size businesses must be included as this rule is finalized. Businesses of that size are bringing on students from the OPT program to meet top talent and grow their operations, not to enrich a software development process.

The American economy, and by extension, the American dream have been built on the hard work, education, and talent of immigrants. Small businesses are the engine of that American dream; to enact a fee that drastically prohibits the small business from accessing the talent they need to grow would stifle this growth.
