comments.title: Comment Submitted by Emily Pottebaum
comments.commentText:
I am a US citizen in the 5th year of my PhD in physics, and I strongly oppose the proposed OPT fee. In the 8 years I have been involved in particle and nuclear physics research, I have worked with many international students on F-1 visas who had invaluable contributions to make to the field. As an undergraduate I was mentored by a postdoc in the OPT program whose guidance motivated me to pursue graduate school, and in graduate school I have seen firsthand how work from students on F-1 visas and those in the STEM OPT program have benefited American science on the daily. Many of my US-based international colleagues have said they would like to pursue a career in research in the United States--our country's scientific leadership is owed in no small part to the immeasurable talent of people from all over the world who come to the US to do science. Especially given the current state of reduced funding from government agencies, very few (if any!) research groups and universities will be able to cover the $70,000-$100,000 fee for OPT/STEM OPT.

These proposed changes will serve to directly harm American science. My own dissertation research is an extension of work done by current and former F-1 visa holders, who I can't imagine would have been inclined to come to the US and stay here after graduating had OPT been as inaccessible as this rule would make it be at the time they were applying to graduate schools and postdoc positions. Several of my collaborators at a national lab near my institution, with whom I work on a near daily basis, are in the STEM OPT program. With these fees in place preventing future positions at this lab for my international colleagues, my research, which relies on collaboration, will suffer for it.

I urge the Department of Homeland Security to withdraw this rule. Respectfully, implementing such a fee will be shooting ourselves in the foot when it comes to American leadership in science.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed OPT fee will harm American science, research groups, and international students.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I oppose the proposed OPT fees. This comment addresses a question DHS asked the public about: how the fees work when a student earns degrees at more than one educational level, often at more than one school. Under the rule, the fee depends on the student's OPT history, not on the school making the recommendation. That breaks the rule's own logic.

1. One student, two schools, two different prices
OPT "can be authorized for up to 12 months at each educational level." Proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)(1) charges $70,000 "the first time" a student is recommended for OPT. Paragraph (i)(2) charges $30,000 for any later recommendation. Nothing ties either charge to the school. So the first school to recommend OPT pays $70,000. Any later school pays $30,000 for its own, separate recommendation. A college that recommends OPT after a bachelor's degree pays the full amount. The university that later recommends the same student after a master's degree pays less than half, though it makes its own decision about a new degree, job and OPT period.

2. The stake DHS wants schools to hold does not follow the decision
DHS says the fee gives schools "a direct stake in the integrity of the OPT program" and makes them "more selective and deliberate." If that is the theory, each school's stake should match its own decision. Under this rule, a graduate school's stake shrinks by $40,000 because a different institution paid years earlier. The first school's payment buys nothing for its own oversight of the later OPT, which it does not recommend or monitor.

3. The price runs opposite to DHS's vetting rationale
DHS sets the initial fee higher because students "may not have been vetted by the U.S. Government since their initial application for an F-1 visa." A student finishing a second degree has usually been in the United States longer, and further from that visa vetting, than a first-time OPT applicant. Under this rule that student is cheaper to recommend. A master's student who came straight from a bachelor's program abroad costs the school $70,000. A master's student who already used OPT in the United States costs $30,000. The fee schedule tracks payment history, not the vetting gap DHS names. Footnote 115 points to extension-of-stay vetting under the Duration of Status rule, which was postponed in Presidents' Alliance v. DHS, No. 26-cv-13799 (D. Mass. Sept. 14, 2026).

4. It distorts admissions and pushes the largest charge to the first school
A graduate program weighing two equal applicants can see that one costs $40,000 less to recommend for OPT. The rule also gives each school a reason to let a later school pay the $70,000. The first school in the chain is often a smaller college, and sometimes a community college recommending OPT after an associate degree. Those schools have the least money and the shortest relationship with the student, yet they would carry the largest charge.

5. DHS did not model any of this
The regulatory impact analysis "applies the initial fee of $70,000 to the OPT participation data and applies the subsequent fee of $30,000 to the STEM OPT participation data." It never counts students who use OPT at more than one educational level, never says which schools would pay which fee, and never estimates the admissions or recommendation shifts described above. DHS cannot judge the alternative it asks about without that count.

6. The alternative DHS floated would make it worse
DHS asks for comment on charging $70,000 again at each new educational level. That would remove the cross-school discount, but only by charging $140,000 or more to students who earn two degrees here and $30,000 more for any STEM extension. It would hit hardest the students who invest most in U.S. education. DHS offers no evidence that second-degree students commit more fraud. DHS should reject this alternative.

7. The text leaves cross-school questions open
Paragraph (i)(2) applies if "the alien has previously participated in OPT and paid the initial OPT fee." The alien does not pay; a school does. The rule does not say how a second school confirms another school's payment, or what happens if the first school later received a refund. DHS states the rule meets E.O. 12988's standard of "a clear legal standard for affected conduct." On this point it does not.

8. Request
DHS should withdraw the proposed rule. If it re-proposes any fee, it should (a) reject the repeat $70,000 alternative; (b) stop making one school's charge depend on another school's past payment; (c) publish SEVIS counts of students with OPT at more than one educational level and at more than one school; and (d) explain how any fee schedule fits its stated vetting and school-accountability goals for these students.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes the proposed OPT fees and argues that the fee structure is illogical.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Brennan Y
comments.commentText:
I am a graduate student in speech-language pathology (SLP), a healthcare field that diagnoses and treats disorders related to language, communication, voice, and swallowing. I am opposed to ICEB-2026-0100 because of the negative effects it will have on my profession and on healthcare as a whole.

Many of my fellow graduate students hold F-1 visas and hope to practice SLP in the US after graduation, which they can only do if they complete a year of fellowship training (i.e., an OPT). This proposed financial barrier will keep my classmates from contributing the demonstrated skill and expertise that only they can bring to this field, at a time when demand for healthcare workers is increasing faster than we can keep up with as a country.

In order to practice as an SLP, one must complete a clinical fellowship year, which qualifies as an OPT for international students holding an F-1 visa. In this sense, it is not an "optional" training period as Section D1 of the proposal describes; yet, these positions fall into this wide category (1). Our field needs more practitioners than are graduating into the field each year, and international students help meet this growing demand. In addition to their labor, international students' diverse perspectives and backgrounds help the field grow, and ensure culturally and linguistically appropriate care for all people who need it. This proposal will reduce the number of qualified professionals across healthcare disciplines in what is a growing shortage of healthcare professionals nationwide.

US healthcare is facing dire staffing shortages across disciplines (2), and SLP is no exception (3). Because of the US's aging population and the over-twofold increase in childhood language delays since the COVID-19 pandemic (4), the demand for SLPs is skyrocketing, with the Bureau of Labor Statistics predicting that SLP as a field will grow by over 15% over the 2024–2034 decade (5). Meanwhile, SLP graduate programs are already failing to keep up with current demands, with 55% of surveyed SLPs reporting that job openings exceeded applicants in their area in 2025 (3). More people need more SLPs than are graduating into the workforce each year, and that is only going to worsen as the population continues to age and children continue to experience COVID-related language consequences. We need international students to help fill these gaps.

International healthcare workers have bolstered the healthcare workforce in the midst of growing professional shortages, and are historically more willing to take on lower-paying jobs in underserved areas when compared to their US-born counterparts (6). International SLP students take on a special commitment to practicing in the US, as an SLP certificate is not valid in other countries.

In a field as demographically homogeneous as SLP, international students are key to ensuring culturally and linguistically appropriate care for all Americans. 80% of SLPs identify as white, and over 90% are women (7). A 2021 report found that less than 10% of SLPs are bilingual (8), while nearly a fifth of all Americans are bilingual (9). People who speak languages other than English and come from other racial and ethnic backgrounds need care that is culturally and linguistically appropriate, and it will only become harder for them to find it if fewer international students enter the workforce in the coming years. A diverse SLP workforce is key to the growth and health of the field, and including international students will help us meet these demands.

International students in healthcare fields train to fill the growing gaps in our healthcare system, and are a vital piece of ensuring that Americans receive the care they need. The passage of ICEB-2026-0100 would keep the American healthcare system from accepting help that it badly needs, and throw a wrench in the lives of people working to provide it.

(Please refer to the attached document for sources.)
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed OPT fee harms healthcare staffing and creates a barrier for speech-language pathology students.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Central Coordinating Committee of TRU-UE Local 197
comments.submitterName: Central Coordinating Committee of TRU-UE Local 197
comments.commentText:
We write as the Central Coordinating Committee of TRU-UE Local 197, the union representing all graduate workers at the Johns Hopkins University in Maryland, urging the administration a reconsideration of the proposed rule change and a return to the long-standing OPT status quo.

For decades, Optional Practical Training (OPT) has provided international students critical access to experiential learning and benefited the U.S. economy and the US workforce. The USA’s reputation as the top destination for global talent and ultimately, its preeminence in research and innovation, will take a devastating hit if OPT fees of this calibre are applied. With 66 percent of international students affirming they would go elsewhere or consider going elsewhere if those opportunities were not available, OPT is one of the main pillars maintaining the US’ standing as the leading destination for global talent.

Over 70% of doctoral graduates at Hopkins use OPT upon graduation according to the Institute For Progress’ SEVIS analysis, which also projects a 79% decline in OPT starts if universities have to pay the full cost of a $100k OPT fee. The impact of this proposed rule is thus completely disproportionate and would functionally close down the entire OPT pipeline.

This is an issue for the U.S. economy too, which benefits an incredible amount from the contributions of international students and the jobs they create for American workers. According to NAFSA, international students and their families contributed $42.9 billion dollars and 355,736 jobs to the U.S. economy during the 2024-2025 academic year. In Maryland, where Johns Hopkins is based, 26,636 international students contributed $1.0 billion dollars to the state and over 9,850 jobs.

The impact that this loss would have would also directly impact the fees of domestic workers, the Institute for Progress estimates that the proposed OPT fee would directly entail about 46,000 fewer Americans enrolling in bachelor’s and master’s programs each year due to rising costs of tuition to compensate for international enrollment losses.

DHS does not account for the effect of these OPT changes on local, regional, or state economies, nor to the broader American research landscape. Hopkins’ international community is a large part of what makes this university an internationally recognized institution. This abusive and arbitrary price tag means losing them, alongside the US’ standing as the leading destination for global talent. It also means fewer opportunities for American workers, higher tuition for American students and a major hit to the American economy.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed OPT fees will harm international students and the U.S. economy.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Re: DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, Optional Practical Training Fees, 91 FR 64566 (Oct. 8, 2026)

This proposal should be withdrawn.

OPT is the bridge between a US degree and US work experience. Students earn the degree, follow every rule, and then use OPT to do the job the degree trained them for. A $70,000 fee before a school can recommend a student for OPT, and $30,000 for each later recommendation, would break that bridge.

The fee is far beyond what schools can absorb, and the proposal itself says schools may pass the cost to students or employers. The predictable result is that schools stop recommending OPT and employers stop hiring OPT graduates. The people harmed would be the ones who did everything right: admitted lawfully, studied lawfully, and graduated.

DHS itself estimates this fee would collect about $12.4 billion a year. A charge of that size is not a processing fee. It is a barrier that ends the program in practice while keeping it on paper. Please withdraw the proposal.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Re: Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, Optional Practical Training Fees (91 FR 64566)

I am a faculty on the West Coast -- a health sciences school. I am commenting in my individual capacity. I strongly oppose the proposed $70,000 initial and $30,000 subsequent OPT fees, and I urge DHS to withdraw the rule.

1. Direct harm to biomedical and health research. At health sciences schools, international graduates on OPT and STEM OPT work as research staff, postdoctoral trainees, data analysts, and laboratory scientists. Their work covers drug development, infectious disease, clinical trials, genomics, and public health research, and much of it is federally funded. A trainee using post-completion OPT plus a STEM extension would cost $100,000 in fees. That is more than a year of a postdoc's salary and benefits. Grants generally cannot pay such fees, and departmental funds cannot absorb them. Labs will lose trained staff, and projects will slow or stop, after taxpayers have already invested in training these scientists.

2. Rationing by wealth, not merit. DHS expects the fee to shrink OPT participation by making schools more selective. But whether a school can pay $70,000 says nothing about a student's merit or the value of their training. Smaller, public, and under-resourced health professions schools will be shut out entirely.

3. Damage to recruitment. Strong international applicants in biomedical sciences, epidemiology, biostatistics, and pharmaceutical sciences will choose Canada, the UK, Australia, and Germany instead. Smaller graduate cohorts mean fewer researchers and less discovery. They also mean a weaker pipeline for future U.S. faculty and industry scientists.

4. Likely unlawful. The proposal cites no statute that expressly authorizes an OPT fee. Instead, it relies on general authority over the conditions of nonimmigrant admission. DHS concedes that ICE cannot keep the money, so it would go to the general Treasury. The amount is benchmarked to tuition and H-1B fees, not to any cost of administering OPT. A charge that is unrelated to the cost of a service and is deposited in the Treasury is a tax, and taxing power belongs to Congress. Courts have already held that general regulatory authority does not allow agencies to charge the public as a condition of an activity, and they have relied on that reasoning against the $100,000 H-1B fee. If finalized, this rule will face Administrative Procedure Act challenges on several grounds: it exceeds statutory authority, it is arbitrary and capricious, it ignores alternatives and reliance interests, and it allows only 30 days of comment on a rule of this significance. Years of litigation and uncertainty would follow, and that is itself a harm DHS has not considered.

5. Better alternatives ignored. DHS considered extending existing STEM OPT safeguards, such as training plans, site visits, and reporting, to all OPT, and rejected that approach. If the problem is fraud by shell companies and suspect employers, the answer is targeted enforcement against those employers. A blanket charge on every school punishes legitimate students and does nothing directly to bad actors.

6. Incomplete economic analysis. DHS's analysis leaves out major costs. DHS must account for lost research output on federally funded projects, lost tuition and teaching capacity, and effects on the health care and life sciences workforce. It must also account for the disproportionate effects on smaller institutions and the costs of litigation and uncertainty.

OPT has strengthened American science and health care for decades. This fee would ration training by institutional wealth and drive talented scientists abroad. I urge DHS to withdraw the proposed rule and to address fraud through targeted enforcement.

Views are my own and do not represent my institution.
comments.reason: The commenter strongly opposes the proposed OPT fees and urges DHS to withdraw the rule.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by TAEYA HILLMAN-JOHNSON
comments.commentText:
In my work with international student recruitment and engagement, I help students learn about the opportunities available at Mt. Hood Community College and consider whether our institution is a good fit for their educational goals.

Students are making a significant investment when they choose to study in the United States. Their decision involves more than the classroom experience; they also consider how their education may prepare them for future employment and career opportunities. The ability to pursue eligible Optional Practical Training is an important part of that conversation.

With the proposed changes, our college would no longer be able to afford to recommend students for OPT. That limitation would affect how we communicate the value of studying here and could influence students’ decisions about where to enroll. It could also undermine the trust students place in their institution when they make plans based on the opportunities available to them.

I urge DHS to reconsider this proposal and avoid creating a fee structure that makes OPT inaccessible to students at institutions with limited financial resources
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed fee makes OPT inaccessible and urges DHS to reconsider.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Gerald Dunne
comments.commentText:
Dear Secretary Mullin,

My name is Gerald Dunne and I am a professor of physics at UConn.

I'm writing to express my opposition to the excessive OPT fees proposed in DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, "Optional Practical Training Fees". As explained in the American Physical Society's public comment (ICEB-2026-0100-2924), the proposed $70,000 initial recommendation fee and subsequent $30,000 extension fee to be levied on universities would likely put OPT out of reach for essentially all international students. Such fees would shatter the U.S. STEM talent pipeline, forcing international, high-skilled students and graduates trained at U.S. institutions to leave the U.S. for competing nations.

The propose increase will be devastating for our ability to attract the best minds in the world to contribute to US research and development.

It is important to attract the very best from all over the world, bringing talent and competition to the research and development process.

Once again, I ask you to withdraw this proposed rule. Our economy, national security, and international influence depend on it.

Sincerely,
Gerald Dunne
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed OPT fees are excessive and asks to withdraw the rule to protect the U.S. STEM talent pipeline.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Van Andel Research Institute
comments.commentText:
Dear Acting Director Venturella,

On behalf of the Van Andel Research Institute (VARI), we write in opposition to the U.S. Department of Homeland Security (DHS)'s proposed rule, Optional Practical Training Fees. While we share DHS's interest in preserving the integrity of the Optional Practical Training (OPT) program, this rule would impose severe burdens on small, independent research institutes like ours and place the cost of OPT misuse on institutions and students who follow the rules, rather than on those who violate them. We urge DHS to withdraw the rule.

The proposed fees would either divert funding from research or end OPT access for our students. VARI is a nonprofit biomedical research institute in Grand Rapids, Michigan with a doctoral program. Our PhD students pay no tuition and receive a fixed stipend. Over one third of our PhD students hold F-1 status, and we expect one to five OPT recommendations per year over the next five years. If each graduate uses the STEM extension, fees for 15 new graduates between 2027 and 2031 ($1,050,000) and 11 extensions ($330,000) would total over $1.3 million in five years. With no tuition revenue, this cost would come from research funds; students living on stipends cannot bear it. DHS's small-institution analysis measures revenue by tuition, room, and board, overlooking tuition-free doctoral programs like ours. DHS acknowledges some small institutions "may be unable to secure such funding." For students at compliant, tuition-free programs, the fee would not ensure "that legitimate participants continue to benefit from its opportunities"; it would end their access.

We also oppose a second initial fee for students who completed OPT at a prior institution. DHS asks for comment on charging a new $70,000 initial fee when a student begins OPT at a higher degree level. Some of our F-1 students completed OPT at another U.S. school; under this rule, VARI would owe $70,000 for a student whose initial fee was already paid, though neither school violated any OPT requirement. One student's practical training should not trigger more than one initial fee.

Additionally, a flat fee does not target fraud; it penalizes compliant institutions. Before recommending OPT, we meet with each student to verify continuity between their degree, training, and planned employment. For STEM OPT, we review each training plan to confirm it is genuine, and that the employer will provide appropriate training. Under the proposed rule, an institution that meets every OPT requirement would pay the same fee as one that knowingly misuses the program. This is unfair and does little to deter bad actors who can pay. A fairer alternative is to increase penalties, with due process, on schools and employers found to have knowingly violated OPT requirements, including substantial monetary penalties and loss of OPT eligibility in confirmed fraud cases.

To our knowledge, no accredited college or university, academic medical center, or nonprofit research institute has failed to comply with OPT requirements. DHS's evidence of noncompliance includes "highly suspect employers," staged worksites, and shell companies selling job letters. The school-related cases DHS cites are F-1 visa fraud prosecutions, largely involving for-profit and language schools, not cases of OPT noncompliance. Targeted enforcement may be more burdensome to administer than uniform fees, but it is far fairer to compliant institutions.

Finally, the fees would interrupt research at VARI, which employs 12 researchers on OPT or STEM OPT who trained at other U.S. universities. Their work spans cancer, including pediatric cancer; Parkinson's, Alzheimer's, and other neurodegenerative diseases; structural biology; metabolism; and epigenetics. If these scientists' former schools declined to pay, these projects could face major delays or elimination. Research continuity at VARI should not depend on the budget decisions of other institutions.

Recommendations. Alongside increased penalties for noncompliance, we urge DHS to:
1. Adopt risk-based enforcement that directs audits and penalties toward schools and employers with documented noncompliance, treating nonprofit research institutions, tuition-free doctoral programs, and low-volume schools with strong compliance records as low-risk.
2. Apply new penalties or requirements only to conduct occurring after the effective date and allow at least one academic year before they take effect for schools and employers to update their procedures.
3. Strengthen STEM OPT oversight through existing tools, such as Form I-983 review and employer site visits, and penalize employers that fail to provide certified training.
4. Assign any penalty solely to the school or employer responsible for a violation.

Thank you for considering these comments.

Jonathan D. Licht, M.D.
President and Chief Scientific Officer, Van Andel Research Institute
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed fees impose severe burdens on research institutes and urges DHS to withdraw the rule.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I oppose the proposal of the new fees to OPT.

This fee does not bring labor protection back to the U.S. nor does it guarantee that students who can reliably pay the fee are any more talented than those who couldn’t. This rule, therefore looks more like a shadow ban on the program due to the U.S.’s own grievances with immigrants, especially immigrants of color (as most international students in the U.S. are people of color) than to truly protect the citizens of the States. Below I would like to demonstrate why I make this statement.

OPT as a system is oftentimes utilized (and in many cases, crucial) by graduates or degree-seekers to be able to work as interns, off-campus resesrch assistants, medical scribes, EMTs, and more as the acquisition of these positions can demand students work more than 20 hours per week which would be pass the CPT limit. Graduates do not have a CPT at all so they rely entirely on OPTs. The point of contention is that students can be sponsored with an H-1B. This is not always true. H-1B requires students to be sponsored and most employers will not sponsor an H-1B before students have demonstrated abilities through an OPT (much like how citizens tend not to be hired for higher, more permanent positions before having worked for an employer for an amount of time). An argument can be made to say that this is a case where the faults lay on the employers and not the legitimacy of the OPT program. However, if that is to be the argument then DHS must fix how H-1B can be sponsored and how easily can it be filed because under current rules, H-1B filing simply doesn’t happen quickly enough. This means that for fields where an H-1B is in play, the loss of OPT will result in a loss in international workforce across the board, harming institutions that rely on these talents.

OPT is even more crucial in healthcare. In this argument, I will use the example of the nursing track. Nurses don’t tend to use H-1B; they use EB-3. Unlike EB-1A (which tend to require a PhD) and EB-2NIW, nurses cannot self-petition for an EB-3. With current barriers like the end to automatic EAD extension, international nursing graduates face uncertainty regarding their statuses and whether or not their paperwork can be cleared before their permitted stay runs out. This will simply deter students enough to significantly exacerbate the aready existing nursing shortage in the U.S. I would like to remind DHS and the federal courts that all healthcare positions must be staffed for the system to function.

These two arguments above point to how this proposal hurts both industries and international students but doesn’t address how it fails at wage and labor protection for U.S. citizens. This paragraph aims to do so. Economically speaking, hiring OPT international students is cheaper which is why wage depression happens. However, this is more an argument for more labor protections and oversight, not an argument against the OPT program and international students. The reason being that the incentive for economic benefits outweighs the need to fill all the vacant spots. Say hiring an OPT international student costs $20/hour and hiring a domestic for the same position costs $27/hour. The fee causes 10 vacancies to open up from international students leaving. Firms have more incentives to hire only 3-5 new domestic workers to fill the spots, increasing work load for everyone and increasing pay to $30/hour instead of hiring all 10 new domestics for $27/hour. While pay did increase, clearly worker welfare did not as the amount of hours they get for themselves decreased disproportionately. That is not to mention, as hiring and production get more expensive without new job protection policies beyond kicking out immigrants, firms with the means to do so will simply shift production abroad (which has already happened).

In conclusion, this proposal fails to protect citizens as it claims and will damage industries extensively, especially in healthcare and academia. This proposal only serves as a chilling effect to depress immigration to the United States while providing no benefits to anyone in the States. It is a case of for the cause of anti-immigration, the administration is willing to harm everyone equally.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes the new OPT fees, arguing they act as a shadow ban and harm international students.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
RE: Docket No. ICEB–2026–0100, RIN 1653–AB01, “Optional Practical Training Fees”
The fee bears no relationship to the cost of the service it purports to fund. DHS’s own Regulatory Impact Analysis estimates the actual cost of reviewing and processing each OPT application at roughly $50–$90 per application (Section VII.A.5.a(2), Table 5) — a few dollars, not tens of thousands. A fee set at 1,000 times the administrative cost of the transaction functions as a tax or a bar to entry, not a service fee, and DHS does not explain how a figure “comparable to” the H-1B fee (rather than tied to OPT’s own costs) is a lawful basis for setting it.
The fee is not targeted at the fraud DHS describes. DHS’s own fraud examples (Section IV.A) involve a relatively small number of shell companies and bad-faith employers. Rather than pursuing the alternatives DHS itself identified and rejected. expanded site visits, stronger DSO training, employer vetting (Section VII.B.6), the rule imposes a blanket, six-figure cost on all 194,554+ lawfully participating students and the institutions that sponsor them. This is not narrowly tailored; it punishes the overwhelming legitimate population to reach a small set of violators.
The fee does not fund fraud enforcement. By DHS’s own description, collected fees go to the Treasury as miscellaneous receipts under 31 U.S.C. 3302 and are not earmarked for SEVP oversight (Section IV.C). DHS cannot credibly claim the fee strengthens its enforcement capacity when the revenue is not directed to that purpose.
The agency’s own cost-benefit analysis cannot justify the rule. For an “economically significant” action under E.O. 12866, DHS lists annualized monetized benefits as “Not Estimated” (Table 1) while estimating transfers as high as $17 billion annually and total 10-year costs up to $69.9 billion (Section VII.A.1). An agency cannot reasonably conclude that unquantified, qualitative benefits outweigh quantified costs of this magnitude.
The rule falls hardest on small and under-resourced institutions. DHS’s own data show 56% of affected SEVP-certified schools are small entities, and that under the post-transition period, over 280 small institutions would see fee impacts exceeding 10% of annual revenue (Table 15). DHS considered and rejected a small-institution exemption, meaning this rule will disproportionately push smaller, often non-profit, schools out of OPT sponsorship altogether - concentrating opportunity at the wealthiest institutions, which has nothing to do with fraud prevention.
The fee effectively creates a shadow visa-cap/fee regime that Congress did not authorize. Congress set specific numerical and fee limits for the H-1B program by statute. Using INA 214(a)’s “time and conditions” authority to impose a fee explicitly designed to be “comparable to” and to “closely align with” H-1B fees (Section IV.C) functions as an end-run around Congress’s statutory scheme for employment-based nonimmigrant visas, which DHS has no delegated authority to replicate through a fee on a different, uncapped visa category.
DHS undervalues reliance interests and the fee’s chilling effect on legitimate students and institutions. Many current F-1 students selected their programs years in advance, in part because of OPT availability, yet the rule applies to anyone without a DSO recommendation as of the effective date — including students already mid-program. DHS also does not meaningfully grapple with the fee’s likely effect on U.S. international-student enrollment and the significant economic contributions those students make, dismissing this impact as merely “speculative” (Section VI).

For these reasons, I urge DHS to withdraw the proposed fee structure, or at minimum, substantially reduce the fee to an amount reasonably related to actual administrative costs, and pursue the fraud-specific enforcement alternatives it already identified instead of a blanket fee on the entire legitimate OPT population.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed OPT fee is excessively high, disconnected from actual costs, and harms students and employers.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
A university education is one of the largest financial commitments a person can make. For international students, that commitment often begins years before they arrive in the United States.

Students compare academic programs, tuition costs, living expenses, and opportunities for practical training before deciding where to study. OPT is an important part of that decision because it allows eligible graduates to apply what they have learned in a professional setting.

The proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee could significantly change those expectations.

My concern is not that immigration regulations should never change. Governments have the responsibility to review programs and address problems. The concern is whether major changes should take effect without meaningful protection for people who made long-term commitments under the existing framework.

The proposed 60-day transition period under 8 CFR § 214.13(i)(3) appears particularly inadequate.

A student who is approaching graduation cannot realistically recover years of tuition payments, transfer an entire degree program, or develop an alternative career plan within two months.

Even if the payment obligation formally falls on educational institutions, students may bear the consequences if their schools cannot afford to support OPT recommendations.

This creates uncertainty that could affect confidence in American higher education.

I request that DHS withdraw the proposed fee under § 214.13(i)(1). If any substantial changes are adopted, DHS should provide meaningful grandfathering protections for students already enrolled before the final rule takes effect.

Regulatory predictability matters. Students and institutions need reasonable notice when government decisions affect educational commitments made years in advance.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Aditya Agarwal
comments.commentText:
Comment on DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, "Optional Practical Training Fees"

I write as an F-1 international student at a large public university, graduating in spring 2027 with majors in computer science, data science, and economics, planning to use post-completion OPT and, if eligible, the STEM OPT extension. I submit this comment anonymously.

Under proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i), my school would pay $70,000 before a designated school official may enter my first OPT recommendation, and $30,000 for each later recommendation. DHS openly acknowledges schools "may pass the financial obligation" to F-1 students, all students, or employers. For a 2027 graduate like me, the initial fee is not abstract: it would attach to my first OPT recommendation in my first months out of school, when I have the least bargaining power and would be asked to absorb — through tuition surcharges or employer pass-through — a $70,000 cost, rising to $100,000 with a STEM OPT extension. The school's decision whether to pay, pass through, or stop recommending OPT would be made per student; students at budget-constrained public universities bear the most risk.

DHS justifies the figure as "comparable to the fee for H-1B visas." But for a new graduate, OPT is not an alternative to the H-1B lottery — it is the bridge employment that lets an employer evaluate a graduate before sponsoring them. Pricing a new graduate's first year of U.S. work at $70,000–$100,000 does not deter fraud; it prices entry-level hiring of international graduates out of reach for most employers, especially small and mid-size companies, and punishes students for timing they cannot defer — post-completion OPT must be filed within 60 days of program end.

I ask DHS to: (1) withdraw or substantially reduce the initial $70,000 fee; (2) not apply the $30,000 subsequent fee to STEM OPT extensions, which cover the graduates the United States most wants to retain; (3) reject the alternative floated in the proposal of charging $70,000 again at each higher degree level; and (4) if any fee survives, cap total per-student liability and set explicit limits on pass-through to students, since the proposal itself anticipates schools shifting the cost to students who cannot pay it.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed OPT fees are excessively high and will harm students and universities.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Accounting and financial compliance are essential functions for American businesses, yet they are often overlooked in discussions about workforce policy.

Small companies need professionals who understand financial reporting, internal controls, audit preparation, taxation, and accounting systems. These responsibilities require practical experience as well as academic training.

OPT can allow eligible international graduates with accounting, finance, or information systems degrees to develop professional skills in American workplaces.

The proposed fees could make that pathway more difficult if universities become unable or unwilling to support OPT recommendations.

For smaller accounting firms and businesses, staffing constraints can be particularly challenging during tax season, financial reporting periods, or regulatory audits.

A reduced pool of qualified candidates may result in longer processing times, increased workloads for existing employees, and higher operating costs.

This does not mean international graduates are the only available source of accounting talent. However, restricting legitimate training opportunities could create additional recruitment difficulties without necessarily improving compliance.

There is also an important distinction between financial capacity and regulatory integrity.

A university's ability to pay a substantial OPT fee does not establish whether an employer maintains appropriate records or whether a graduate is participating in legitimate training.

I request that DHS withdraw the proposed fees under § 214.13(i)(1) and (i)(2), and examine their potential effects on accounting workforce development and small business compliance.

Targeted verification of employers and training arrangements would provide a more direct method of addressing documented immigration violations.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
What should determine whether a graduate qualifies for practical training?

Their education? Their compliance with immigration rules? Whether the training is related to their degree?

Or whether their university can afford an enormous fee?

That is the question I keep coming back to when reading about this proposal.

OPT is intended to connect academic education with practical professional experience. Students spend years completing degree requirements, developing specialized knowledge, and preparing to enter their chosen fields.

The proposed $70,000 initial fee and $30,000 subsequent fee could introduce a financial obstacle that has little connection to those educational objectives.

Two graduates with identical qualifications could face very different outcomes simply because their universities have different financial resources.

I find that difficult to justify.

I understand the importance of preventing fraud. But legitimate students should be evaluated according to clear eligibility and compliance requirements. A large payment does not demonstrate honesty, professional competence, or the legitimacy of a training opportunity.

I am also concerned that these fees could disproportionately affect students attending smaller institutions, including those that serve communities with fewer financial resources.

The Department should explain why a uniform financial requirement is necessary instead of strengthening verification of individual training arrangements and investigating institutions with documented compliance problems.

I request withdrawal of the proposed provisions under 8 CFR § 214.13(i)(1) and (i)(2).

A fair regulatory system should distinguish between legitimate participants and actual violations. Financial resources should not become a substitute for that distinction.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
RE: Docket No. ICEB–2026–0100, RIN 1653–AB01, “Optional Practical Training Fees”
The “transition period” fee structure is punitive and procedurally unfair to students already enrolled. Under proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)(3), any student receiving a DSO recommendation on or after the effective date pays the full $70,000 “initial” fee — including students who are already mid-degree and chose their program years ago, in part because OPT was an expected, affordable benefit of F-1 status. DHS acknowledges this reliance interest exists (Section VI) but dismisses it by asserting, without real evidentiary support, that OPT availability is merely “one of many factors” in a student’s enrollment decision. That conclusion is not supported by data DHS itself collected; DHS did not survey students or institutions on this question, it simply asserted the conclusion it needed to reach.

DHS’s own numbers undercut its “widespread fraud” premise. Section VI states that only about 20% of F-1 nonimmigrants participate in OPT at all, and the fraud examples DHS cites (Section IV.A) — a handful of shell-company prosecutions spanning over a decade, plus one 2025–2026 investigation — amount to a small fraction of the 194,554+ students who used OPT in 2024 alone. Imposing a fee on the entire remaining population to address conduct DHS itself describes as concentrated among identifiable bad actors (shared addresses, fake worksites, specific employer clusters) is not a proportionate response; DHS has the tools to target those employers directly (site visits, SEVIS data matching) without a blanket fee on all students and schools.

The pre-/post-completion fee differential ($100,000 vs. $70,000) is arbitrary and not explained by any fraud-prevention rationale. DHS admits (Section V.A, VII.A.5.d(3)) that this structure exists only because of how DHS chose to define “initial” vs. “subsequent” fees — not because pre-completion OPT carries more fraud risk than post-completion OPT. DHS even states it expects schools to steer students away from pre-completion OPT specifically to avoid the extra $30,000, which is a $30,000 regulatory distortion with no integrity-related justification.

The 30-day comment period is inadequate for a rule of this magnitude. DHS designated this an “economically significant” action under E.O. 12866 with a primary cost estimate of $35.1 billion and a high-end estimate near $70 billion over 10 years (Section VII.A.1) — yet gave the public just 30 days to review a rule built on dozens of tables, cost models, and regulatory impact assumptions. For a rule of this fiscal scale affecting over 1.4 million F-1 students and 2,478 institutions, a comment period this short limits the public’s meaningful ability to identify errors in DHS’s modeling (e.g., the participation-scenario assumptions in Table 3) before the rule is finalized.

The rule does not address the stated FICA-exemption “incentive” problem it blames for part of the harm. Sections IV.B and footnote 108 attribute some of the alleged wage suppression to the FICA tax exemption for F-1 nonimmigrants, not to OPT itself. If that exemption is the actual driver of any hiring incentive, a six-figure OPT fee does nothing to fix it — DHS is imposing a massive cost on students to address a problem its own analysis attributes to a separate provision of the tax code that this rule does not touch.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed OPT fee is punitive, procedurally unfair, and based on unsupported assumptions.
